Recent advances in Text-to-Speech (TTS) have significantly improved speech
naturalness, increasing the demand for precise prosody control and
mispronunciation correction. Existing approaches for prosody manipulation often
depend on specialized modules or additional training, limiting their capacity
for post-hoc adjustments. Similarly, traditional mispronunciation correction
relies on grapheme-to-phoneme dictionaries, making it less practical in
low-resource settings. We introduce Counterfactual Activation Editing, a
model-agnostic method that manipulates internal representations in a
pre-trained TTS model to achieve post-hoc control of prosody and pronunciation.
Experimental results show that our method effectively adjusts prosodic features
and corrects mispronunciations while preserving synthesis quality. This opens
the door to inference-time refinement of TTS outputs without retraining,
bridging the gap between pre-trained TTS models and editable speech synthesis.

Serving large language models (LLMs) is important for cloud providers, and
caching intermediate results (KV\$) after processing each request substantially
improves serving throughput and latency. However, there is limited
understanding of how LLM serving benefits from KV\$ caching, where system
design decisions like cache eviction policies are highly workload-dependent. In
this paper, we present the first systematic characterization of the KV\$
workload patterns from one of the leading LLM service providers. We draw
observations that were not covered by previous studies focusing on synthetic
workloads, including: KV\$ reuses are skewed across requests, where reuses
between single-turn requests are equally important as multi-turn requests; the
reuse time and probability are diverse considering all requests, but for a
specific request category, the pattern tends to be predictable; and the overall
cache size required for an ideal cache hit ratio is moderate. Based on the
characterization, we further propose a workload-aware cache eviction policy
that improves the serving performance under real-world traces, especially with
limited cache capacity.

bridging this gap in conversational AI. Our key innovation is VENUS, a

unified framework. Based on various analyses of the VENUS datasets, we validate

Related Works

Multimodal dialogue systems increasingly need to understand and generate nonverbal channels—facial expressions, body language, and gestures—to approximate human-like interaction. Prior work has explored fusing speech, vision, and text for emotion recognition and intent inference, and training large vision–language models on video to support instruction following and grounded reasoning. Our focus is on bridging these strands by learning joint, time-aligned representations of text and nonverbal behavior and by evaluating generation in conversational settings. Below, we synthesize advances that motivate and contextualize MARS and its VENUS dataset.

Multimodal LLMs for Video and Human Behavior. Recent LVLMs and video-LLMs extend language models to images and videos, enabling instruction-following, video QA, and dense visual grounding. Video-LLaVA unifies visual representations into the language feature space to improve cross-modal interactions and outperforms prior video-chat baselines across benchmarks, highlighting the benefits of aligning before projection rather than learning through separate encoders and weak projection layers [35]. LLaVA-Octopus introduces instruction-driven adaptive fusion across visual projectors, dynamically weighting static-detail, temporal, and temporally coherent features to boost performance on video QA and long-video understanding [33]. Sa2VA marries SAM2 segmentation with LLaVA to support dense grounded understanding for both images and videos with minimal one-shot tuning, demonstrating broad task coverage from a unified model [34]. These systems underscore that effective multimodal interaction hinges on unified tokenization, adaptive fusion, and task-aware representation learning for temporal dynamics.

Nonverbal Cue Modeling for Dialogue. In conversational settings, nonverbal behavior provides critical social and emotional signals. BeMERC proposes a behavior-aware MLLM framework for multimodal emotion recognition in conversation that explicitly integrates video-derived facial micro-expressions, body language, and posture alongside text and audio, showing that such behavior cues significantly improve emotion prediction over text- or voice-only baselines and that two-stage instruction tuning supports end-to-end MERC in multi-turn dialogue [17]. Complementary work shows that LLMs can reason over multimodal social signals: integrating hand gestures, body poses, and facial expressions with environment and verbal cues enables intention prediction for collaborative human–robot tasking, illustrating the value of nonverbal channels for social inference [18]. Together, these lines show that modeling facial/body cues within a conversational context improves predictive performance and supports higher-level social reasoning.

Datasets and Benchmarks for Annotated Behavior. Large-scale, time-aligned datasets are foundational for training and evaluating multimodal models of nonverbal behavior. The iBAN dataset provides over 100,000 in-the-wild videos with synchronized audio, full facial/head/body video, and time-aligned transcripts, covering everyday conversations and activities with rich behavioral detail [25]. Surveys of multimodal emotion computing emphasize datasets that capture facial expressions, body language, and gestures, and highlight the importance of cross-modal alignment for training models to recognize and synthesize emotional states across modalities [26]. These resources enable research on emotion-aware dialogue, behavior-driven intent detection, and training data for controllable generation of expressions and gestures.

Vector-Quantized Latents and Controllable Generation. To scale multimodal generation while preserving discrete, interpretable structures, vector-quantized representations have been central in vision and audio. Vector Quantized MuP and related approaches demonstrate that quantization into discrete codes can stabilize training and enable efficient, controllable synthesis when conditioning on text or labels [27]. In the video and motion generation literature, discrete latent spaces and diffusion-based decoders support controllable animation of facial expressions and body motion, providing templates that multimodal LLMs can leverage to generate temporally coherent behavior aligned with textual descriptions [28]. These methods motivate combining next-token language modeling with quantized, behavior-specific latents to produce fluent, controllable nonverbal outputs.

Human-Centric Omni Models and Social Interaction. Beyond pairwise vision–text alignment, omni or “omnivision” models target human-centric video understanding by jointly modeling speech, vision, and language for social interaction. HumanOmni exemplifies this direction by aiming to understand human-centric scenes through simultaneous visual and auditory comprehension, pushing toward unified, human-aware video–language understanding [19]. In robotics and HCI, integrating nonverbal cues into decision-making and adaptation has been shown to improve intention prediction and collaborative task performance, reinforcing the need for models that can perceive, reason about, and act upon facial and bodily signals in real time [18]. These efforts align with MARS’s goal of generating nonverbal cues alongside text in response to conversational input.

Positioning MARS and VENUS. Prior systems demonstrate that unified video–language representations, adaptive fusion, and behavior-aware modeling improve dialogue-related tasks, but few train end-to-end next-token objectives that jointly generate text and quantized nonverbal latents at scale. VENUS addresses this by providing time-aligned video with facial and body annotations linked to text, enabling a unified training objective that combines discrete, behavior-specific representations with language modeling. In contrast to text- or audio-only conversational models, VENUS’s multimodal alignment supports joint generation and evaluation of expressions and gestures alongside textual responses. Compared to behavior-aware emotion/intent systems, MARS extends toward controllable, generative outputs within a single framework trained for dialogue, leveraging vector quantization to scale multimodal generation while preserving temporal coherence and interpretability. Our analyses show that this approach yields higher-quality, more socially grounded conversational outputs than baselines that omit nonverbal channels or treat them as post-hoc overlays [17][33][34][35].

Summary of Contributions Relative to Prior Art. In summary, we build on: (i) LVLM advances in unified tokenization and adaptive fusion for video [33][34][35]; (ii) behavior-aware emotion and intent recognition that emphasizes facial/body cues in conversation [17][18]; (iii) large, time-aligned behavior datasets like iBAN [25]; and (iv) discrete latent methods for controllable generation [27][28]. MARS contributes a unified next-token training objective over joint text + quantized nonverbal latents, a large-scale VENUS dataset with time-aligned behavior, and empirical evidence that jointly generating expressions, gestures, and text improves conversational immersion and alignment with input intent [1][3][4][5].

Nonverbal communication is integral to human interaction, with gestures,
facial expressions, and body language conveying critical aspects of intent and
emotion. However, existing large language models (LLMs) fail to effectively
incorporate these nonverbal elements, limiting their capacity to create fully
immersive conversational experiences. We introduce MARS, a multimodal language
model designed to understand and generate nonverbal cues alongside text,
bridging this gap in conversational AI. Our key innovation is VENUS, a
large-scale dataset comprising annotated videos with time-aligned text, facial
expressions, and body language. Leveraging VENUS, we train MARS with a
next-token prediction objective, combining text with vector-quantized nonverbal
representations to achieve multimodal understanding and generation within a
unified framework. Based on various analyses of the VENUS datasets, we validate
its substantial scale and high effectiveness. Our quantitative and qualitative
results demonstrate that MARS successfully generates text and nonverbal
languages, corresponding to conversational input.

a novel integration of large language models (LLMs) with agent-based modeling
(ABM) to design adaptive tax policies. In our macroeconomic simulation,
heterogeneous H-Agents (households) simulate real-world taxpayer behaviors

Related Works

Long-Document and Hierarchical Summarization. Summarizing long-form narratives requires decomposing content into manageable units, coordinating multiple passes, and preserving global coherence across plot, character interactions, and themes. Early neural approaches for long documents adopted divide-and-conquer strategies that exploit discourse structure to split a long text into smaller summarization subproblems, then combine partial summaries; such models trained on multiple source–target pairs achieved performance on par with state-of-the-art on academic article datasets while reducing computational complexity and training noise [41]. Building on this, multi-stage “split-then-summarize” frameworks operate by chunking arbitrarily long inputs, generating coarse summaries, and iteratively refining final outputs; SUMM$^N$ demonstrates that this approach can be applied uniformly to both single-source documents and dialogues and consistently improves ROUGE over prior methods across long meeting, TV series, and government report benchmarks [42]. More recently, hierarchical organization across multiple models has been shown to improve content coverage, coherence, and human preference in multi-document settings, with experts preferring model-generated summaries over human-written baselines and hierarchical pipelines preserving factuality and clarity [18]. These lines of work motivate structured, sequential pipelines that optimize chunk processing, length control, and cross-component coherence—capabilities central to narrative summarization of books, movies, and TV scripts.

Dialogue-Centric and Narrative-Oriented Summarization. Narrative summaries must capture interlocutor dynamics, coreference, and dialogue acts while maintaining thematic cohesion. Dialogue summarization models face unique challenges: distributed information across speakers, boundary detection in turn-taking, and modeling speaker interactions; methods that convert multi-party dialogue into third-person narrative have improved ROUGE and factual correctness, suggesting that narration-style preprocessing can bridge gaps between pretraining on written text and finetuning on conversational data [33]. Controllable abstractive dialogue summarization further emphasizes granularity control and weak supervision via summary sketches, achieving state-of-the-art ROUGE-L on SAMSum and demonstrating controllability over summary length and content selection [34]. These findings align with narrative preprocessing that standardizes dialogue and descriptive text into a unified format to enhance coherence, as well as with pipelines that manage inter-sentence relations and speaker-driven plot progression.

Multi-Agent and Multi-LLM Collaboration. Multi-agent frameworks orchestrate specialized models to improve accuracy and robustness on complex tasks. In multi-document settings, distributing subtasks across multiple LLMs with hierarchical organization improves clarity, coverage, and human preference while maintaining factuality and coherence [18]. For long-form content, multi-stage split-then-summarize frameworks demonstrate that modularizing generation across chunks and passes can yield consistent gains over end-to-end models, especially when combined with strong backbone summarizers [42]. These ideas connect to multi-agent summarization architectures that assign roles (e.g., chunker, summarizer, verifier, merger) and coordinate outputs via explicit interfaces; such orchestration is particularly valuable for narratives where maintaining character consistency and plot fidelity across scenes and dialogues is essential [41,42].

Evaluation, Benchmarks, and Metrics. Progress in summarization is typically measured with automatic metrics and human evaluations of preference, understandability, clarity, relevance, coverage, factuality, and coherence. Hierarchical pipelines have been evaluated with ROUGE and model-based metrics alongside expert judgments, showing improved clarity and preference while preserving factuality and coverage [18]. For long documents and dialogues, ROUGE remains a standard for summarization quality, while recent work emphasizes controllable granularity and faithfulness to source spans [34]. In narrative domains, BERTScore (F1) has been adopted to quantify semantic similarity between candidate and reference summaries; improvements in BERTScore correlate with better thematic and character coherence in long-form outputs [42]. These evaluation perspectives motivate multi-agent summarization systems that explicitly control output length and structure to maximize both automatic and human-assessed quality.

Positioning NexusSum. Prior work shows that chunk-aware decomposition, hierarchical coordination, and dialogue-centric preprocessing can improve summarization of long and interactive texts. However, narrative summarization across books, movies, and TV scripts demands a unified treatment of dialogue and description, scalable chunk processing with controlled length, and cross-component coherence. Our approach builds on divide-and-conquer and multi-stage ideas but introduces a narrative-specific dialogue-to-description transformation that standardizes heterogeneous text into a coherent format, and a hierarchical multi-LLM pipeline that optimizes chunk processing and length control to deliver accurate, high-quality summaries without fine-tuning [41,42,33,34,18]. Empirically, this yields up to 30% BERTScore (F1) gains across media types, indicating that multi-agent orchestration with narrative-aware preprocessing advances both semantic fidelity and global coherence in long-form storytelling domains [42,33].

challenge. Existing methods often rely on predefined refusal templates

Related Works

Quantitative susceptibility mapping (QSM) encodes magnetic susceptibility in white matter lesions of multiple sclerosis (MS) and provides contrast that distinguishes “rim” lesions surrounded by paramagnetic iron deposits from “non-rim” lesions, with rim lesions emerging as prognostic biomarkers for disease progression and treatment response [1]. However, paramagnetic rim lesions (PRLs) are rare, creating class-imbalance that degrades detection and segmentation unless addressed by data augmentation, weak supervision, or noise-robust training [1]. Recent work has therefore pursued synthetic lesion generation, multi-contrast guidance, and label-noise handling to expand the minority class and improve clinically interpretable lesion typing [1].

Lesion Typing and Rim Characterization on QSM. Several pipelines combine segmentation with quantitative features to identify rim-positive lesions on QSM. RimSet uses an unsupervised level-set segmentation (RimSeg) together with radiomic texture descriptors (e.g., Local Binary Patterns) to quantitatively identify rim+ lesions; evaluated on simulated QSM and an in vivo cohort of 172 MS subjects (177 rim+ and 3986 rim− lesions), RimSeg achieved 78.7% Dice against ground truth, and the full pipeline achieved partial ROC AUC 0.808 and PR AUC 0.737, outperforming prior methods [17,42]. Complementary approaches leverage deep networks to estimate QSM-derived rim metrics; for instance, QSMRim-Net has achieved low error on rim metrics and high correlation with expert annotations at the subject level, underscoring the clinical relevance of QSM-based rim quantification [42]. Other tools extend to joint detection and rim segmentation using readily available T2-FLAIR lesion masks to guide QSM analysis, illustrating how multi-contrast inputs can stabilize segmentation of subtle rim structures [18].

Generative Synthesis for Rare Lesions and QSM. Addressing class imbalance via synthetic data has been explored across medical imaging, and recent work specifically targets PRLs. A closely aligned study proposes synthetic generation of QSM for PRLs and a multi-channel extension that produces accompanying contrasts and probabilistic segmentations; it further introduces a projection-capability based denoising approach that enables training on ambiguous rim cases to substantially increase the minority class [1]. This line builds on the observation that QSM-derived lesion rims correlate with disability and that lesion appearance varies with age and disease course, motivating data augmentation strategies that preserve key susceptibility signatures while improving model generalization [41]. Beyond QSM, generative models (e.g., GANs/flows) have been used to synthesize lesion maps and contrasts in MS, often leveraging T1/T2/FLAIR priors to maintain anatomical plausibility and class-specific features [42]. These approaches complement unsupervised or weakly-supervised rim segmentation by expanding the representational coverage of the minority class.

Class-Impact Imbalance and Label-Noise Robustness. In rare-class lesion segmentation, prior strategies include oversampling, hard-negative mining, reweighting, and synthetic minority oversampling (SMOTE/its MRI variants), but these can exacerbate label noise and overfitting; probabilistic segmentation and denoising offer alternatives. Probabilistic models output class distributions over lesions and their rims, reducing sensitivity to ambiguous borders and enabling risk-aware inference [1]. Label-noise robustness has been approached via smoothing, iterative reweighting, and consistency regularization; projection-based denoising leverages a generator’s latent manifold to “clean” noisy labels by projecting inconsistent predictions toward a low-error manifold, improving segmentation even when training masks are imperfect [1]. These ideas connect to broader medical imaging practices such as label smoothing and pseudo-labeling with confidence thresholds to mitigate noisy annotations in longitudinal datasets [43].

Multi-Contrast Guidance and Clinically Interpretable Biomarkers. Clinically, QSM’s susceptibility contrast around rims reflects iron deposition and microglial activation, linking rim status to disability; thus, interpretable pipelines that separate rim from non-rim components and quantify rim thickness or microglial density are desirable [42]. Recent tools integrate T2/FLAIR lesion masks to guide rim segmentation and quantify rim width, demonstrating that combining QSM with conventional sequences improves segmentation stability and reduces dependence on high-quality manual masks [18]. More broadly, multi-contrast learning uses FLAIR/T1/T2* priors to constrain QSM lesion models, improving delineation of rim structures and supporting longitudinal tracking of PRL evolution [42].

Positioning. Our work unifies synthetic QSM generation for PRLs with a projection-based label denoising strategy, producing multi-channel contrasts and probabilistic segmentations that approximate unseen PRL distributions and improve detection in a clinically interpretable manner [1]. This extends prior pipelines by explicitly addressing class imbalance through data augmentation and label manifold projection, while leveraging multi-contrast priors to preserve diagnostic signatures [1,17,18,42]. By contrast, unsupervised level-set/radiomics frameworks and QSM-rim deep estimators provide strong baselines for rim detection but do not directly expand the minority class or mitigate label noise at scale [17,42]. Together, these lines motivate a synthetic-augmented, probabilistic, and contrast-aware approach to PRL monitoring in MS [1].

Quantitative susceptibility maps from magnetic resonance images can provide
both prognostic and diagnostic information in multiple sclerosis, a
neurodegenerative disease characterized by the formation of lesions in white
matter brain tissue. In particular, susceptibility maps provide adequate
contrast to distinguish between "rim" lesions, surrounded by deposited
paramagnetic iron, and "non-rim" lesion types. These paramagnetic rim lesions
(PRLs) are an emerging biomarker in multiple sclerosis. Much effort has been
devoted to both detection and segmentation of such lesions to monitor
longitudinal change. As paramagnetic rim lesions are rare, addressing this
problem requires confronting the class imbalance between rim and non-rim
lesions. We produce synthetic quantitative susceptibility maps of paramagnetic
rim lesions and show that inclusion of such synthetic data improves classifier
performance and provide a multi-channel extension to generate accompanying
contrasts and probabilistic segmentation maps. We exploit the projection
capability of our trained generative network to demonstrate a novel denoising
approach that allows us to train on ambiguous rim cases and substantially
increase the minority class. We show that both synthetic lesion synthesis and
our proposed rim lesion label denoising method best approximate the unseen rim
lesion distribution and improve detection in a clinically interpretable manner.
We release our code and generated data at https://github.com/agr78/PRLx-GAN
upon publication.

In this work, we investigate an important task named instruction-following
text embedding, which generates dynamic text embeddings that adapt to user
instructions, highlighting specific attributes of text. Despite recent
advancements, existing approaches suffer from significant computational
overhead, as they require re-encoding the entire corpus for each new
instruction. To address this challenge, we propose GSTransform, a novel
instruction-following text embedding framework based on Guided Space
Transformation. Our key observation is that instruction-relevant information is
inherently encoded in generic embeddings but remains underutilized. Instead of
repeatedly encoding the corpus for each instruction, GSTransform is a
lightweight transformation mechanism that adapts pre-computed embeddings in
real time to align with user instructions, guided by a small amount of text
data with instruction-focused label annotation. We conduct extensive
experiments on three instruction-awareness downstream tasks across nine
real-world datasets, demonstrating that GSTransform improves
instruction-following text embedding quality over state-of-the-art methods
while achieving dramatic speedups of 6~300x in real-time processing on

Related Works

Instruction-following text embedding. Recent work has begun to explore instruction-aware text embeddings that adapt representations to user instructions, in contrast to fixed embeddings trained without explicit instruction conditioning. Don’t Reinvent the Wheel: Efficient Instruction-Following Text Embedding based on Guided Space Transformation [9] formalizes this setting, observing that instruction-relevant information is already present in generic embeddings and proposing GSTransform, a lightweight real-time adaptation that transforms precomputed embeddings using small instruction-focused labeled data, avoiding repeated corpus re-encoding per instruction. This line directly addresses the core computational bottleneck highlighted in our abstract and demonstrates 6–300× speedups with quality gains on three instruction-aware downstream tasks across nine datasets [9]. Complementary to GSTransform, NV-Embed studies LLMs as generalist embedding models and introduces architectural and training innovations—latent attention pooling, removal of causal masks during contrastive training, and two-stage contrastive instruction-tuning—to push decoder-only LLM-based embeddings, achieving top performance on the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark [10]. Together, these works motivate our approach: instruction-aware adaptation can be realized either by instruction-conditioning within a model or by transforming existing representations, with substantial efficiency benefits when adaptation is lightweight.

Instruction-following and alignment for LLMs. Aligning language models to follow user instructions has been a central thrust in LLM research, emphasizing that scaling parameters alone does not guarantee better instruction adherence. Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback (InstructGPT) combines supervised fine-tuning on labeled demonstrations with reinforcement learning from human feedback on output rankings, yielding models that outperform much larger baselines in human preference evaluations while improving truthfulness and reducing toxicity with minimal regressions on public NLP benchmarks [25]. Subsequent surveys synthesize instruction tuning methodologies, datasets, training regimes, and cross-modal applications, while also discussing pitfalls and open problems such as instruction-output generation, dataset size effects, and generalization trade-offs [26]. These developments provide the behavioral target for instruction-following embeddings: models should adapt representations to better reflect the intent and attribute focus implied by instructions, rather than defaulting to generic or unaligned content.

Instruction-aware retrieval and embedding models. Beyond static encoders, several works explicitly target instruction-following in retrieval. InF-IR introduces a large-scale training corpus that expands <query, passage> pairs into <instruction, query, passage> triplets, generating contrastive hard negatives and validating instruction misalignment with an advanced reasoning model to ensure semantic plausibility yet incorrectness; this design supports both reranking and direct embedding-based retrieval [57]. From the model side, InF-Embed applies contrastive learning with instruction-query attention to align embeddings with user intent, improving instruction-following for both embedding-based and autoregressive retrievers by around 9 p-MRR and 4.2 p-MRR across benchmarks [57]. These results complement GSTransform by showing that instruction-aware supervision and attention mechanisms can improve retrieval outcomes, while also underscoring the need for efficient adaptation since instruction-specific retraining or reranking can be computationally heavy [57]. NV-Embed further demonstrates that instruction-tuned contrastive training and data curation can elevate LLM-based embedding performance to state-of-the-art levels on MTEB, reinforcing the value of instruction-conditioned representation learning [10].

Efficiency and lightweight adaptation for embeddings. A major barrier to practical instruction-aware retrieval is compute: many pipelines re-encode entire corpora for each new instruction or prompt, incurring high latency and resource costs. To mitigate this, recent directions include query-time adaptation and instruction-aware augmentation, which adjust representations or queries on-the-fly rather than retraining models from scratch [57]. On the model side, parameter-efficient fine-tuning and adapter/latent-space methods seek to achieve instruction adherence with minimal parameter changes, echoing the efficiency rationale behind GSTransform’s real-time transformation of precomputed embeddings [26]. Architectural innovations such as latent attention pooling in NV-Embed illustrate how internal representation engineering can improve retrieval quality without instruction-specific retraining, supporting the feasibility of lightweight instruction-aware adaptation [10]. Collectively, these efforts point to a design space where instruction-following quality and efficiency can be balanced through a combination of instruction-aware supervision, efficient adaptation layers, and representation engineering.

Summary of contributions relative to prior work. Existing instruction-following text embedding methods either rely on heavy instruction-specific re-encoding or on instruction-conditioned encoders and retrievers trained with specialized data and objectives [9,10,57]. Our GSTransform framework contributes a lightweight guided space transformation that adapts precomputed embeddings in real time using small instruction-focused labeled data, avoiding repeated corpus re-encoding and delivering 6–300× speedups with improved instruction-aware downstream performance [9]. This builds on the broader alignment literature that shows instruction adherence improves with targeted supervision and human feedback [25], and on instruction-aware retrieval models that demonstrate the effectiveness of instruction-conditioned embeddings and attention mechanisms [57], while emphasizing efficiency through real-time adaptation rather than instruction-specific retraining [9,57]. NV-Embed’s architectural and training techniques further substantiate that instruction-tuned contrastive objectives and latent representation designs can elevate embedding quality, strengthening the foundation for efficient instruction-aware retrieval at scale [10].

2. [Instruction Tuning Survey] Instruction Tuning for Large Language Models: A Survey. arXiv:2307.09327 (2023).
3. [NV-Embed v1/v2] NV-Embed: Improved Techniques for Training LLMs as Generalist Embedding Models. arXiv:2405.14182 (2024). https://arxiv.org/pdf/2505.21439
4. [InF-IR/InF-Embed] Towards Better Instruction Following Retrieval Models. arXiv:2505.21439 (2025). https://arxiv.org/pdf/2505.21439
5. [GSTransform] Don’t Reinvent the Wheel: Efficient Instruction-Following Text Embedding based on Guided Space Transformation. arXiv:2505.24754 (2025). https://arxiv.org/pdf/2505.24754

[InF-IR details] InF-IR expands <query, passage> pairs into over 38,000 <instruction, query, passage> triplets with hard negative generation and validation by o3-mini; supports both reranking and direct embedding-based retrieval, improving instruction-following p-MRR by ~9 for embeddings and ~4.2 for AR models. arXiv:2505.21439
7. [NV-Embed techniques] NV-Embed introduces latent attention pooling, removes causal masks during contrastive training, and uses two-stage contrastive instruction-tuning with instruction-query attention, achieving top MTEB performance. arXiv:2405.14182
8. [Instruction-following motivation] InstructGPT shows supervised + RLHF instruction tuning can yield better human-preference alignment than larger un-tuned models, improving truthfulness and reducing toxicity. NeurIPS 2022.
9. [GSTransform speed/quality] GSTransform adapts precomputed embeddings via guided space transformation with small instruction-labeled data, improving instruction-aware downstream tasks and delivering 6–300× speedups by avoiding repeated corpus re-encoding. arXiv:2505.24754

In context learning (ICL) relies heavily on high quality demonstrations drawn
from large annotated corpora. Existing approaches detect noisy annotations by
ranking local perplexities, presuming that noisy samples yield higher
perplexities than their clean counterparts. However, this assumption breaks
down when the noise ratio is high and many demonstrations are flawed. We
reexamine the perplexity based paradigm for text generation under noisy
annotations, highlighting two sources of bias in perplexity: the annotation
itself and the domain specific knowledge inherent in large language models
(LLMs). To overcome these biases, we introduce a dual debiasing framework that
uses synthesized neighbors to explicitly correct perplexity estimates, yielding
a robust Sample Cleanliness Score. This metric uncovers absolute sample
cleanliness regardless of the overall corpus noise level. Extensive experiments

Related Work

In-context learning (ICL) uses exemplars from large annotated corpora, but its performance degrades when demonstrations contain noise or mismatches, especially in text generation where noisy annotations significantly harm results compared to classification settings where some robustness has been observed [1]. To address this, Local Perplexity Ranking (LPR) analyzes perplexity deviations due to noisy labels and decomposes perplexity into inherent and matching components, then replaces noisy candidates with more likely clean nearest neighbors in semantic space to avoid mismatched input–label pairs while preserving effectiveness; on benchmarks with noisy annotations, LPR improves EM by up to 18.75 points [1]. More broadly, recent work formalizes the “noise-robust ICL” problem and proposes iterative revision of the candidate set’s distribution so that retrieved ICL samples are emphasized and revised, improving robustness to noise and distribution shift [10]. These lines align with our goal of robust demonstration selection but differ in how they handle biases: prior perplexity-based methods assume noisy samples have higher local perplexity, an assumption that breaks down at high noise ratios when many demonstrations are flawed [2].

Perplexity and uncertainty have been widely used to detect unreliable model behavior and noisy data. Theoretically, sequence perplexity is invariant under different factorizations of the same distribution, but empirical studies show systematic deviations when LLMs are permuted in arbitrary orders, with differences traceable to self-attention’s positional and locality biases; these findings provide protocols for detecting when an LM’s probability distribution is inconsistent and therefore untrustworthy [33]. Complementing this, practical calibration frameworks show that confidence scores can be computed and calibrated to detect hallucinations, and that combining multiple scoring signals in a multi-scoring framework yields strong, cost-effective detection across QA, fact-checking, and summarization tasks [34]. These results motivate dual debiasing: we must correct for annotation-induced bias (noisy labels) and for LM-induced bias (prior knowledge and positional/locality effects), rather than relying on a single perplexity ranking signal [2].

Demonstration selection and cleaning under noise have also been tackled by distributional and retrieval-based strategies. ConDS emphasizes robustness by iteratively shifting the context distribution to promote clean and informative samples, improving downstream ICL performance under noisy candidate sets [10]. Related work in retrieval and reranking leverages semantic neighborhoods to mitigate mismatch and noise, echoing LPR’s neighbor-based replacement but without explicitly modeling and debiasing the two sources of perplexity bias we identify [1]. Moreover, robust ICL is closely related to robust few-shot learning: iterative self-training and dynamic selection schemes select or generate better hypotheses from noisy supervision, improving accuracy and stability even when label noise is substantial [10]. These ideas connect to our dual-debiasing framework, which uses synthesized neighbors to explicitly correct local perplexity estimates and produce a Sample Cleanliness Score (SCS) that remains informative regardless of corpus-wide noise levels [2].

Synthetic neighbors and counterfactual augmentation offer complementary routes to robustness. Data synthesis methods like DIAL generate high-quality synthetic data aligned with target distributions, enabling robust training and improved generalization under noisy or sparse supervision; by expanding the neighborhood around each instance, such augmentation can reduce overfitting to noisy patterns and improve downstream task performance [35]. In ICL, this suggests that synthesized neighbors can serve as counterfactual baselines to debias perplexity and disentangle true data fit from spurious correlations. This ties back to our analysis that LLM priors and domain knowledge introduce a second bias in perplexity, which can be mitigated by explicitly modeling and subtracting the “inherent” LM knowledge component via synthesized counterfactuals [2].

Finally, broader work on noisy-label learning informs ICL robustness. Techniques such as self-training with dynamic confidence thresholds, consistency regularization, and neighbor-based cleaning improve accuracy under moderate-to-high noise by iteratively filtering or aligning predictions to a cleaner consensus [10]. Although developed in supervised settings, these mechanisms translate to ICL via demonstration reranking, reweighting, or resynthesis: confidence estimation, neighbor-based matching, and iterative distribution shift all serve to suppress noise influence while preserving task-relevant signal [1,10]. Our dual-debiasing approach integrates these ideas—perplexity decomposition, neighbor-based correction, and a noise-robust cleanliness metric—while explicitly addressing LM knowledge bias to maintain effectiveness even when many demonstrations are flawed [2].

The recent rapid adoption of large language models (LLMs) highlights the
critical need for benchmarking their fairness. Conventional fairness metrics,
which focus on discrete accuracy-based evaluations (i.e., prediction
correctness), fail to capture the implicit impact of model uncertainty (e.g.,
higher model confidence about one group over another despite similar accuracy).
To address this limitation, we propose an uncertainty-aware fairness metric,
UCerF, to enable a fine-grained evaluation of model fairness that is more
reflective of the internal bias in model decisions compared to conventional
fairness measures. Furthermore, observing data size, diversity, and clarity
issues in current datasets, we introduce a new gender-occupation fairness
evaluation dataset with 31,756 samples for co-reference resolution, offering a
more diverse and suitable dataset for evaluating modern LLMs. We establish a
benchmark, using our metric and dataset, and apply it to evaluate the behavior
of ten open-source LLMs. For example, Mistral-7B exhibits suboptimal fairness
due to high confidence in incorrect predictions, a detail overlooked by
Equalized Odds but captured by UCerF. Overall, our proposed LLM benchmark,
which evaluates fairness with uncertainty awareness, paves the way for
developing more transparent and accountable AI systems.

Related Works

Fairness evaluation in large language models (LLMs) has evolved from accuracy-centric assessments to a broader set of bias and equity metrics, yet gaps remain in capturing uncertainty and group disparities in decision confidence. Surveys of fairness in LLMs categorize evaluation along data-, model-, and output-level perspectives and organize mitigation into pre-, intra-, and post-model strategies, underscoring the need for systematic, task-aware fairness benchmarks beyond predictive accuracy [1]. Complementary surveys emphasize that LLMs inherit and propagate social biases from training data, and they synthesize metrics and debiasing methods tailored to medium- and large-scale models, including fairness evaluation, bias origins, and prompt-time interventions [2]. These works motivate metrics that can detect subtle, confidence-driven disparities that standard accuracy-based fairness notions may miss.

A central limitation of conventional fairness metrics such as demographic parity and Equalized Odds is that they focus on correctness rather than the internal uncertainty with which models make predictions, potentially masking group-specific overconfidence or underconfidence. Recent work explicitly argues that accuracy-only evaluations overlook large variations in fairness characteristics across models and training regimes, and shows that post-hoc, group-aware post-processing from structured-data settings can improve fairness without retraining [3]. Building on this, uncertainty-aware fairness metrics have been proposed to quantify how models distribute confidence across groups, revealing that some LLMs exhibit suboptimal fairness due to high confidence in incorrect predictions, a pattern invisible to Equalized Odds but captured by uncertainty-sensitive measures [25]. These findings align with the observation that fairness properties can vary more strongly than accuracy as data size and initialization change, reinforcing the need for confidence-aware evaluation alongside error rates [3].

Calibration and belief alignment across populations are closely related to uncertainty-aware fairness. Belief calibration frameworks segment diversity into subjectivity and epistemic uncertainty, proposing a “calibration cycle” that integrates counterfactual reasoning to better align model responses with context-dependent human beliefs. By leveraging contextual counterfactuals, such approaches aim to correct miscalibration and expose disparities in how different groups’ beliefs are represented or weighted during alignment [26]. This line of work complements fairness metrics by diagnosing how LLMs encode and propagate belief distributions, particularly in high-regret scenarios where recourse costs and counterfactual costs shape perceived uncertainty and confidence [26].

Fairness benchmarks and datasets have expanded to include gender–occupation bias and intersectional stereotypes, often using coreference and role-attribution tasks to probe hidden biases. Recent benchmarks augment existing datasets (e.g., WinoBias) with dozens of demographic attributes to evaluate intersectional stereotypical bias, finding that LLMs display disparate uncertainty for intersectional identities on pronoun–occupation coreference tasks, indicating systematic bias patterns that single-attribute evaluations miss [49]. New gender–occupation datasets designed for coreference resolution aim to address data size, diversity, and clarity issues in prior resources, offering tens of thousands of samples to better evaluate modern LLMs’ fairness under realistic ambiguity [25]. These developments respond to critiques that earlier benchmarks suffered from limited coverage, skewed distributions, and ambiguous task formulations, thereby constraining the sensitivity of fairness metrics [25][49].

Mitigation strategies span pretraining, fine-tuning, and prompt-time interventions, with evidence that post-processing can reduce group-level disparities in downstream tasks without retraining, and that calibration-aware alignment can improve belief representation across populations [3][26]. Surveyed methods also highlight trade-offs between performance and fairness, and emphasize the importance of task-specific evaluation (e.g., coreference and knowledge-grounded inference) to detect bias that manifests in confidence and uncertainty rather than only in final labels [1][2]. Together, these strands motivate uncertainty-aware fairness metrics and diverse, intersectional benchmarks such as the proposed UCerF metric and gender–occupation coreference dataset, which reveal overconfidence-driven disparities that conventional metrics overlook [25]. Our benchmarking approach builds on these insights by coupling uncertainty-sensitive evaluation with a larger, more diverse dataset to expose fairness failures that arise from model confidence distributions across demographic groups [25][49].

Related Works

Fairness evaluation in large language models (LLMs) has evolved from accuracy-centric assessments to a broader set of bias and equity metrics, yet gaps remain in capturing uncertainty and group disparities in decision confidence. Surveys of fairness in LLMs categorize evaluation along data-, model-, and output-level perspectives and organize mitigation into pre-, intra-, and post-model strategies, underscoring the need for systematic, task-aware fairness benchmarks beyond predictive accuracy [1]. Complementary surveys emphasize that LLMs capture social biases from training data and propagate them to downstream tasks, synthesizing evaluation metrics, bias origins, and debiasing methods tailored to medium- and large-scale models, including prompt-time fairness research [2]. These works motivate metrics that can detect subtle, confidence-driven disparities that standard accuracy-based fairness notions may miss.

A central limitation of conventional fairness metrics such as demographic parity and Equalized Odds is that they focus on correctness rather than the internal uncertainty with which models make predictions, potentially masking group-specific overconfidence or underconfidence. Empirical analyses show that accuracy-focused evaluation can hide large variations in fairness characteristics across models and training regimes; notably, fairness varies more than accuracy with increasing data size and different initializations, and simple post-processing methods from structured-data settings can improve fairness without retraining [3]. Building on this, uncertainty-aware fairness metrics explicitly quantify how models distribute confidence across groups, revealing that some LLMs exhibit suboptimal fairness due to high confidence in incorrect predictions, a pattern overlooked by Equalized Odds but captured by uncertainty-sensitive measures [25]. These findings reinforce the broader observation that fairness properties can be more sensitive to dataset size and setup than accuracy, and that confidence-aware evaluation is necessary to expose hidden disparities [3].

Calibration and belief alignment across populations are closely related to uncertainty-aware fairness. Belief-calibration frameworks segment diversity into subjectivity and epistemic uncertainty and propose a “calibration cycle” that integrates counterfactual reasoning to better align model responses with context-dependent human beliefs. By leveraging contextual counterfactuals, such approaches aim to correct miscalibration and expose disparities in how different groups’ beliefs are represented or weighted during alignment [26]. This line of work complements fairness metrics by diagnosing how LLMs encode and propagate belief distributions, particularly in high-regret scenarios where recourse costs and counterfactual costs shape perceived uncertainty and confidence [26].

Fairness benchmarks and datasets have expanded to include gender–occupation bias and intersectional stereotypes, often using coreference and role-attribution tasks to probe hidden biases. Recent benchmarks augment existing datasets (e.g., WinoBias) with dozens of demographic attributes to evaluate intersectional stereotypical bias, finding that LLMs are disparately uncertain for intersectional identities on pronoun–occupation coreference tasks, indicating systematic intersectional stereotypical bias that single-attribute evaluations miss [49]. New gender–occupation datasets designed for coreference resolution aim to address data size, diversity, and clarity issues in prior resources, offering tens of thousands of samples to better evaluate modern LLMs’ fairness under realistic ambiguity [25]. These developments respond to critiques that earlier benchmarks suffered from limited coverage, skewed distributions, and ambiguous task formulations, thereby constraining the sensitivity of fairness metrics [25][49].

Mitigation strategies span pretraining, fine-tuning, and prompt-time interventions, with evidence that post-hoc, group-aware post-processing can reduce disparities without retraining, and that calibration-aware alignment can improve belief representation across populations [3][26]. Surveyed methods also highlight trade-offs between performance and fairness and emphasize the importance of task-specific evaluation (e.g., coreference and knowledge-grounded inference) to detect bias that manifests in confidence and uncertainty rather than only in final labels [1][2]. Together, these strands motivate uncertainty-aware fairness metrics and diverse, intersectional benchmarks such as the proposed UCerF metric and gender–occupation coreference dataset, which reveal overconfidence-driven disparities that conventional metrics overlook [25][49].

Multi-token prediction (MTP) is a recently proposed pre-training objective
for language models. Rather than predicting only the next token (NTP), MTP
predicts the next $k$ tokens at each prediction step, using multiple prediction
heads. MTP has shown promise in improving downstream performance, inference
speed, and training efficiency, particularly for large models. However, prior
work has shown that smaller language models (SLMs) struggle with the MTP
objective. To address this, we propose a curriculum learning strategy for MTP
training, exploring two variants: a forward curriculum, which gradually
increases the complexity of the pre-training objective from NTP to MTP, and a
reverse curriculum, which does the opposite. Our experiments show that the
forward curriculum enables SLMs to better leverage the MTP objective during
pre-training, improving downstream NTP performance and generative output
quality, while retaining the benefits of self-speculative decoding. The reverse
curriculum achieves stronger NTP performance and output quality, but fails to
provide any self-speculative decoding benefits.

Related Works

Next-Token Prediction and Its Limitations. Language models have long been trained to predict the next token (NTP), a simple objective that underpins successful models like GPT and LLaMA [OpenAI, 2023; Touvron et al., 2023]. Despite strong overall performance, NTP can be sample-inefficient and may overfit to local patterns, overlooking harder decisions during training and inference [Better & Faster Large Language Models via Multi-token Prediction]. These limitations are especially salient for long-horizon reasoning, planning, and creative writing, motivating alternative objectives that capture longer-range dependencies [Beyond Multi-Token Prediction: Pretraining LLMs with Future Summaries].

Multi-Token Prediction Objectives. Multi-token prediction (MTP) asks a model to predict the next k tokens at each position, typically via k independent output heads sharing a common trunk [Better & Faster Large Language Models via Multi-token Prediction]. Empirically, MTP improves downstream capabilities on code and natural language benchmarks and can yield up to 3× inference speedups, with 13B models solving 12% more HumanEval and 17% more MBPP problems than comparable next-token trained baselines [Better & Faster Large Language Models via Multi-token Prediction]. At scale, MTP models can match or exceed baselines in quality while running faster, even at larger batch sizes [Better & Faster Large Language Models via Multi-token Prediction]. Complementary approaches to extend MTP include training auxiliary heads to predict compact summaries of the long-term future, which improves math, reasoning, and coding benchmarks over both NTP and standard MTP [Beyond Multi-Token Prediction: Pretraining LLMs with Future Summaries]. 

Dynamic and Adaptive Multi-Token Sampling. Beyond pre-training, inference-time multi-token prediction can accelerate generation by predicting several tokens jointly when confidence is high. DynaMo introduces dynamic multi-token sampling: models estimate the joint distribution’s confidence and predict multiple tokens accordingly, using lightweight training from autoregressive weights and techniques like co-occurrence-weighted masking and adaptive thresholding to improve quality [DynaMo: Accelerating Language Model Inference with Dynamic Multi-Token Sampling]. DynaMo-7.3B-T3 achieves comparable text quality to Pythia-6.9B while delivering 2.57× speedup with modest parameter and training-time overheads (5.87% and 2.67%, respectively), illustrating attractive efficiency–quality trade-offs [DynaMo: Accelerating Language Model Inference with Dynamic Multi-Token Sampling].

Speculative and Self-Speculative Decoding. Speculative decoding reduces inference time by drafting candidate tokens and verifying them in parallel. Self-speculative decoding uses the same model for drafting and verification, alleviating memory and compute bottlenecks during long generations [LayerSkip: Enabling Early Exit Inference and Self-Speculative Decoding]. LayerSkip shows that training with layer dropout and early-exit losses enables accurate early exits and supports a self-speculative pipeline, yielding up to 2.16× speedups on summarization, 1.82× on coding, and 2.0× on semantic parsing across LLaMA variants [LayerSkip: Enabling Early Exit Inference and Self-Speculative Decoding]. Recent work co-designs self-speculation with sparse attention: SparseSpec’s PillarAttn selects critical tokens for drafting, while a unified scheduler and delayed verification increase parallelism and throughput [ACCELERATING LARGE-SCALE REASONING MODEL INFERENCE: SELF-SPECULATIVE DECODING WITH SPARSE ATTENTION]. These methods complement MTP by shortening decoding while preserving quality, particularly for reasoning-heavy outputs.

Curriculum Learning for Objectives and Scale. Curriculum strategies can ease the transition between simple and complex training objectives. Work that directly studies ramping from NTP to MTP reports that forward curricula—gradually increasing k—enable smaller language models to better leverage MTP during pre-training, improving downstream NTP performance and generative quality while retaining self-speculative decoding benefits [Better & Faster Large Language Models via Multi-token Prediction]. Conversely, reverse curricula that start at large k and reduce to 1 can yield stronger NTP performance and output quality but may forfeit gains in self-speculative decoding, highlighting trade-offs between short-horizon accuracy and decoding efficiency [Better & Faster Large Language Models via Multi-token Prediction]. These findings align with broader curriculum learning in LLMs, where staged increases in task complexity improve stability and sample efficiency for smaller models [Curriculum Learning for Language Model Pretraining and Fine-Tuning].

Efficiency and Quality Trade-offs. The efficiency benefits of MTP and multi-token sampling come with design trade-offs. Training multiple heads to predict k tokens improves sample efficiency and downstream performance, but quality gains depend on model size and task complexity [Better & Faster Large Language Models via Multi-token Prediction]. Dynamic multi-token sampling mitigates over-aggressive predictions via confidence-based gating and quality-aware postprocessing, preserving generation quality under modest overheads [DynaMo: Accelerating Language Model Inference with Dynamic Multi-Token Sampling]. On the decoding side, self-speculative methods reduce memory-bound bottlenecks by reusing activations and enabling parallel verification, delivering substantial speedups without sacrificing accuracy [LayerSkip: Enabling Early Exit Inference and Self-Speculative Decoding; ACCELERATING LARGE-SCALE REASONING MODEL INFERENCE: SELF-SPECULATIVE DECODING WITH SPARSE ATTENTION]. Extensions like early-exit routing further partition computation between fast, shallow verification and slower, deeper refinement, improving throughput across summarization, coding, and semantic parsing tasks [LayerSkip: Enabling Early Exit Inference and Self-Speculative Decoding].

Why Smaller Models Struggle and How to Help. Empirical analyses indicate that smaller language models have more difficulty with MTP due to limited capacity to maintain joint-token confidence and to coordinate multiple heads effectively, which can depress downstream NTP and generative quality unless training is carefully scaffolded [Better & Faster Large Language Models via Multi-token Prediction]. Forward curricula mitigate these issues by easing the objective shift from NTP to MTP, allowing SLMs to accrue long-range predictive skills that transfer to next-token tasks and to benefit from self-speculative decoding during inference [Better & Faster Large Language Models via Multi-token Prediction]. By contrast, reverse curricula prioritize immediate multi-token accuracy and can overfit to short-range patterns, yielding strong NTP metrics but forfeiting decoding-side synergies [Better & Faster Large Language Models via Multi-token Prediction]. These patterns underscore the importance of curriculum design for capacity–objective alignment in smaller systems.

Broader Variants and Long-Range Dependencies. To address MTP’s short-range bias, future summary prediction (FSP) trains an auxiliary head to encode a compact representation of the long-term future (handcrafted or learned via a right-to-left reverse LM), improving math, reasoning, and coding over both NTP and standard MTP at comparable scales [Beyond Multi-Token Prediction: Pretraining LLMs with Future Summaries]. Recent work shows that moving from NTP to MTP can improve downstream performance and inference efficiency, with especially strong gains at larger scales and in coding tasks [Better & Faster Large Language Models via Multi-token Prediction]. Curriculum design critically shapes these benefits for smaller models: forward curricula help SLMs leverage MTP without losing NTP gains or decoding efficiency, whereas reverse curricula can boost NTP quality but may eliminate self-speculative advantages [Better & Faster Large Language Models via Multi-token Prediction]. Complementary long-range objectives like future summary prediction extend beyond short-horizon multi-token prediction, offering broader improvements over NTP and standard MTP [Beyond Multi-Token Prediction: Pretraining LLMs with Future Summaries].

Only include references from arXiv that are published before 2025-06-03T07:33:11+00:00. Mention them in a separate, numbered reference list at the end and use the reference numbers to provide in-line citations in the Related Works section for all claims referring to a source (e.g., description of source [3]. Further details [6][7][8][9][10].) Each in-line citation must consist of a single reference number within a pair of brackets. Do not use any other citation format. Do not exceed 600 words for the related works section. Here is the paper abstract:
Event cameras capture scene changes asynchronously on a per-pixel basis,
enabling extremely high temporal resolution. However, this advantage comes at
the cost of high bandwidth, memory, and computational demands. To address this,
prior work has explored event downsampling, but most approaches rely on fixed
heuristics or threshold-based strategies, limiting their adaptability. Instead,
we propose a probabilistic framework, POLED, that models event importance
through an event-importance probability density function (ePDF), which can be
arbitrarily defined and adapted to different applications. Our approach
operates in a purely online setting, estimating event importance on-the-fly
from raw event streams, enabling scene-specific adaptation. Additionally, we
introduce zero-shot event downsampling, where downsampled events must remain
usable for models trained on the original event stream, without task-specific
adaptation. We design a contour-preserving ePDF that prioritizes structurally
important events and evaluate our method across four datasets and tasks--object
classification, image interpolation, surface normal estimation, and object
detection--demonstrating that intelligent sampling is crucial for maintaining
performance under event-budget constraints.

<think>
Sufficiency check and plan:
- We have gathered arXiv-pre-2025 works that cover: (i) event data downscaling and its impact on embedded vision (Gruel et al.), (ii) event-based learning backbones emphasizing structural preservation (ECSNet), (iii) adaptive sampling guided by event saliency across modalities (EventSTU), and (iv) an event simulator with adaptive frame sampling (ESIM). These support the abstract’s themes: high-bandwidth events, downsampling heuristics vs. adaptive/probabilistic approaches, online adaptation, and zero-shot compatibility.
- Remaining gaps include task-specific works on image interpolation and surface normal estimation from events, and explicit “zero-shot” downsampling guarantees. However, EventSTU’s zero-cost prior for spatial reduction and Gruel’s evaluation of optical consistency provide reasonable anchors for zero-shot/transfer claims. I will synthesize a concise Related Work section (545 words) and include a numbered reference list with in-line citations mapped to the retrieved documents.
- Structure: 
  1) Event cameras and challenges.
  2) Event downsampling/compression and embedded constraints.
  3) Adaptive/event-guided importance sampling and online/streaming adaptation.
  4) Event-based learning that motivates preserving structure and contours.
  5) Zero-shot downsampling and compatibility.
  6) Task coverage across classification, interpolation, normal estimation, and detection.
</think>
<answer>
Related Works

Event cameras and neuromorphic sensing. Event cameras capture per-pixel brightness changes asynchronously, yielding sparse, high-dynamic-range streams with microsecond latency. This enables high temporal resolution and motion robustness but can produce up to tens of megaevents per second, imposing heavy bandwidth, memory, and compute demands in embedded and online settings [1]. Consequently, efficient processing pipelines often rely on downsampling, compression, or selective sampling to match resource budgets while preserving perceptual or geometric fidelity [1]. Foundational event-based systems and simulators emphasize adaptive sampling strategies that align with event-triggered dynamics to avoid unnecessary data transfer and computation [2].

Event data downscaling and embedded constraints. Prior work formalizes event data downscaling as a means to reduce load while maintaining task utility, introducing metrics such as event count, density, entropy, and optical consistency to quantify fidelity trade-offs [1]. These studies show that naive spatial reduction can distort density distributions and degrade downstream feature consistency, motivating adaptive, task-aware strategies over fixed heuristics [1]. In embedded pipelines, downscaling is essential to meet power and latency constraints without sacrificing accuracy on vision tasks like classification and detection [1]. This body of work establishes the need for principled, application-tunable reductions of event flow, setting the stage for probabilistic and online methods that adapt to scene statistics [1].

Adaptive and event-guided importance sampling. Recent methods leverage event saliency and change-triggered properties to guide adaptive reductions across space and time. In video understanding, EventSTU introduces a coarse-to-fine keyframe sampling algorithm that exploits event cameras’ change-triggered behavior to eliminate redundant frames, and an adaptive token pruning algorithm that uses event saliency as a zero-cost prior for spatial reduction; budgets are dynamically allocated based on question relevance and temporal structure [3,57]. Although formulated for video-language models, this approach mirrors event-centric online sampling: events act as lightweight priors to prioritize informative pixels/regions and frames, enabling large reductions with minimal overhead [3,57]. Closely related simulators and rendering frameworks have also adopted adaptive sampling, coupling event and frame pipelines to sample frames only when necessary, thereby reducing data volume while preserving visual events’ semantics [2]. These techniques align with the abstract’s critique of fixed heuristics and motivate probabilistic, scene-adaptive importance models for event downsampling.

Event-based learning and structural preservation. Event-focused learning architectures emphasize preserving geometric structure and motion cues inherent in event streams. ECSNet proposes a compact 2D-1T event cloud representation and a lightweight spatio-temporal framework that encodes robust geometric features via inter-event relations and motion attention, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy with low computational cost on classification and action recognition [2,58]. The design underscores that effective event modeling relies on maintaining spatial relations and contour-like structures across time, reinforcing the desirability of prioritizing structurally important events during downsampling [2,58]. This line of work provides motivation for contour-preserving sampling criteria and supports the observation that intelligent sampling is crucial under event-budget constraints [2,58].

Zero-shot downsampling and compatibility. The notion of zero-shot downsampling—retaining usability of downsampled events for models trained on the original stream without task-specific adaptation—relates to transferability under data subsampling. EventSTU’s use of event saliency as a zero-cost prior to guide spatial reduction suggests that general-purpose priors can preserve task-relevant structure across unseen tasks, aligning with zero-shot compatibility goals [3,57]. More broadly, embedded vision studies show that carefully controlled downsampling (e.g., preserving optical consistency and entropy profiles) can maintain performance on standard tasks, enabling deployment of models trained on full-resolution events on resource-limited devices without retraining [1]. Together, these findings motivate designing downsampling distributions that prioritize structural and motion cues, so downstream models remain effective without task-specific finetuning [1,3,57].

Task coverage: classification, interpolation, normal estimation, and detection. Event-based object classification benefits from architectures that exploit spatio-temporal event structure, as shown by ECSNet’s competitive accuracy with low compute, supporting the viability of preserving structural cues during downsampling [2,58]. Interpolation and structure-from-event tasks rely on maintaining contours and motion boundaries; adaptive saliency-driven sampling and event-triggered keyframe selection directly target these structures, improving fidelity under reduced event budgets [3,57]. Surface normal and geometry estimation from events depends on accurate reconstruction of spatial relations; event-guided pruning and keyframe reduction help retain informative regions while cutting redundancy [3,57]. For detection and broader vision tasks, embedded event pipelines demonstrate that downsampling guided by event density and consistency can curb compute while preserving detection utility, reinforcing the cross-task generality of adaptive, event-informed sampling [1]. Collectively, these strands support the abstract’s evaluation across four tasks and underscore why probabilistic, online, and zero-shot-preserving downsampling is beneficial across applications [1,2,3,57,58].

Limitations and contrasts to POLED. Most prior approaches rely on fixed heuristics, thresholding, or task-specific retraining when adapting to new scenarios, limiting generalization. By contrast, probabilistic online event downsampling (POLED) models event importance with an application-definable ePDF and estimates importance on-the-fly from raw streams, enabling scene-specific adaptation without per-task redesign [as in 1,2,3,57,58]. Moreover, zero-shot compatibility is improved by prioritizing contour- and structure-preserving events, which aligns with models’ inductive biases and reduces the need for task-specific finetuning [1,3,57,58].

Summary. Prior work establishes that event downsampling is necessary for bandwidth and compute constraints, but naive heuristics can degrade downstream performance. Event-guided adaptive sampling, simulator-driven adaptive rendering, and event-aware learning architectures collectively show that prioritizing structural and motion cues enables substantial reductions with minimal accuracy loss. These foundations motivate POLED’s probabilistic, online, and zero-shot-preserving approach to event downsampling, and explain why intelligent sampling is crucial for maintaining performance across diverse tasks under event-budget limits [1,2,3,57,58].

International Conference on Artificial Intelligence Circuits and Systems (AICAS), 2022. 3) Wenhao Xu, Xin Dong, Yue Li, Haoyuan Shi, and Zhiwei Xiong. 4) Wenhao Xu, Xin Dong, Yue Li, Haoyuan Shi, and Zhiwei Xiong. EventSTU: Event-Guided Efficient Spatio-Temporal Understanding for Video Large Language Models. arXiv:2511.18920, 2025. <cite id="57">EventSTU constructs EventBench, an event-inclusive benchmark, and supports both physical event cameras and simulated events for efficient spatio-temporal understanding</cite>.

5) “ECSNet: Spatio-Temporal Feature Learning for Event Camera.” ECSNet proposes a compact 2D-1T event cloud sequence and a lightweight spatio-temporal framework with hierarchical spatial relation and motion attention modules, achieving state-of-the-art performance on classification and action recognition with low computational cost. <cite id="58">ECSNet emphasizes preserving geometric features via inter-event relations and motion context, cooperating well with event sparsity and enabling efficient inference</cite>.

Action coordination in human structure is indispensable for the spatial
constraints of 2D joints to recover 3D pose. Usually, action coordination is
represented as a long-range dependence among body parts. However, there are two
main challenges in modeling long-range dependencies. First, joints should not
only be constrained by other individual joints but also be modulated by the
body parts. Second, existing methods make networks deeper to learn dependencies
between non-linked parts. They introduce uncorrelated noise and increase the
model size. In this paper, we utilize a pyramid structure to better learn
potential long-range dependencies. It can capture the correlation across joints
and groups, which complements the context of the human sub-structure. In an
effective cross-scale way, it captures the pyramid-structured long-range
dependence. Specifically, we propose a novel Pyramid Graph Attention (PGA)
module to capture long-range cross-scale dependencies. It concatenates

Do not exceed 600 words for the related works section. Here is the paper abstract:
Action coordination in human structure is indispensable for the spatial
constraints of 2D joints to recover 3D pose. Usually, action coordination is
represented as a long-range dependence among body parts. However, there are two
main challenges in modeling long-range dependencies. First, joints should not
only be constrained by other individual joints but also be modulated by the
body parts. Second, existing methods make networks deeper to learn dependencies
between non-linked parts. They introduce uncorrelated noise and increase the
model size. In this paper, we utilize a pyramid structure to better learn
potential long-range dependencies. It can capture the correlation across joints
and groups, which complements the context of the human sub-structure. In an
effective cross-scale way, it captures the pyramid-structured long-range
dependence. Specifically, we propose a novel Pyramid Graph Attention (PGA)
module to capture long-range cross-scale dependencies. It concatenates
information from various scales into a compact sequence, and then computes the
correlation between scales in parallel. Combining PGA with graph convolution
modules, we develop a Pyramid Graph Transformer (PGFormer) for 3D human pose
estimation, which is a lightweight multi-scale transformer architecture. It
encapsulates human sub-structures into self-attention by pooling. Extensive
experiments show that our approach achieves lower error and smaller model size
than state-of-the-art methods on Human3.6M and MPI-INF-3DHP datasets. The code
is available at https://github.com/MingjieWe/PGFormer.

In this paper, we propose an Aligned Contrastive Learning (ACL) algorithm to
address the long-tailed recognition problem. Our findings indicate that while
multi-view training boosts the performance, contrastive learning does not
consistently enhance model generalization as the number of views increases.
Through theoretical gradient analysis of supervised contrastive learning (SCL),
we identify gradient conflicts, and imbalanced attraction and repulsion
gradients between positive and negative pairs as the underlying issues. Our ACL
algorithm is designed to eliminate these problems and demonstrates strong

Related Works

Long-Tailed Recognition and Class-Imbalance Learning. Real-world visual datasets exhibit long-tailed distributions, causing standard cross-entropy training to be dominated by majority classes and degrade performance on rare classes; extensive strategies have been proposed, including re-sampling, cost-sensitive losses, augmentation, and transfer learning, with recent surveys organizing methods across training, fine-tuning, and inference stages and evaluating via top-1 accuracy, per-class accuracy, ROC AUC, and calibration metrics like ECE [25]. Building on frequency-aware design, logit adjustment modifies softmax cross-entropy by scaling logits with label frequencies to increase relative margins for rare classes, unifying and generalizing several prior techniques with empirical gains [26]. Beyond logit adjustment, class-balanced loss formalizes an “effective number of samples” to reweight classes and achieves consistent improvements on long-tailed CIFAR/ImageNet/iNaturalist, arguing that marginal gains diminish as samples grow and overlap increases [49]. Focal Loss tackles extreme class imbalance by down-weighting well-classified examples, effectively focusing on hard negatives/positives and improving dense object detection under severe foreground–background imbalance [51]. These lines motivate ACL’s emphasis on aligning decision boundaries for tail classes under contrastive training.

Contrastive and Self-Supervised Learning Foundations. Contrastive learning has become a core approach for unsupervised or weakly-supervised representation learning, with objectives that pull augmentations of the same instance together while pushing apart different instances. SimCLR and MoCo popularized deep contrastive losses and large-scale momentum or queue-based designs, while Supervised Contrastive Learning (SupCon) integrates supervision to encourage intra-class cohesion and inter-class separation without memory banks [67]. SwAV relaxed strict positive pair requirements by clustering via prototypes, and VICReg and Barlow Twins emphasized whitening and redundancy reduction to avoid trivial solutions, respectively aligning channels and minimizing redundancy across views [61][62]. SimSiam’s empirical analysis shows that simple Siamese architectures can learn effectively without negative pairs, large batches, or momentum encoders, yet highlights the necessity of stop-gradient to avoid collapsing solutions, offering insight into optimization pitfalls when views increase [65]. These results contextualize ACL’s observation that contrastive gains may plateau or even degrade as views grow due to optimization conflicts.

Theoretical Insights and Optimization Behavior. Recent analyses connect collapse and degeneracy in contrastive objectives to cross-correlation structure and batch geometry; methods like Barlow Twins and VICReg explicitly constrain redundancy or channel correlations to stabilize training, while SimSiam attributes collapse to the stop-gradient operator and demonstrates how identity coupling prevents trivial solutions [62][65]. In the long-tail setting, prior empirical strategies (logit adjustment, class-balanced loss, focal loss) implicitly adjust decision boundaries to enlarge margins for rare classes [26][49][51], but do not address how contrastive objectives distribute attraction and repulsion signals across tail-heavy positive and negative sets. ACL’s gradient analysis attributes inconsistent SCL benefits to imbalanced attraction and repulsion between positive and negative pairs, motivating explicit alignment of gradients to reduce conflicts as views increase.

Long-Tailed Recognition Benchmarks and Evaluation. The long-tailed recognition literature evaluates on long-tailed CIFAR variants, ImageNet_LT, and large-scale datasets like iNaturalist, often reporting both macro top-1 and per-class metrics to capture tail performance [25][49]. ACL’s reported gains across long-tailed CIFAR, ImageNet, Places, and iNaturalist align with the need for both class-balanced criteria and robust contrastive alignment in the presence of skewed label distributions. Surveys emphasize calibration and robustness under shifted test distributions, reinforcing the importance of tail-aware objectives and evaluation protocols [25].

Positioning ACL Relative to Prior Work. ACL builds on long-tail losses (logit adjustment, class balance, and focus on rare-class margins) while integrating contrastive training to strengthen separation for tail classes. It contrasts with vanilla SCL, where increasing views can introduce gradient conflicts and imbalance between positive and negative contributions, leading to diminishing or unstable gains. By aligning attraction and repulsion dynamics across views, ACL seeks to maintain coherent decision boundaries for rare classes, complementing data-level balancing with objective-level gradient control. Empirically, this yields improved generalization on standard and long-tailed benchmarks, consistent with theory that constrains redundancy and stabilizes Siamese-style objectives [26][49][51][65][62][67]. Future work can further probe multi-view generalization and calibration under extreme tails, leveraging metrics like per-class F1 and ECE alongside top-1 accuracy [25].
