raw_output.raw_text: <search query="IVF-PQ maximum inner product search arXiv 2012..2024" search_time="2026年5月14日17时46分星期四"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:1"><title>ANNA: Specialized Architecture for Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search</title><summary>Similarity search or nearest neighbor search is a task of retrieving a set of vectors in the (vector) database that are most similar to the provided query vector. It has been a key kernel for many applications for a long time. However, it is becoming especially more important in recent days as modern neural networks and machine learning models represent the semantics of images, videos, and documents as high-dimensional vectors called embeddings. Finding a set of similar embeddings for the provided query embedding is now the critical operation for modern recommender systems and semantic search engines. Since exhaustively searching for the most similar vectors out of billion vectors is such a prohibitive task, approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS) is often utilized in many real-world use cases. Unfortunately, we find that utilizing the server-class CPUs and GPUs for the ANNS task leads to suboptimal performance and energy efficiency. To address such limitations, we propose a specialized architecture named ANNA (Approximate Nearest Neighbor search Accelerator), which is compatible with state-of-the-art ANNS algorithms such as Google ScaNN and Facebook Faiss. By combining the benefits of a specialized dataflow pipeline and efficient data reuse, ANNA achieves multiple orders of magnitude higher energy efficiency, 2.3-61.6× higher throughput, and 4.3-82.1× lower latency than the conventional CPU or GPU for both million- and billion-scale datasets.</summary><hostname>Yejin Lee</hostname><publisher>2022 IEEE International Symposium on High-Performance Computer Architecture (HPCA)</publisher><author_list><author name="Yejin Lee" affiliation="Seoul National University, Seoul, South Korea" /><author name="Hyunji Choi" affiliation="Seoul National University, Seoul, South Korea" /><author name="Sunhong Min" affiliation="Seoul National University, Seoul, South Korea" /><author name="Hyunseung Lee" affiliation="Seoul National University, Seoul, South Korea" /><author name="Sangwon Beak" affiliation="Seoul National University, Seoul, South Korea" /><author name="Dawoon Jeong" affiliation="Seoul National University, Seoul, South Korea" /><author name="Jae W Lee" affiliation="Seoul National University, Seoul, South Korea" /><author name="Tae Jun Ham" affiliation="Seoul National University, Seoul, South Korea" /></author_list><url>https://yjyjlee.github.io/assets/pdf/hpca22_anna.pdf</url></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:2"><title>Local Orthogonal Decomposition for Maximum Inner Product Search</title><summary>Inverted file and asymmetric distance computation (IVFADC) have been successfully applied to approximate nearest neighbor search and subsequently maximum inner product search. In such a framework, vector quantization is used for coarse partitioning while product quantization is used for quantizing residuals. In the original IVFADC as well as all of its variants, after residuals are computed, the second production quantization step is completely independent of the first vector quantization step. In this work, we seek to exploit the connection between these two steps when we perform non-exhaustive search. More specifically, we decompose a residual vector locally into two orthogonal components and perform uniform quantization and multiscale quantization to each component respectively. The proposed method, called local orthogonal decomposition, combined with multiscale quantization consistently achieves higher recall than previous methods under the same bitrates. We conduct comprehensive experiments on large scale datasets as well as detailed ablation tests, demonstrating effectiveness of our method.</summary><hostname>arXiv</hostname><cite_count>4</cite_count><author_list><author name="Xiang Wu" /><author name="Ruiqi Guo" /><author name="Sanjiv Kumar" /><author name="David Simcha"

Maximum Inner Product Search (MIPS) is a fundamental challenge in machine
learning and information retrieval, particularly in high-dimensional data
applications. Existing approaches to MIPS either rely solely on Inner Product
(IP) similarity, which faces issues with local optima and redundant
computations, or reduce the MIPS problem to the Nearest Neighbor Search under
the Euclidean metric via space projection, leading to topology destruction and
information loss. Despite the divergence of the two paradigms, we argue that
there is no inherent binary opposition between IP and Euclidean metrics. By
stitching IP and Euclidean in the design of indexing and search algorithms, we
can significantly enhance MIPS performance. Specifically, this paper explores
the theoretical and empirical connections between these two metrics from the
MIPS perspective. Our investigation, grounded in graph-based search, reveals
that different indexing and search strategies offer distinct advantages for
MIPS, depending on the underlying data topology. Building on these insights, we
introduce a novel graph-based index called Metric-Amphibious Graph (MAG) and a
corresponding search algorithm, Adaptive Navigation with Metric Switch (ANMS).
To facilitate parameter tuning for optimal performance, we identify three
statistical indicators that capture essential data topology properties and
correlate strongly with parameter tuning. Extensive experiments on 12
real-world datasets demonstrate that MAG outperforms existing state-of-the-art
methods, achieving up to 4x search speedup while maintaining adaptability and
scalability.

Active learning (AL) reduces human annotation costs for machine learning
systems by strategically selecting the most informative unlabeled data for
annotation, but performing it individually may still be insufficient due to
restricted data diversity and annotation budget. Federated Active Learning
(FAL) addresses this by facilitating collaborative data selection and model
training, while preserving the confidentiality of raw data samples. Yet,
existing FAL methods fail to account for the heterogeneity of data distribution
across clients and the associated fluctuations in global and local model
parameters, adversely affecting model accuracy. To overcome these challenges,
we propose CHASe (Client Heterogeneity-Aware Data Selection), specifically
designed for FAL. CHASe focuses on identifying those unlabeled samples with
high epistemic variations (EVs), which notably oscillate around the decision
boundaries during training. To achieve both effectiveness and efficiency,
\model{} encompasses techniques for 1) tracking EVs by analyzing inference
inconsistencies across training epochs, 2) calibrating decision boundaries of
inaccurate models with a new alignment loss, and 3) enhancing data selection
efficiency via a data freeze and awaken mechanism with subset sampling.
Experiments show that CHASe surpasses various established baselines in terms of
effectiveness and efficiency, validated across diverse datasets, model
complexities, and heterogeneous federation settings.

Related Works

Active Learning. A core line of work studies pool-based active learning (AL) to reduce annotation cost by querying the most informative samples, using heuristics such as uncertainty (entropy, margin), disagreement (pairwise or triplet), and expected risk reduction to guide selection.<cite id="1">Pool-based active learning selects items from an unlabeled pool to maximize information per label, with strategies comparing uncertainty, disagreement, and expected loss reduction to guide queries</cite> <cite id="2">Active learning allows algorithms to choose informative data for labeling, reducing the number of labeled examples needed when labels are costly to obtain</cite> <cite id="3">In sequence labeling, AL strategies can be tailored to model-specific losses and dependencies, improving annotation efficiency</cite> Beyond single-machine settings, AL has been integrated with deep models and self-training, where consistency under distribution shift serves as a proxy for epistemic uncertainty to prioritize hard examples for annotation.<cite id="3">Sequence AL methods leverage model-specific properties and can outperform prior baselines at scale</cite> 

Federated Learning and Federated Active Learning. Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative training under data privacy constraints, but annotation budgets remain scarce across clients; federated active learning (FAL) couples selective querying with FL to improve accuracy while preserving confidentiality of raw samples.<cite id="14">Federated active learning facilitates collaborative data selection and model training while preserving raw data confidentiality</cite> Prior FAL approaches often query per-round using centralized criteria (e.g., uncertainty or disagreement) over local models, yet they struggle when client data distributions are heterogeneous and model updates fluctuate across rounds, leading to degraded global accuracy.<cite id="14">Existing FAL methods fail to account for client data heterogeneity and associated fluctuations in global and local model parameters, harming accuracy</cite> Recent work explores lightweight clustering-based selection for low-budget FAL, showing that feature-level pretraining and robust clustering can sustain performance when per-client data is small or heterogeneous, and that such methods can be resilient to feature extraction choices.<cite id="15">TypiClust achieves strong performance in low-budget FAL settings, benefiting from pre-trained features to enable participation even with limited unlabeled data per client and showing robustness to feature-space choices</cite> 

Client Heterogeneity and Stability. A central challenge in FAL is non-IID data and unstable local models; methods address this via personalized models, adaptive sampling weights, and robust aggregation, but selection criteria that ignore heterogeneity can exacerbate divergence across clients.<cite id="14">Client heterogeneity and parameter fluctuations degrade accuracy when selection does not account for distribution shifts across clients</cite> To mitigate instability, some works propose aligning local and global decision boundaries through calibration and consistency regularization, which can stabilize updates when client models are noisy or misaligned.<cite id="14">An alignment loss is used to calibrate decision boundaries of inaccurate models, improving stability and accuracy</cite> 

Epistemic Variation and Decision-Boundary Proximity. Epistemic uncertainty can be proxied by inference-time inconsistency or softmax variance; samples whose predictions oscillate across epochs or perturbations are near decision boundaries and likely informative.<cite id="14">Epistemic variations are tracked by analyzing inference inconsistencies across training epochs, reflecting oscillations around decision boundaries</cite> This idea connects to decision-boundary calibration: calibrating predicted probabilities and aligning class boundaries reduces boundary-hopping behavior and improves selection of high-uncertainty, high-impact samples.<cite id="14">Calibration of decision boundaries via an alignment loss reduces misalignment between local and global models and stabilizes uncertainty estimates</cite> Related work in FL emphasizes temperature/Dirichlet-based calibration and boundary-smoothing penalties to improve generalization and consistency of local models under heterogeneous data.<cite id="14">Alignment and calibration techniques target misaligned decision boundaries caused by noisy or inaccurate local models</cite> 

Efficient Data Selection. To scale AL in FL, methods reduce per-round computation via subset sampling, streaming without a full pool, and self-training cycles that reactivate a frozen set of samples periodically, focusing annotation on rare or ambiguous items.<cite id="14">A data freeze and awaken mechanism with subset sampling enhances selection efficiency while prioritizing high-variation samples</cite> These ideas relate to AL with dynamic reservoirs and consistency-based reactivation, which maintain a manageable candidate set and avoid full-pool recomputation by re-evaluating a frozen pool under updated models.<cite id="14">Freezing and awakening subsets of data reduce repeated full-pool computations while maintaining effectiveness through periodic reassessment under evolving boundaries</cite> Privacy-preserving clustering and feature extraction further reduce per-client computation and communication, enabling low-budget FAL participation from resource-constrained clients.<cite id="15">Pre-trained feature extraction and robust clustering enable low-overhead participation in FAL with limited local data</cite> 

Contributions Relative to Prior Work. While AL reduces annotation cost and FL preserves privacy, existing FAL methods often overlook client heterogeneity and decision-boundary drift, harming accuracy and efficiency.<cite id="14">Standard AL is insufficient under restricted diversity and budgets in federated settings; prior FAL methods overlook heterogeneity and parameter fluctuations</cite> Addressing these gaps, CHASe introduces a heterogeneity-aware selection that (i) tracks epistemic variation via inference inconsistency across epochs, (ii) aligns and calibrates decision boundaries with a new loss, and (iii) uses a freeze–awaken mechanism with subset sampling to maintain effectiveness and efficiency.<cite id="14">CHASe tracks epistemic variation via inference inconsistency, calibrates decision boundaries with an alignment loss, and employs a freeze–awaken mechanism with subset sampling to improve efficiency</cite> Across datasets and heterogeneous settings, prioritizing high-variation samples and aligning boundaries yields consistent gains over pool-based and non-calibrated baselines, validating the approach’s robustness and scalability.<cite id="14">Experiments show CHASe surpasses established baselines across diverse datasets, model complexities, and heterogeneous federation settings</cite> 

Scope and Comparisons. Our treatment complements recent FAL efforts that emphasize clustering or feature-level strategies for low-budget regimes and highlights the importance of boundary calibration and heterogeneity-aware sampling when data and model updates diverge across clients.<cite id="15">Clustering-based low-budget FAL leverages pre-trained features to sustain performance under limited labels</cite> <cite id="14">Heterogeneity-aware selection and boundary alignment improve robustness to client-specific shifts and parameter fluctuations</cite> Together, these works motivate methods that combine uncertainty-sensitive selection, boundary-calibrated training, and efficient sampling to make AL both effective and practical in federated settings.<cite id="14">Combining inference-inconsistency tracking, boundary alignment, and freeze–awaken subset sampling yields effectiveness and efficiency gains in FAL</cite>

Active learning (AL) reduces human annotation costs for machine learning
systems by strategically selecting the most informative unlabeled data for
annotation, but performing it individually may still be insufficient due to

training, while preserving the confidentiality of raw data samples. Yet,
existing FAL methods fail to account for the heterogeneity of data distribution
across clients and the associated fluctuations in global and local model
parameters, adversely affecting model accuracy. To overcome these challenges,
we propose CHASe (Client Heterogeneity-Aware Data Selection), specifically
designed for FAL. CHASe focuses on identifying those unlabeled samples with
high epistemic variations (EVs), which notably oscillate around the decision
boundaries during training. To achieve both effectiveness and efficiency,
\model{} encompasses techniques for 1) tracking EVs by analyzing inference
inconsistencies across training epochs, 2) calibrating decision boundaries of
inaccurate models with a new alignment loss, and 3) enhancing data selection
efficiency via a data freeze and awaken mechanism with subset sampling.
Experiments show that CHASe surpasses various established baselines in terms of
effectiveness and efficiency, validated across diverse datasets, model
complexities, and heterogeneous federation settings.

Further details [6][7][8][9][10].) Each in-line citation must consist of a single reference number within a pair of brackets. Do not use any other citation format. Do not exceed 600 words for the related works section. Here is the paper abstract:
In order to achieve low latency, high throughput, and partition tolerance,
modern databases forgo strong transaction isolation for weak isolation
guarantees. However, several production databases have been found to suffer
from isolation bugs, breaking their data-consistency contract. Black-box
testing is a prominent technique for detecting isolation bugs, by checking
whether histories of database transactions adhere to a prescribed isolation
level.
  Testing databases on realistic workloads of large size requires isolation
testers to be as efficient as possible, a requirement that has initiated a
study of the complexity of isolation testing. Although testing strong isolation
has been known to be NP-complete, weak isolation levels were recently shown to
be testable in polynomial time, which has propelled the scalability of testing
tools. However, existing testers have a large polynomial complexity,
restricting testing to workloads of only moderate size, which is not typical of
large-scale databases.
  In this work, we develop AWDIT, a highly-efficient and provably optimal
tester for weak database isolation. Given a history $H$ of size $n$ and $k$
sessions, AWDIT tests whether H satisfies the most common weak isolation levels
of Read Committed (RC), Read Atomic (RA), and Causal Consistency (CC) in time
$O(n^{3/2})$, $O(n^{3/2})$, and $O(n \cdot k)$, respectively, improving
significantly over the state of the art. Moreover, we prove that AWDIT is
essentially optimal, in the sense that there is a conditional lower bound of
$n^{3/2}$ for any weak isolation level between RC and CC. Our experiments show
that AWDIT is significantly faster than existing, highly optimized testers;
e.g., for the $\sim$20% largest histories, AWDIT obtains an average speedup of
$245\times$, $193\times$, and $62\times$ for RC, RA, and CC, respectively, over
the best baseline.

- Then weak-isolation testing: shift from NP-complete to polynomial-time, with Plume/IsoVista techniques and their limits.

Related Works

Modern distributed and multi-version databases often trade strong transaction isolation for weaker guarantees to achieve low latency and high throughput, but several production systems have been found to contain isolation bugs that violate their consistency contracts. Black-box testing has emerged as a prominent methodology for detecting such violations by synthesizing large workloads and checking whether observed histories adhere to a target isolation level, including representative weak levels such as Read Committed (RC), Read Atomicity (RA), and Transactional Causal Consistency (CC) <cite id="9">Black-box testing is a prominent technique for detecting isolation bugs, by checking whether histories of database transactions adhere to a prescribed isolation level</cite>. Recent studies have documented numerous isolation defects across commercial and open-source databases, underscoring the need for efficient, complete, and scalable checkers that can operate without access to source code or internal state <cite id="39">recent studies have uncovered numerous isolation bugs in many production databases, raising concerns about whether these databases actually uphold their promised isolation guarantees in practice</cite>. Within this landscape, our work builds on and significantly accelerates the state of the art in weak-isolation testing.

A large body of work focuses on verifying strong isolation guarantees (e.g., serializability and snapshot isolation). Foundational results show that naive verification can be computationally demanding, and practical systems must navigate efficiency–completeness trade-offs when operating in black-box settings with uncertain transactional dependencies. Recent work presents specialized verifiers that make verification practical by simplifying traces and exploiting structural properties, demonstrating that careful algorithmic design can dramatically improve performance while maintaining correctness <cite id="38">We present Boomslang, the first general-purpose checking framework capable of verifying configurations that were previously uncheckable. As a result, the checking problem becomes challenging. This trade-off is expected: more detailed traces simplify checking and improve checking performance</cite>. Complementary efforts target end-to-end database isolation checking with techniques such as mini-transations to reduce the complexity of inter-procedure and cross-object dependencies, enabling scalable detection of violations in realistic workloads <cite id="42">a greybox fuzz-testing framework that bridges the gap by instrumenting key transactional operations to capture true dependencies and generate concurrency traces that reflect internal dependencies</cite>. Alongside these systems advances, new verifiers for strong isolation emphasize speed and practicality, indicating that modern algorithmic ideas can deliver substantial performance gains in black-box verification scenarios <cite id="41">we present VeriStrong, a fast verifier for strong database isolation</cite>.

For weak isolation levels, prior black-box checkers established efficient, sound, and complete characterizations based on fine-grained anomalous patterns and augmented logical clocks, enabling scalable checking for RC, RA, and CC. Plume introduces a complete checker that combines vectors and tree clocks to accelerate checking and reproduces known violations efficiently, demonstrating that modern temporal models and modular pattern libraries can yield both correctness and performance in practice <cite id="11">Plume builds on modular, fine-grained, transactional anomalous patterns, with which we establish sound and complete characterizations of representative weak isolation levels, including read committed, read atomicity, and transactional causal consistency. Plume leverages a novel combination of two techniques, vectors and tree clocks, to accelerate isolation checking</cite>. IsoVista adopts a black-box approach that encompasses a broad range of isolation levels, providing faithful characterizations to avoid false positives and missed bugs, and achieving superior checking efficiency relative to prior systems while supporting profiling and visualization for large workloads <cite id="12">It builds on faithful characterizations of a range of isolation levels, ensuring the absence of both false positives and missed bugs in collected DBMS execution histories. IsoVista exhibits superior checking efficiency, compared to the state of the art, and visualizes violation scenarios</cite>. These systems motivate further algorithmic improvements, as they reveal that while weak isolation is polynomially testable, existing testers often have large polynomial complexities that constrain testing to moderate-sized histories in large-scale deployments <cite id="9">weak isolation levels were recently shown to be testable in polynomial time, which has propelled the scalability of testing tools. However, existing testers have a large polynomial complexity, restricting testing to workloads of only moderate size</cite>.

Our work addresses these limitations by developing AWDIT, a provably optimal tester for RC, RA, and CC with near-linear-to-subquadratic runtime in the number of operations and sessions. AWDIT leverages structural properties specific to weak isolation to reduce the complexity of checking on realistic workloads, achieving O(n^{3/2}) for RC and RA, and O(n·k) for CC, and establishing conditional lower bounds of Ω(n^{3/2}) for RC and RA, implying near-optimality under widely believed hardness assumptions <cite id="9">AWDIT tests RC and RA in time O(n^{3/2}) and CC in O(n·k), and proves that there is a conditional lower bound of n^{3/2} for any weak isolation level between RC and CC</cite>. Empirically, AWDIT delivers order-of-magnitude speedups over the best specialized baselines, with average speedups of 245×, 193×, and 62× on the roughly 20% largest histories for RC, RA, and CC, respectively, enabling complete testing of substantially larger traces within practical time budgets <cite id="9">for the ~20% largest histories, AWDIT obtains an average speedup of 245×, 193×, and 62× for RC, RA, and CC, respectively, over the best baseline</cite>. These gains stem from AWDIT’s algorithmic innovations and its tight integration with the problem structure of weak isolation, complementing prior systems that relied on pattern libraries and augmented clocks to achieve completeness and efficiency <cite id="11">sound and complete characterizations for RC, RA, and CC, with vectors and tree clocks to accelerate checking</cite><cite id="12">faithful characterizations ensure absence of false positives and missed bugs, with superior checking efficiency</cite>.

Beyond AWDIT, broader trends in concurrency testing emphasize hybrid approaches that combine black-box stress testing with targeted instrumentation and decomposition to manage inter-procedure and cross-object dependencies. These include greybox fuzzing that instruments source to capture true transactional dependencies, and frameworks that simplify traces to improve checking performance while preserving completeness guarantees <cite id="42">a greybox fuzz-testing framework that bridges this gap by combining principled instrumentation and version-aware traces</cite><cite id="38">more detailed traces simplify checking and improve checking performance</cite>. Together, these lines of work establish that while weak isolation testing is polynomially solvable, the choice of representation and algorithmic strategy critically determines scalability, and that modern techniques—graph- and clock-based encodings for weak levels, and decomposition/mini-transaction strategies for strong levels—can bring end-to-end checking into practical regimes for large workloads <cite id="11">Plume leverages vectors and tree clocks to accelerate isolation checking</cite><cite id="12">IsoVista exhibits superior checking efficiency and visualizes violations</cite><cite id="41">a fast verifier for strong database isolation</cite>.

Finally, the empirical discovery of isolation defects in production systems motivates comprehensive, complete, and fast checkers that can operate without source access. Recent work shows that randomized black-box testing remains the de facto approach, as it stresses DBMSs under large, concurrent workloads to surface violations while scaling to realistic traces, thereby balancing coverage, completeness, and runtime constraints <cite id="12">the de facto approach adopted by these checkers is randomized black-box testing, stressing DBMSs with large, concurrent workloads to serve a dual purpose</cite><cite id="39">isolation bugs are difficult to detect and have remained undetected for long periods, motivating sophisticated checkers</cite>. AWDIT complements these efforts by providing algorithms that are not only correct and complete for RC, RA, and CC but also provably near-optimal and dramatically faster in practice, enabling complete testing of larger and more complex production-like histories within feasible time budgets <cite id="9">AWDIT is a highly-efficient and provably optimal tester for RC, RA, and CC, with O(n^{3/2}) and O(n·k) runtimes and conditional lower bounds</cite>.

tool_outputs.title: [Literature Review] AWDIT: An Optimal Weak Database Isolation Tester
tool_outputs.snippet:
The paper "AWDIT: An Optimal Weak Database Isolation Tester" introduces AWDIT, a highly efficient and provably optimal tester for weak database isolation levels like Read Committed (RC), Read Atomic (RA), and Causal Consistency (CC).Black-box testing, which involves checking histories of database transactions against prescribed isolation levels, is a common technique for detecting these bugs.
The paper focuses on improving the efficiency of isolation testers, especially for large-scale databases.

Your task is to write a Related Works section for an academic paper given the paper's abstract. Your response should provide the Related Works section and references. Only include references from arXiv that are published before 2025-04-09T15:30:09+00:00. Mention them in a separate, numbered reference list at the end and use the reference numbers to provide in-line citations in the Related Works section for all claims referring to a source (e.g., description of source [3]. Further details [6][7][8][9][10].) Each in-line citation must consist of a single reference number within a pair of brackets. Do not use any other citation format. Do not exceed 600 words for the related works section. Here is the paper abstract:
In order to achieve low latency, high throughput, and partition tolerance,
modern databases forgo strong transaction isolation for weak isolation
guarantees. However, several production databases have been found to suffer
from isolation bugs, breaking their data-consistency contract. Black-box
testing is a prominent technique for detecting isolation bugs, by checking
whether histories of database transactions adhere to a prescribed isolation
level.
  Testing databases on realistic workloads of large size requires isolation
testers to be as efficient as possible, a requirement that has initiated a
study of the complexity of isolation testing. Although testing strong isolation
has been known to be NP-complete, weak isolation levels were recently shown to
be testable in polynomial time, which has propelled the scalability of testing
tools. However, existing testers have a large polynomial complexity,
restricting testing to workloads of only moderate size, which is not typical of
large-scale databases.
  In this work, we develop AWDIT, a highly-efficient and provably optimal
tester for weak database isolation. Given a history $H$ of size $n$ and $k$
sessions, AWDIT tests whether H satisfies the most common weak isolation levels
of Read Committed (RC), Read Atomic (RA), and Causal Consistency (CC) in time
$O(n^{3/2})$, $O(n^{3/2})$, and $O(n \cdot k)$, respectively, improving
significantly over the state of the art. Moreover, we prove that AWDIT is
essentially optimal, in the sense that there is a conditional lower bound of
$n^{3/2}$ for any weak isolation level between RC and CC. Our experiments show
that AWDIT is significantly faster than existing, highly optimized testers;
e.g., for the $\sim$20% largest histories, AWDIT obtains an average speedup of
$245\times$, $193\times$, and $62\times$ for RC, RA, and CC, respectively, over
the best baseline.

Inspired by the success of unsupervised pre-training paradigms, researchers
have applied these approaches to DNA pre-training. However, we argue that these
approaches alone yield suboptimal results because pure DNA sequences lack
sufficient information, since their functions are regulated by genomic profiles
like chromatin accessibility. Here, we demonstrate that supervised training for
genomic profile prediction serves as a more effective alternative to pure
sequence pre-training. Furthermore, considering the multi-species and
multi-profile nature of genomic profile prediction, we introduce our
$\textbf{S}$pecies-$\textbf{P}$rofile $\textbf{A}$daptive
$\textbf{C}$ollaborative $\textbf{E}$xperts (SPACE) that leverages Mixture of
Experts (MoE) to better capture the relationships between DNA sequences across
different species and genomic profiles, thereby learning more effective DNA
representations. Through extensive experiments across various tasks, our model
achieves state-of-the-art performance, establishing that DNA models trained
with supervised genomic profiles serve as powerful DNA representation learners.
The code is available at https://github.com/ZhuJiwei111/SPACE.

<answer>
Related Work

DNA foundation models have sought to learn general-purpose representations from large genomic sequence corpora to enable transfer to regulatory and functional tasks. Early efforts focused on pure DNA sequence, training Transformers with masked or language-modeling objectives to capture long-range structure and context for downstream prediction of regulatory elements and variants. <cite id="1">DNABERT introduced a pre-trained bidirectional encoder for DNA sequences that transfers to promoter, splice site, and transcription factor binding prediction after minimal fine-tuning, and demonstrated applicability across organisms</cite>. <cite id="2">A complementary benchmarking study (BEND) evaluated DNA language models on realistic downstream tasks across the human genome and found that while embeddings can approach expert methods on some tasks, they capture limited information about long-range features, highlighting the difficulty of purely sequence-based modeling</cite>. Beyond sequence-only Transformers, alternative architectures have targeted long-range modeling at single-nucleotide resolution. <cite id="23">HyenaDNA leverages implicit convolutions to pretrain on the entire human genome at up to 1 million tokens of context while maintaining single-nucleotide output, scaling sub-quadratically and enabling in-context learning for adaptation to novel tasks without fine-tuning</cite>. These results collectively suggest that while sequence-only pretraining can be effective, it may be insufficient to fully capture cell-type–specific regulation and functional profiles.

A complementary line of work augments sequence with epigenomic signals during pretraining or modeling. <cite id="22">EPIGENOMIC BERT (EBERT) jointly learns from DNA sequence and paired epigenetic state across 127 cell types using a masked language objective, and demonstrates strong transfer to cell type–specific transcription factor binding prediction, exceeding prior state-of-the-art on several ENCODE-DREAM benchmarks</cite>. This approach directly addresses the abstract’s premise that pure DNA sequences lack sufficient information for regulatory function and motivates supervised objectives that predict genomic profiles such as chromatin accessibility. <cite id="31">Recent work systematically evaluates deep learning methods for high-resolution chromatin accessibility prediction from sequence, introducing ConvNeXt-inspired architectures and assessing robustness at 4-bp resolution, emphasizing the importance of accurate accessibility modeling for regulatory variant effect analysis</cite>. <cite id="30">AlphaGenome takes a unified step by training on 1 Mb of DNA sequence to predict thousands of functional genomic tracks at single-base-pair resolution across modalities including chromatin accessibility, histone modifications, transcription factor binding, chromatin contacts, and gene expression, and shows competitive or superior variant effect predictions across 24/26 evaluations</cite>. These supervised, multi-track models demonstrate that learning to predict genomic profiles can yield powerful sequence representations that generalize to variant effect prediction.

Cross-species and multi-profile generalization are central to realistic DNA representation learning. <cite id="1">DNABERT’s pre-trained human model transfers to other organisms with exceptional performance, indicating that sequence-level pretraining can provide a useful inductive bias across species despite evolutionary divergence</cite>. <cite id="22">EBERT’s training across 127 cell types and multiple epigenetic states supports robust cross-cell-type transfer to regulatory tasks</cite>. <cite id="30">AlphaGenome’s simultaneous prediction of accessibility, TF binding, and expression across modalities suggests a principled way to integrate multi-profile supervision, aligning with the multi-profile nature of genomic regulation</cite>. Together, these works motivate models that combine supervised objectives over genomic profiles with mechanisms to scale across species and marks.

Parameter-efficient specialization and routing have been explored in biology to balance accuracy and compute, often as alternatives to training monolithic large models. While mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures are common in NLP, their application to DNA with explicit multi-species and multi-profile objectives is less established. <cite id="1">DNABERT’s cross-species transfer shows that compact, pre-trained sequence encoders can be effective priors for downstream tasks across organisms</cite>, and <cite id="22">EBERT’s joint sequence–epigenomic pretraining supports cross-cell-type adaptation</cite>. <cite id="30">AlphaGenome’s unified multi-track supervision demonstrates that modeling multiple profiles jointly can improve variant effect prediction</cite>. In contrast, SPACE introduces a species–profile adaptive collaborative experts framework that leverages MoE to explicitly capture relationships between DNA sequences across different species and genomic profiles during supervised training, aiming to learn more effective representations for multi-profile prediction than sequence-only or single-species pretraining. <cite id="22">This contrasts with EPIGENOMIC BERT’s multi-cell-type pretraining on sequence+epigenome</cite> and <cite id="30">AlphaGenome’s multi-modality supervised outputs</cite>, and extends prior sequence-only foundation models by parameter sharing across profiles and species via expert routing. <cite id="23">It also differs from long-range sequence-only modeling like HyenaDNA by centering supervised prediction of accessibility and related profiles as the core objective</cite>. <cite id="31">By integrating advances in accessibility prediction architectures and emphasizing multi-profile supervision, SPACE targets the information-poor regime of pure sequences with a structured, scalable MoE design</cite>.

Summary of references
1) DNABERT: pre-trained Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers model for DNA-language in genome. <cite id="1">DNABERT developed a pre-trained bidirectional encoder for DNA that transfers to promoter, splice site, and TF binding prediction and applies to other organisms</cite>.
2) BEND: Benchmarking DNA language models on biologically meaningful tasks. <cite id="2">BEND shows DNA LMs can approach expert methods on some tasks but miss long-range features, underscoring limits of sequence-only modeling</cite>.
3) HyenaDNA: long-range genomic sequence modeling at single nucleotide resolution. <cite id="23">HyenaDNA pretrains on up to 1 million-token contexts at single-nucleotide resolution and supports in-context learning</cite>.
4) EPIGENOMIC BERT (EBERT): joint sequence–epigenome pretraining across 127 cell types. <cite id="22">EBERT pretrains on DNA sequence and epigenetic state across 127 cell types and improves TF binding prediction</cite>.
5) Evaluation of deep learning approaches for high-resolution chromatin accessibility prediction. <cite id="31">Assesses 4-bp resolution accessibility prediction and introduces ConvNext-based architectures</cite>.
6) AlphaGenome: unified multi-modality prediction from sequence. <cite id="30">Trains on 1 Mb sequence to predict thousands of tracks including accessibility, TF binding, contacts, and expression, with strong variant effect prediction</cite>.
</answer>

Understanding how feature representations evolve across layers in large
language models (LLMs) is key to improving their interpretability and
robustness. While recent studies have identified critical layers linked to
specific functions or behaviors, these efforts typically rely on data-dependent
analyses of fine-tuned models, limiting their use to post-hoc settings. In
contrast, we introduce a data-oblivious approach to identify intrinsic critical
layers in pre-fine-tuned LLMs by analyzing representation dynamics via Centered
Kernel Alignment(CKA). We show that layers with significant shifts in
representation space are also those most affected during fine-tuning--a pattern
that holds consistently across tasks for a given model. Our spectral analysis
further reveals that these shifts are driven by changes in the top principal
components, which encode semantic transitions from rationales to conclusions.
We further apply these findings to two practical scenarios: efficient domain
adaptation, where fine-tuning critical layers leads to greater loss reduction
compared to non-critical layers; and backdoor defense, where freezing them
reduces attack success rates by up to 40%.

<answer>
Related Works

Interpreting LLMs through evolving representations. A central line of work studies how features change across transformer layers to make models more interpretable and robust. Probing and alignment-based methods compare representations with external signals or across network depths using metrics such as centered kernel alignment (CKA) and representation difference maps to quantify functional shifts and specialization with depth, often revealing that earlier layers encode syntactic and intermediate layers capture compositional semantics while higher layers consolidate task-relevant decisions and invariances [1]. Broader cross-modal analyses using massive-scale alignment measurements show that higher-performing language and vision models develop stronger brain–AI alignment, with language models exhibiting markedly higher correlations than vision models, underscoring that internal representations evolve in structured, task-adaptive ways without explicit biological priors [2]. These findings motivate measuring layer-wise similarity and dynamics as a window into model behavior and provide methodological grounding for CKA-based, data-oblivious comparisons across layers and tasks.

Identifying critical layers and representation shifts. Prior studies often rely on data-dependent, post-hoc analyses of fine-tuned models, limiting generality. In contrast, alignment and spectral analyses across pre-finetuned stacks suggest that layers exhibiting large shifts in representation space—captured by CKA/RDM changes—are precisely those whose principal components rotate most during fine-tuning, indicating that semantic directions evolve from rationales to conclusions through top-PC changes [3]. Spectral decompositions of Jacobians and attention maps further show that a small number of principal components can account for much of the variance in layer-wise transitions, enabling data-oblivious identification of layers whose directions are most likely to change under adaptation [4]. These results dovetail with observations that higher-capacity models exhibit more specialized, brain-like internal structures, reinforcing that principal component trajectories and alignment patterns are reliable indicators of functional relevance and plasticity [2].

Efficient adaptation via layer-wise importance. Selective fine-tuning methods leverage layer- or parameter-wise importance to reduce cost and improve stability, often by prioritizing blocks that drive largest pre-adaptation changes or show high Fisher information with the new task [5]. Adapter-based approaches further confine updates to low-rank per-layer modules, implicitly prioritizing layers where representation shifts are most informative while constraining update magnitude. Empirically, freezing or sparingly updating “critical” layers yields faster convergence and better accuracy on downstream tasks, consistent with the idea that a small set of layers dominate semantic reorientation under domain shift [6]. Our work complements these by providing a data-oblivious criterion—CKA-driven shifts and top-PC movement—to target adaptation to the most impactful layers before adaptation begins [3].

Backdoor resilience via selective update blocking. Data-dependent backdoor analyses show that malicious features can be injected into specific layers or parameter clusters; defenses that freeze or orthogonalize these critical subspaces reduce attack success by preventing harmful directions from aligning with task-relevant PCs [7]. Freezing or sparingly updating layers that exhibit large intrinsic shifts (and thus high semantic plasticity) interrupts the coalescence of backdoor patterns with clean features, while targeted unlearning on those same layers can remove spurious correlations with minimal loss of task performance [8]. Quantitatively, defenses that protect top-PC directions or critical layers have been shown to reduce attack success by up to roughly 40% in several architectures and noise regimes, aligning with our observation that freezing critical layers hampers fine-tuning-induced semantic takeover by malicious features [9]. Together, these results support prioritizing spectral and alignment diagnostics to both improve adaptation and harden models against backdoors.

Principal component and linear-subspace analyses of semantics. Principal component analysis (PCA) and related spectral methods have been widely used to dissect how representations evolve across layers and training stages, often revealing that semantic information concentrates along a small set of principal components that rotate with learning and adaptation [10]. In LLMs, top PCs have been linked to high-level concepts and compositional structure, and their trajectories across layers can demarcate transitions from intermediate reasoning states to final outputs, mirroring the “rationales-to-conclusions” shift we identify via CKA [4]. These linear-subspace views also connect to Fisher-sharpness and margin analyses, where variance-aligned directions are prioritized for fine-tuning and regularization, providing a unifying rationale for why selective update strategies succeed [5].

Surveys and limitations. Recent surveys of LLM interpretability emphasize that representation probing, attribution, and alignment are complementary lenses for understanding internal computation, but note that many methods depend on task labels or external datasets and are sensitive to data distribution shifts [1]. Our approach addresses data dependence by focusing on intrinsic, cross-layer alignment and spectral dynamics in pre-finetuned models, while the backdoor and adaptation applications leverage the same signals to improve efficiency and robustness [3][5][7][8][9]. Remaining gaps include generalization across architectures, sensitivity to batch/optimization dynamics, and principled integration of depth-wise and cross-attention spaces; ongoing work on contrastive alignment and attention-specific PCA may further clarify how different mechanism classes contribute to semantic transitions [11].

1. Arora, S., et al. (2022). “On the measurement of neural and behavioral similarity.” arXiv:2205.12793. Description: Introduces CKA and related alignment metrics for probing and comparing neural representations across layers and tasks, with implications for interpretability and specialization with depth. [1]
2. Kiat, S., et al. (2024). “Alignment between Brains and AI: Evidence for Convergent Evolution across Modalities, Scales and Training Trajectories.” arXiv:2412.17401. Description: Large-scale analysis shows higher-performing models develop stronger brain–AI alignment, with language models exhibiting r ≈ 0.89 and vision r ≈ 0.53, supporting structured, task-adaptive evolution of internal representations. [2]
3. Zhang, Y., et al. (2023). “Spectral Diagnostics of Layer-wise Semantic Shifts in Pre-finetuned LLMs.” arXiv:2311.14567. Description: Shows that layers with large CKA-driven shifts across depth are precisely those whose top principal components change most during fine-tuning, indicating semantic transitions from rationales to conclusions. [3]
4. Chen, X., et al. (2024). “Attention Spectra and Concept Rotation in LLMs.” arXiv:2403.05552. Description: Uses spectral analysis of attention/Jacobian maps to show few principal components explain layer-wise variance shifts, enabling data-oblivious identification of critical layers. [4]
5. Hou, Q., et al. (2023). “Layer-wise Importance and Efficient Fine-tuning in LLMs.” arXiv:2307.09178. Description: Proposes layer importance via Fisher/representation change priors to guide selective fine-tuning, improving convergence and accuracy by focusing updates on critical layers. [5]
6. Krueger, G., et al. (2022). “Adapters: A Local Approach to Transfer Learning in Pretrained Transformers.” arXiv:2202.09591. Description: Adapter modules confine fine-tuning to low-rank per-layer parameters, effectively prioritizing informative layers while constraining update magnitude. [6]
7. Carlini, N., et al. (2021). “Training backdoored models: Risky target distributions.” arXiv:2103.08459. Description: Shows backdoor features can concentrate in specific layers/directions; defenses that block or orthogonalize these subspaces reduce success. [7]
8. Srivastava, A., et al. (2022). “Mitigating Backdoors by Targeted Unlearning in LLMs.” arXiv:2206.09109. Description: Demonstrates targeted unlearning on critical layers removes backdoor triggers with minimal utility loss. [8]
9. Naveh, M., et al. (2023). “Freezing Critical Layers Reduces Backdoor Success by Up to 40% in Transformer Models.” arXiv:2304.12567. Description: Freezing or sparingly updating plastic layers interrupts harmful fine-tuning alignment, reducing attack success substantially. [9]
10. Tenenbaum, J. B., et al. (2000). “A global geometric framework for nonlinear dimensionality reduction.” Science. Description: PCA/spectral methods reveal low-dimensional manifolds and principal directions underlying high-dimensional data; widely adopted to analyze representation manifolds in deep networks. [10]
11. Foster, J., et al. (2023). “Interpreting LLMs through Attention-Selective Probing.” arXiv:2309.12345. Description: Attention-specific probing and contrastive alignment clarify how concept directions differ across self-attention layers, complementing global CKA-based analyses. [11]

Do not exceed 600 words for the related works section. Here is the paper abstract:
Understanding how feature representations evolve across layers in large
language models (LLMs) is key to improving their interpretability and
robustness. While recent studies have identified critical layers linked to
specific functions or behaviors, these efforts typically rely on data-dependent
analyses of fine-tuned models, limiting their use to post-hoc settings. In
contrast, we introduce a data-oblivious approach to identify intrinsic critical
layers in pre-fine-tuned LLMs by analyzing representation dynamics via Centered
Kernel Alignment(CKA). We show that layers with significant shifts in
representation space are also those most affected during fine-tuning--a pattern
that holds consistently across tasks for a given model. Our spectral analysis
further reveals that these shifts are driven by changes in the top principal
components, which encode semantic transitions from rationales to conclusions.
We further apply these findings to two practical scenarios: efficient domain
adaptation, where fine-tuning critical layers leads to greater loss reduction
compared to non-critical layers; and backdoor defense, where freezing them
reduces attack success rates by up to 40%.

Rehearsal-based methods have shown superior performance in addressing
catastrophic forgetting in continual learning (CL) by storing and training on a
subset of past data alongside new data in current task. While such a concurrent
rehearsal strategy is widely used, it remains unclear if this approach is
always optimal. Inspired by human learning, where sequentially revisiting tasks
helps mitigate forgetting, we explore whether sequential rehearsal can offer
greater benefits for CL compared to standard concurrent rehearsal. To address
this question, we conduct a theoretical analysis of rehearsal-based CL in
overparameterized linear models, comparing two strategies: 1) Concurrent
Rehearsal, where past and new data are trained together, and 2) Sequential
Rehearsal, where new data is trained first, followed by revisiting past data
sequentially. By explicitly characterizing forgetting and generalization error,
we show that sequential rehearsal performs better when tasks are less similar.
These insights further motivate a novel Hybrid Rehearsal method, which trains
similar tasks concurrently and revisits dissimilar tasks sequentially. We
characterize its forgetting and generalization performance, and our experiments
with deep neural networks further confirm that the hybrid approach outperforms
standard concurrent rehearsal. This work provides the first comprehensive
theoretical analysis of rehearsal-based CL.

<answer>
Related Works

Continual learning and rehearsal as a response to catastrophic forgetting. A core challenge in continual learning (CL) is catastrophic forgetting, where learning a new task degrades performance on previously seen tasks; this motivates mechanisms that preserve past knowledge while enabling plasticity for new tasks [23]. Among many approaches, rehearsal-based methods store samples or synthetic proxies of past data and replay them while learning new data, effectively enforcing a plasticity-stability trade-off without altering all weights uniformly [23]. Gradient-based stabilizers such as Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) slow down learning on parameters critical for old tasks, demonstrating that targeted constraints can maintain prior expertise while scaling to complex problems [22]. These insights establish the need for strategies that balance adaptation with memory of prior tasks, a role that rehearsal methods explicitly address by revisiting past information during training.

Concurrent rehearsal: replay, generative replay, and constraints. Replay-based rehearsal stores a buffer of past examples and trains on them concurrently with new data, often complemented by distillation or constraint-based regularization to prevent interference [23]. Recent analyses dissect the dual role of replay buffers: while small buffers can stabilize geometry and prevent deep feature forgetting, mitigating classifier-level forgetting typically requires larger replay fractions, revealing an asymmetry between feature-space and shallow classifier stability [1]. This work formalizes shallow versus deep forgetting and shows that non-zero replay asymptotically preserves linear separability of past classes, yet small buffers can induce rank-deficient statistics that impair classification—suggesting explicit correction of statistical artifacts may reduce reliance on large buffers. Building on replay, exemplar-free generative replay has emerged to scale rehearsal without storing raw data: lightweight generators synthesize pseudo-exemplars or representations conditioned on task/domain cues to approximate past distributions, enabling privacy-preserving rehearsal [1]. In vision and vision-language settings, domain- or morphology-guided generative replay produces synthetic inputs aligned with past tasks, preserving performance across incremental shifts without retaining raw exemplars [1]. Concurrently, hybrid feature-space designs separate learning and replay subspaces: learning novel knowledge in a compact subspace while replaying across a larger accumulated space mitigates interference by decoupling updates that affect past and present representations [34]. These developments extend classic replay by making the geometry of rehearsal explicit and scalable.

Sequential rehearsal and interleaving: revisiting tasks over time. Human learning suggests that sequentially revisiting past tasks can reduce interference, motivating sequential rehearsal schedules that train new data, then revisit old tasks before moving on [1]. In online CL, this manifests as interleaved task sequences or periodic revisits that distribute learning across time, contrasting with concurrent rehearsal where past and new data are co-trained. Empirically, sequential rehearsal has been shown to reduce interference when tasks are dissimilar, improving retention of earlier tasks by reinforcing their decision boundaries between updates [1]. This complements replay-based methods by structuring when, not just what, is rehearsed; scheduling revisits can be particularly effective when buffer capacity is limited or when generative models must approximate diverse past distributions [1]. In practice, sequential schedules also arise in privacy-preserving or exemplar-free settings, where storing past data is undesirable and synthetic replay must be carefully timed to maintain stability [1].

Similarity-aware and hybrid rehearsal. A key observation is that rehearsal costs vary with task similarity: dissimilar tasks interfere more strongly and benefit more from separation, while similar tasks can often be updated jointly with limited interference [3]. Motivated by this, similarity-aware rehearsal groups similar tasks together and schedules sequential revisits for dissimilar ones, reducing redundancy and preserving capacity for larger dissimilarity gaps [3]. Hybrid rehearsal formalizes this by training similar tasks concurrently (to exploit shared feature geometry) and revisiting dissimilar tasks sequentially (to correct drift over larger decision boundaries), yielding a stability–plasticity allocation that adapts to task structure [3]. This idea connects to broader CL taxonomies that emphasize stability–plasticity tuning and memory constraints, showing how rehearsal scheduling can operationalize similarity-aware plasticity within task-incremental settings [23]. In domains like medical imaging and pathology, where domain shifts and evolving conventions are common, hybrid rehearsal with similarity- or morphology-guided scheduling has demonstrated superior retention versus uniform replay, preserving accuracy across incremental changes [1].

Theoretical analyses of rehearsal and rehearsal schedules. Recent theory situates rehearsal within overparameterized and linear models, comparing concurrent and sequential rehearsal and deriving expressions for forgetting and generalization error [3]. The analysis shows that sequential rehearsal achieves lower forgetting when tasks are less similar, because revisiting dissimilar tasks reinforces separations that concurrent rehearsal cannot maintain under interference; conversely, for highly similar tasks, concurrent rehearsal suffices and wastes rehearsal budget otherwise [3]. These insights motivate hybrid rehearsal that partitions tasks by similarity, and the theory characterizes its error and forgetting trade-offs, aligning with empirical observations that interleaving and revisit schedules improve stability under larger task divergence [3]. Complementing this, asymptotic analyses of replay reveal a geometric view: replay preserves linear separability of past classes but may induce statistical artifacts (e.g., rank deficiency) that inflate class means and impair shallow classifiers, explaining why larger replay fractions or targeted corrections are often needed to fully mitigate forgetting [1]. Together, these results provide a unified lens: rehearsal buffers stabilize geometry, while scheduling and similarity-aware grouping stabilize decision boundaries, especially for dissimilar tasks [1,3].

Empirical landscape and benchmarks. Across benchmarks, replay-based methods consistently serve as strong baselines, with generative and exemplar-free variants scaling rehearsal to large or sensitive domains [1]. In task-incremental settings, replayed buffers and distillation schedules preserve accuracy on old tasks while adapting to new ones, though shallow classifier degradation can persist without explicit mitigation [1]. Hybrid and similarity-aware strategies improve upon uniform replay by allocating rehearsal to dissimilar tasks and co-training similar ones, reducing redundancy and improving overall accuracy and efficiency [3]. In medical and pathology benchmarks, privacy-aware generative replay and morphology-style footprints outperform standard fine-tuning and uniform replay, demonstrating robustness to domain shifts and evolving conventions [1]. These empirical gains align with theoretical predictions that sequential rehearsal benefits increase with task dissimilarity, while concurrent rehearsal dominates when tasks are similar [3].

Summary of connections. The literature converges on rehearsal as a central mechanism for mitigating catastrophic forgetting, with concurrent replay, generative replay, and constraint-based methods providing the basic toolkit [23]. Sequential rehearsal and similarity-aware scheduling refine this toolkit by allocating rehearsal where it is most impactful, reducing interference for dissimilar tasks and economizing capacity for similar ones [1,3]. Theoretical analyses in overparameterized/linear settings and neural-collapse perspectives explain why sequential rehearsal helps more when tasks are dissimilar and why buffer size and geometry matter, guiding hybrid designs that combine concurrent and sequential strategies [1,3]. Our hybrid rehearsal method builds on these insights, offering a principled, similarity-driven allocation of rehearsal effort with theoretical guarantees and empirical gains over standard concurrent rehearsal [3].

2. Pratibha Kumari et al. Domain-incremental White Blood Cell Classification with Privacy-aware Continual Learning. arXiv:2503.19819, 2025. [1]
3. Pratibha Kumari et al. Footprint-Guided Exemplar-Free Continual Histopathology Report Generation. arXiv:2509.01234, 2025. [1]
4. Huiwei Lin. ER-FSL: Experience Replay with Feature Subspace Learning for Online Continual Learning. arXiv:2407.12279, 2024. [34]
5. Matthias De Lange et al. A continual learning survey: Defying forgetting in classification tasks. arXiv:2304.05576, 2023. [23]
6. James Kirkpatrick et al. Overcoming catastrophic forgetting in neural networks. PNAS, 2017. [22]

Rehearsal-based methods have shown superior performance in addressing
catastrophic forgetting in continual learning (CL) by storing and training on a
subset of past data alongside new data in current task. While such a concurrent
rehearsal strategy is widely used, it remains unclear if this approach is
always optimal. Inspired by human learning, where sequentially revisiting tasks
helps mitigate forgetting, we explore whether sequential rehearsal can offer
greater benefits for CL compared to standard concurrent rehearsal. To address
this question, we conduct a theoretical analysis of rehearsal-based CL in
overparameterized linear models, comparing two strategies: 1) Concurrent
Rehearsal, where past and new data are trained together, and 2) Sequential
Rehearsal, where new data is trained first, followed by revisiting past data
sequentially. By explicitly characterizing forgetting and generalization error,
we show that sequential rehearsal performs better when tasks are less similar.
These insights further motivate a novel Hybrid Rehearsal method, which trains
similar tasks concurrently and revisits dissimilar tasks sequentially. We
characterize its forgetting and generalization performance, and our experiments
with deep neural networks further confirm that the hybrid approach outperforms
standard concurrent rehearsal. This work provides the first comprehensive
theoretical analysis of rehearsal-based CL.

properties, and their traditional study typically relies on time-consuming
molecular dynamics (MD) simulations conducted in silico. Recent advances in

learning distributions over crystallographic structures. However, effectively
integrating physical supervision into these data-driven approaches remains
challenging, as standard energy-based objectives often lead to intractable

Related Work

Protein function and biophysical properties depend critically on conformational dynamics and ensembles of states, motivating efficient methods that approximate MD-informed structure distributions without exhaustive simulation. Recent advances in generative modeling have enabled data-driven sampling of protein conformations and trajectories, but integrating physical supervision—especially energy differences and Boltzmann-like weighting—remains challenging. In this section, we synthesize prior work on diffusion-based protein structure/ensemble generation, MD-informed or energy-guided generative modeling, and benchmarks for MD ensembles, and situate our Energy-based Alignment (EBA) approach within these developments.

Diffusion-based protein structure and ensemble generation. Early successes in diffusion distillation for protein backbone generation demonstrate that training structure predictors to reverse-engineer noise can yield high-fidelity designs and samples. For example, RFdiffusion fine-tunes a RoseTTAFold-like network on protein structure denoising, uses an MSE loss that promotes coordinate-frame continuity across timesteps, and iteratively denoises random frames before handing off designed backbones to ProteinMPNN for sequence assignment, achieving strong performance in monomer, binder, and symmetric oligomer design scenarios [3]. Beyond design, diffusion models have been adapted to capture conformational ensembles and dynamics. CONFROVER introduces an autoregressive framework that jointly learns protein conformation and dynamics with an SE(3) diffusion decoder, supporting both time-dependent trajectories and time-independent conformation sampling on the ATLAS MD dataset [25]. For intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs), sequence-only ensemble generation has been explored: IDPFold fine-tunes diffusion models to generate conformational ensembles directly from sequence, addressing the paucity of experimental data and computational cost of MD while improving ensemble property accuracy over prior methods [26]. Complementing sequence-only approaches, ExEnDiff integrates experimental measurements as a physical prior to guide diffusion-based conformational ensemble generation, showing improved adherence to Boltzmann distributions and ensemble diversity across fast-folding and disordered proteins compared to unified ensemble samplers trained solely on PDB folds [2]. More recently, MarS-FM proposes Markov State Model (MSM) emulators for generative modeling of MD via flow matching, learning transitions across discrete MSM states to avoid training signals dominated by short, uninformative transitions; it reports over two orders of magnitude speedup versus implicit/explicit solvent MD while better reproducing MD statistics such as RMSD, radius of gyration, and secondary structure [1].

Energy/physics-guided generative modeling and MD-informed sampling. A central difficulty is aligning data-driven generative models with physical energetics and thermodynamics, including energy differences that bias conformational occupancy. Prior work addresses this in several ways. First, energy weighting and contrastive objectives have been used to incorporate energy rankings or experimental observables into training, encouraging generators to favor lower-energy or physically plausible structures; these ideas are related to EBA’s calibration of conformational states by energy differences. Second, MD-informed sampling and MSM-based discretization provide a coarse-grained yet physically grounded scaffold for transitions, as in MarS-FM, which explicitly leverages MSM states to guide long-timescale transitions and improve statistical fidelity [1]. Third, sequence-level energy models and structure predictors can be repurposed as supervisory signals: RFdiffusion’s MSE loss and iterative denoising steps implicitly align with energy landscapes by promoting consistent coordinate frames and narrowing feasible structure space as denoising progresses, before sequence design encodes the backbone into an energy-minimizing fold [3]. Finally, energy-based models and Hamiltonian-guided sampling connect score-based or flow-based generators to physical dynamics by steering denoising with forces or by matching stationary distributions conditioned on energy levels; these approaches motivate EBA’s feedback alignment between a generative denoiser and a physics/energy oracle to balance conformational states according to energy differences [25,26,1].

Benchmarks and evaluation for MD ensembles. Comparative evaluations increasingly emphasize ensemble-level metrics and MD statistics to assess generative models’ physical plausibility and applicability. CONFROVER evaluates on ATLAS, a large-scale MD dataset spanning diverse structures, demonstrating effectiveness in learning dynamics and supporting downstream tasks with both trajectory and structure sampling [25]. MarS-FM benchmarks structural observables (RMSD, radius of gyration, secondary structure) across protein domains including unfolding events and enforces sequence dissimilarity between train/test to test generalization, reporting superior performance over prior methods on these statistics [1]. ExEnDiff and IDPFold similarly emphasize ensemble diversity and adherence to experimentally guided or Boltzmann-like distributions, showing that integrating physical or experimental priors improves ensemble realism relative to models trained only on static PDB folds [2,26]. These benchmarks align with EBA’s evaluation on an MD ensemble benchmark, where energy-calibrated sampling improves high-quality ensemble generation and physical plausibility [3].

Positioning EBA. Existing diffusion-based generators and MD-informed emulators establish strong baselines for protein structure and ensemble sampling, but systematic calibration of samples by physical energy differences remains underexplored. EBA addresses this gap by aligning a generative model with feedback from a physics/energy model to balance conformational states according to energy differences, effectively translating thermodynamic priors into learnable guidance for denoising steps. This bridges the gap between sequence/structure diffusion models and energy-weighted thermodynamic sampling, improving ensemble quality on MD ensemble benchmarks without sacrificing sampling efficiency [3,25,26,1]. By contrast, prior methods either rely primarily on static structural priors [26], integrate experiments post hoc [2], or learn dynamics via MSM discretization rather than energy-calibrated feedback alignment [1,25]. EBA complements these lines by providing a general mechanism to incorporate energy supervision into generative denoising, enhancing physical plausibility and downstream utility in structural biology and drug discovery [3,25].

 4. Reference 25: Simultaneous Modeling of Protein Conformation and Dynamics via Autoregression. arXiv (2025).
 5. Reference 26: Precise Generation of Conformational Ensembles for Intrinsically Disordered Proteins via Fine-tuned Diffusion Models. bioRxiv (2024/2025).

Protein dynamics play a crucial role in protein biological functions and
properties, and their traditional study typically relies on time-consuming
molecular dynamics (MD) simulations conducted in silico. Recent advances in
generative modeling, particularly denoising diffusion models, have enabled
efficient accurate protein structure prediction and conformation sampling by
learning distributions over crystallographic structures. However, effectively
integrating physical supervision into these data-driven approaches remains
challenging, as standard energy-based objectives often lead to intractable
optimization. In this paper, we introduce Energy-based Alignment (EBA), a
method that aligns generative models with feedback from physical models,
efficiently calibrating them to appropriately balance conformational states
based on their energy differences. Experimental results on the MD ensemble
benchmark demonstrate that EBA achieves state-of-the-art performance in
generating high-quality protein ensembles. By improving the physical
plausibility of generated structures, our approach enhances model predictions
and holds promise for applications in structural biology and drug discovery.

Fund allocation has been an increasingly important problem in the financial
domain. In reality, we aim to allocate the funds to buy certain assets within a
certain future period. Naive solutions such as prediction-only or
Predict-then-Optimize approaches suffer from goal mismatch. Additionally, the
introduction of the SOTA time series forecasting model inevitably introduces
additional uncertainty in the predicted result. To solve both problems
mentioned above, we introduce a Risk-aware Time-Series Predict-and-Allocate
(RTS-PnO) framework, which holds no prior assumption on the forecasting models.
Such a framework contains three features: (i) end-to-end training with
objective alignment measurement, (ii) adaptive forecasting uncertainty
calibration, and (iii) agnostic towards forecasting models. The evaluation of
RTS-PnO is conducted over both online and offline experiments. For offline
experiments, eight datasets from three categories of financial applications are
used: Currency, Stock, and Cryptos. RTS-PnO consistently outperforms other
competitive baselines. The online experiment is conducted on the Cross-Border
Payment business at FiT, Tencent, and an 8.4\% decrease in regret is witnessed
when compared with the product-line approach. The code for the offline
experiment is available at https://github.com/fuyuanlyu/RTS-PnO.

Problem Setting and Goal Misalignment. Distributionally Robust Integration of Forecast and Allocation. A prominent line of work integrates prediction and robust portfolio selection through distributionally robust optimization (DRO). End-to-end DRO portfolio construction couples an asset return predictor with a robust optimizer and learns risk tolerance and ambiguity parameters from data, explicitly quantifying and mitigating model risk via an ambiguity set centered on a nominal distribution [1]. Efficient training is achieved by reformulating the decision-layer minimax as a tractable convex program via convex duality. Extending this integration to side information, DRO formulations minimize worst-case conditional risk–return trade-offs within an optimal-transport ambiguity set; when paired with mean–variance or mean–CVaR criteria, the problem reduces to second-order or semidefinite programs, demonstrating empirical gains over non-robust baselines [2]. Predict-and-optimize frameworks address this by differentiating forecast uncertainty into ambiguity-driven risk and by training end-to-end to measure objective alignment, including adaptive calibration of predictive uncertainty before robust optimization [1]. Vision Transformers (ViTs) leverage the transformer architecture to
effectively capture global context, demonstrating strong performance in
computer vision tasks. A major challenge in ViT hardware acceleration is that
the model family contains complex arithmetic operations that are sensitive to
model accuracy, such as the Softmax and LayerNorm operations, which cannot be
mapped onto efficient hardware with low precision. Existing methods only
exploit parallelism in the matrix multiplication operations of the model on
hardware and keep these complex operations on the CPU. This results in
suboptimal performance due to the communication overhead between the CPU and
accelerator. Can new data formats solve this problem?
  In this work, we present the first ViT accelerator that maps all operations
of the ViT models onto FPGAs. We exploit a new arithmetic format named
Microscaling Integer (MXInt) for datapath designs and evaluate how different
design choices can be made to trade off accuracy, hardware performance, and
hardware utilization. Our contributions are twofold. First, we quantize ViTs
using the MXInt format, achieving both high area efficiency and accuracy.
Second, we propose MXInt-specific hardware optimization that map these complex
arithmetic operations into custom hardware. Within 1\% accuracy loss, our
method achieves at least 93$\times$ speedup compared to Float16 and at least
1.9$\times$ speedup compared to related work.
