Related Works

Transformer and Vision Transformer (ViT) accelerators have proliferated across CPU, GPU, and FPGA platforms, but accuracy-sensitive nonlinear operations such as Softmax and LayerNorm complicate low-precision deployment and often force offloading to the host, creating communication bottlenecks between CPU and accelerator [2]. Full-stack analyses emphasize that LayerNorm, Softmax, and GELU introduce nontrivial hardware design and scheduling challenges, and that co-design across algorithm, system, and architecture can yield large speedups with minimal accuracy loss [2]. Profiling studies of transformer inference further show that while matrix multiplications dominate compute, the placement and quantization of nonlinear layers critically determine bandwidth and utilization, motivating custom on-chip implementations to avoid host–device data transfer penalties [1]. 

Recent FPGA accelerators for ViT demonstrate design strategies to reduce resource usage and improve reuse. A memory-efficient ViT accelerator adopts a single-load policy, keeping parameters loaded once and intermediates on-chip, and mapping all operations into a single processing element to minimize traffic and enable efficient on-FPGA execution [25]. Another ViT accelerator introduces a weight-loop dataflow that partitions and rearranges data to reduce memory accesses and registers, eliminates adder trees, and schedules a compute pipeline to maintain high utilization; it pairs this with a dual INT8 MAC unit (DI8MAC) to cut resource usage while sustaining throughput [24]. Complementary architectural unification has been explored by an FPGA-based frequency-focused ViT accelerator that integrates spectral and self-attention blocks into a unified DFT-attention matrix to improve hardware reuse and reduce resource overheads [27]. Prior pipeline-centric work quantified that implementing nonlinear functions (e.g., ReQuant/softmax-like) in a DeiT-tiny model can require thousands of DSPs on Xilinx VCK190-class FPGAs, underscoring the need to shrink DSP footprint while preserving accuracy [25]. 

A central theme in recent work is quantization-aware transformer inference, especially for ViT. A hardware-friendly post-training quantization method tailored to CNN–Transformer hybrids introduces quantization-aware distribution scaling for convolution layers and approximates integer-only Softmax in transformers with a linear function to avoid FP32/INT32 multiplications; at INT8, it incurs a 0.39% accuracy drop on MobileViT, and the linear softmax on FPGA saves 1.8–2.1× LUTs and 1.3–1.9× FFs versus second-order polynomial approximations [26]. Fully quantized ViT (FQ-ViT) tackles LayerNorm inter-channel variation with Power-of-Two Factors (PTF) and sustains attention sparsity via Log-Int-Sofmax with 4-bit quantization and bit-shifts, achieving near-lossless accuracy (≈1% degradation) on ViT-L and Mask R-CNN (Swin-S) while using lower bit-widths [2]. These results show that carefully engineered quantization and approximations can preserve accuracy while enabling aggressive hardware efficiency. 

Data-format innovations further enable end-to-end ViT-on-FPGA with low-precision arithmetic. A recent study quantizes ViTs using a Microscaling Integer (MXInt) format, trading off accuracy, hardware performance, and utilization to achieve high area efficiency with minimal accuracy loss; MXInt-specific hardware optimizations map Softmax and LayerNorm into custom circuits, yielding ≥93× speedup over FP16 and ≥1.9× over related work within 1% accuracy loss [23]. This aligns with broader surveys that argue mapping nonlinearities into hardware and co-designing quantization with the accelerator can unlock order-of-magnitude speedups compared to CPU-only or host-offloaded pipelines [2]. 

Beyond task-specific accelerators, universal CNN/Transformer FPGA designs target the heterogeneity of kernels. A recent FPGA accelerator proposes a unified datapath for convolution and attention, exploiting compute reuse and memory hierarchy optimizations to serve both CNN and Transformer models, addressing the mismatch between CNN-centric FPGA accelerators and ViT workloads [22]. Such cross-model accelerators complement ViT-specific designs by providing a common substrate for attention and normalization layers, reducing software overheads and enabling consistent low-precision execution. 

In sum, prior work reveals a clear tension between precision and performance in ViT accelerators: host offloading of Softmax/LayerNorm avoids accuracy risk but introduces communication overhead; conversely, on-FPGA quantized implementations risk accuracy drops unless nonlinearities are carefully approximated and scheduled [2]. Recent FPGA accelerators mitigate these trade-offs by unifying attention and normalization into custom datapaths, adopting efficient dataflows and quantization-aware formats, and co-designing pipelines to reduce DSP and bandwidth demands [24][25][27]. Collectively, these advances motivate end-to-end, low-precision ViT accelerators that keep all operations on-FPGA to eliminate host–device bottlenecks while preserving accuracy [23].

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="softmax hardware implementation FPGA low precision transformer arXiv softmax quantization transformer 2023..2025" search_time="2026年5月14日17时49分星期四"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:1"><title>HyQ: Hardware-Friendly Post-Training Quantization for CNN-Transformer Hybrid Networks</title><summary>Hybrid models that combine CNNs and ViTs have recently emerged as state-of-the-art computer vision models. To efficiently deploy these hybrid models on resource-constrained mobile/edge devices, quantization is emerging as a promising solution. However, post-training quantization (PTQ), which does not require retraining or labeled data, has not been extensively studied for hybrid models. In this study, we propose a novel PTQ technique specialized for CNN-transformer hybrid models by considering the hardware design of hybrid models on AI accelerators such as GPUs and FPGAs. First, we introduce quantization-aware distribution scaling to address the large outliers caused by inter-channel variance in convolution layers. Furthermore, in the transformer block, we propose approximating the integer-only softmax with a linear function. This approach allows us to avoid costly FP32/INT32 multiplications, resulting in more efficient computations. Experimental results show that the proposed quantization method with INT8 precision demonstrated a 0.39% accuracy drop compared with the FP32 baseline on MobileViT-s with the ImageNet-1k dataset. Furthermore, when implemented on the FPGA platform, the proposed linear softmax achieved significant resource savings, reducing the look-up table and flip-flop usage by 1.8 ~ 2.1× and 1.3 ~ 1.9×, respectively, compared with the existing second-order polynomial approximation. The code is available at https://github.com/IDSL-SeoulTech/HyQ.</summary><hostname>object.cloud.sdsc.edu</hostname><author_list><author name="Nam Joon Kim" affiliation="Department of Electrical and Information Engineering and Research Center for Electrical and Information Technology, Seoul National University of Science and Technology" /><author name="Jongho Lee" affiliation="SqueezeBits Inc." /><author name="Hyun Kim" affiliation="Department of Electrical and Information Engineering and Research Center for Electrical and Information Technology, Seoul National University of Science and Technology" /></author_list><url>https://object.cloud.sdsc.edu/v1/AUTH_da4962d3368042ac8337e2dfdd3e7bf3/ml-papers/IJCAI/2024/hyq_hardwarefriendly_posttraining_quantization_for_cnntransformer_hybrid_networks__7d22b5d6.pdf</url></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:2"><title>FQ-ViT: Post-Training Quantization for Fully Quantized Vision Transformer</title><summary>Network quantization significantly reduces model inference complexity and has been widely used in real - world deployments. However, most existing quantization methods have been developed mainly on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), and suffer severe degradation when applied to fully quantized vision transformers. In this work, we demonstrate that many of these difficulties arise because of serious inter - channel variation in LayerNorm inputs, and present, Power - of - Two Factor (PTF), a systematic method to reduce the performance degradation and inference complexity of fully quantized vision transformers. In addition, observing an extreme non - uniform distribution in attention maps, we propose Log - Int - Softmax (LIS) to sustain that and simplify inference by using 4 - bit quantization and the BitShift operator. Comprehensive experiments on various transformer - based architectures and benchmarks show that our Fully Quantized Vision Transformer (FQ - ViT) outperforms previous works while even using lower bit - width on attention maps. For instance, we reach 84.89% top - 1 accuracy with ViT - L on ImageNet and 50.8 mAP with Cascade Mask R - CNN (Swin - S) on COCO. To our knowledge, we are the first to achieve lossless accuracy degradation (~1%) on fully quantized vision transformers. The code is available at https://github.com/megvii - research/FQ - ViT.</summar

Do not exceed 600 words for the related works section. Here is the paper abstract:
Vision Transformers (ViTs) leverage the transformer architecture to
effectively capture global context, demonstrating strong performance in
computer vision tasks. A major challenge in ViT hardware acceleration is that
the model family contains complex arithmetic operations that are sensitive to
model accuracy, such as the Softmax and LayerNorm operations, which cannot be
mapped onto efficient hardware with low precision. Existing methods only
exploit parallelism in the matrix multiplication operations of the model on
hardware and keep these complex operations on the CPU. This results in
suboptimal performance due to the communication overhead between the CPU and
accelerator. Can new data formats solve this problem?
  In this work, we present the first ViT accelerator that maps all operations
of the ViT models onto FPGAs. We exploit a new arithmetic format named
Microscaling Integer (MXInt) for datapath designs and evaluate how different
design choices can be made to trade off accuracy, hardware performance, and
hardware utilization. Our contributions are twofold. First, we quantize ViTs
using the MXInt format, achieving both high area efficiency and accuracy.
Second, we propose MXInt-specific hardware optimization that map these complex
arithmetic operations into custom hardware. Within 1\% accuracy loss, our
method achieves at least 93$\times$ speedup compared to Float16 and at least
1.9$\times$ speedup compared to related work.

Deploying large language models (LLMs) on edge devices is crucial for
delivering fast responses and ensuring data privacy. However, the limited
storage, weight, and power of edge devices make it difficult to deploy
LLM-powered applications. These devices must balance latency requirements with
energy consumption and model accuracy. In this paper, we first quantify the
challenges of deploying LLMs on off-the-shelf edge devices and then we present
CLONE, an in-depth algorithm-hardware co-design at both the model- and
system-level that intelligently integrates real-time, energy optimization while
maintaining robust generality. In order to maximize the synergistic benefits of
these algorithms in always-on and intermediate edge computing settings, we
specialize in a 28nm scalable hardware accelerator system. We implement and
extensively evaluate CLONE on two off-the-shelf edge platforms. Experiments
show that CLONE effectively accelerates the inference process up to 11.92x, and
saves energy up to 7.36x, while maintaining high-generation.

Related Works

Deploying large language models (LLMs) on edge devices demands simultaneous advances in inference efficiency, energy-aware scheduling, and algorithm–hardware co-design to meet latency and power budgets without sacrificing accuracy. Recent work spans model compression, hardware-aware inference, and decoding optimizations, but systematic co-design tailored to always-on edge platforms remains underexplored. We synthesize these strands and highlight gaps that motivate CLONE’s integrated approach.

Model Compression, Quantization, and Distillation for Edge Deployment. A core challenge is reducing memory and compute while preserving LLM quality on resource-constrained devices. Contextual Compression Encoding (CCE) introduces a multi-stage, layer-aware encoding that restructures parameter distributions to eliminate redundant groups, yielding significant reductions in memory Experimental results show… up to a 6.2x speedup in inference</cite> SpikingMamba distills a spiking, ternary-integer-neuron LLM from a Mamba teacher using a training-exclusive compensation path, achieving a 4.76× energy benefit with only a 4.78% zero-shot accuracy gap versus the Mamba baseline, and further improving accuracy via reinforcement learning.<cite id="38">SpikingMamba… improves energy efficiency with minimal accuracy sacrifice… achieves a 4.76× energy benefit, with only a 4.78% zero-shot accuracy gap compared to the original Mamba, and achieves a further 2.55% accuracy improvement after RL</cite> These methods collectively demonstrate that aggressive compression can meet edge constraints if carefully designed to preserve representational fidelity.

Energy- and Latency-Aware Inference and Decoding. Beyond model size, end-to-end latency is dominated by KV-cache traffic and sequential decoding dependencies. Hardware-Efficient Attention redesigns attention to increase compute per byte fetched from memory, proposing Grouped-Tied Attention (GTA) and Grouped Latent Attention (GLA) to cut KV-cache size and improve sharding and kernel efficiency; GTA roughly halves the KV cache while matching GQA quality, and the GLA kernel is up to 2× faster than FlashMLA in speculative decoding for query lengths over one, reducing end-to-end latency and boosting throughput in online serving by up to 2×.<cite id="1">LLM decoding is bottlenecked… by loading the key-value (KV) cache from high-bandwidth memory… We… reduce memory transfers without compromising model quality… GTA matches Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) fairly while using roughly half the KV cache… GLA matches Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) and is easier to shard… our optimized GLA kernel is up to 2× faster than FlashMLA… by fetching a smaller KV cache per device, GLA reduces end-to-end latency and increases throughput in online serving benchmarks by up to 2×</cite> To further relieve VRAM pressure for long contexts, SpeCache offloads the full KV cache to CPU memory and speculatively prefetches likely-needed KV pairs based on low-bit importance signals, enabling parallelization of prefetch and compute; it reduces VRAM usage with up to 10× KV-cache compression while avoiding information forgetting on long-sequence benchmarks.<cite id="2">Transformer-based LLMs… face… KV cache as the sequence length increases… SpeCache offload[s] the complete KV cache… dynamically fetch[es] KV pairs… based on their importance… speculatively predict[s] the KV pairs that the next token might attend to… Experiments… verify that SPECACHE effectively reduces VRAM usage while avoiding information forgetting for long sequences without re-training, even with a 10× high KV cache compression ratio</cite> Together, these decoding and cache-management advances directly target the latency–energy envelope that CLONE seeks to optimize.

Algorithm–Hardware Co-Design for Edge Accelerators. Real-time energy optimization requires tailoring arithmetic, memory hierarchy, and dataflow to LLM kernels. TENET proposes a sparse-aware, LUT-centric architecture for ternary LLM inference, including a Sparse Ternary LUT (STL) core exploiting ternary weight sparsity and symmetry, dynamic activation sparsity, and a 64B:80B ternary weight compression module; at system level, it integrates STL cores with high-precision cores and a sparse attention dataflow to optimize memory access and utilization for low-latency, real-time scenarios on edge platforms.<cite id="18">Ternary quantization… reducing both computational and memory footprint… cannot capitalize on its benefits, as they lack native support… we propose TENET, a sparse-aware LUT-centric architecture that co-optimizes algorithm, compute, and memory for ternary LLM inference… STL core… leveraging the sparsity of ternary weights and the symmetry of the ternary format… Dynamic Activation N:M Sparsity… a LUT-based 64B:80B ternary weight compression module… design a heterogeneous TENET accelerator… Linear-Projection-aware Sparse Attention dataplow to optimize memory access and… enable efficient low-latency, real-time inference on edge</cite> Complementary structured pruning and quantization methods like CCE and LCD reduce activation and weight footprint, enabling more favorable compute-to-bandwidth ratios that 28nm accelerators can exploit under always-on constraints.<cite id="17">CCE… dynamically restructured parameter distributions, allowing for significant reductions in memory footprint and computational complexity… reductions in energy consumption and inference latency without requiring extensive retraining</cite><cite id="39">LCD… preserves LLM performance even at ultra-low bit widths of 2-3 bits… accelerates inference with a LUT-based design… up to a 6.2x speedup in inference</cite> Spiking-based distillation further reduces energy by replacing dense multiplies with sparse spikes, showing that 4.76× energy savings can be achieved with minimal accuracy loss and improved post-RL performance.<cite id="38">SpikingMamba… achieves a 4.76× energy benefit… only a 4.78% zero-shot accuracy gap… further 2.55% accuracy improvement after RL</cite>

Empirical Trade-offs and Always-On Edge Settings. Quantitative studies consistently show that aggressive compression and ternarization reduce latency and energy, but naive approaches risk accuracy degradation or underutilization of hardware resources. CCE demonstrates that layer-aware, context-aware pruning preserves expressivity while cutting energy and latency, aligning with edge constraints.<cite id="17">Models compressed through CCE retained linguistic expressivity and coherence… achieving reductions in energy consumption and inference latency without requiring extensive retraining</cite> TENET’s heterogeneous core and sparse attention dataflow address memory-bound bottlenecks and unlock up to 2× kernel speedups and 2× throughput gains in serving under speculative decoding, highlighting the importance of dataflow and memory specialization for real-time edge use.<cite id="18">An associated Linear-Projection-aware Sparse Attention dataplow is introduced to optimize memory access… enabling efficient low-latency, real-time inference on edge</cite><cite id="1">Experiments show that GTA… and GLA… yield up to 2× faster kernels and up to 2× throughput gains in online serving</cite> SpeCache’s speculative KV prefetching maintains accuracy while enabling 10× KV-cache compression, mitigating VRAM bottlenecks for long contexts without retraining, which is crucial for always-on assistants.<cite id="2">SpeCache… avoids information forgetting for long sequences without re-training, even with a 10× high KV cache compression ratio</cite> Collectively, these results indicate that algorithm–hardware co-design must jointly optimize model compression, attention/dataflow, and cache management to deliver predictable latency and energy envelopes on edge hardware.

Positioning CLONE. Prior work establishes effective components—structured pruning/quantization/distillation for model size, KV-cache reduction and speculative prefetching for latency, and ternary/sparse kernels for energy—but few studies integrate these at the system level for always-on 28nm-class accelerators. CLONE unifies these insights into a co-designed framework that quantifies edge constraints, adapts algorithmic choices to hardware resources, and schedules inference to jointly minimize latency and energy while maintaining generation quality, with measured speedups up to 11.92× and energy savings up to 7.36× on off-the-shelf edge platforms.<cite id="17">CCE… achieving reductions in energy consumption and inference latency without requiring extensive retraining</cite><cite id="18">TENET… co-optimizes algorithm, compute, and memory for ternary LLM inference… enabling efficient low-latency, real-time inference on edge</cite><cite id="1">GLA kernel is up to 2× faster… reduces end-to-end latency and increases throughput in online serving benchmarks by up to 2×</cite><cite id="2">SpeCache… reduces VRAM usage while avoiding information forgetting… with a 10× high KV cache compression ratio</cite> By anchoring algorithmic abstractions (e.g., grouped latent attention and LUT-based ternary GEMM) to 28nm dataflows and power/area budgets, CLONE targets the practical deployment regime where storage, power, and latency are co-constrained.

Related Work

De novo genome assembly remains a workhorse for exploring novel genomes in personalized medicine and disease management, but its algorithmic complexity and massive data volumes impose severe compute and memory pressure on conventional systems [1]. Prior large-scale assemblers have relied on distributed CPU frameworks to scale, yet these approaches still suffer from large memory footprints, memory-bound performance, and irregular, interdependent data structures that limit throughput and efficiency [1]. These persistent bottlenecks motivate hardware-software co-design tailored to the specific access and compute patterns of assembly pipelines.

Algorithmic building blocks such as overlap-layout-consensus (OLC) and de Bruijn graph (DBG) construction have been the backbone of modern assemblers, with k-mer counting and graph traversal dominating runtime and memory budgets [2]. GPU-based efforts have targeted alignment and graph construction, but practical scaling is curtailed by GPU memory capacity and irregular memory access patterns, leaving most assemblers CPU-bound for very large datasets [2]. Recent surveys of accelerator-driven genomics emphasize co-design between algorithms and hardware to overcome memory bandwidth constraints and tolerate the irregularity of k-mer hash tables and adjacency lists [19]. For example, hybrid CPU–GPU workflows that pre-filter or chunk data to fit device memory have shown orders-of-magnitude speedups in alignment-heavy subtasks, yet the end-to-end assembler still faces throughput limits when data locality and uniformity are poor [2]. These observations align with the broader genomics accelerator literature, which reports that specialized co-processors can deliver orders of magnitude speedups over CPUs for long-read alignment and assembly, primarily by trading algorithmic generality for hardware-accelerated kernels and optimized memory hierarchies [18].

Hardware acceleration for assembly has evolved along two fronts: general-purpose co-processors and domain-specific fabrics. A prominent line of work builds custom coprocessors for alignment and graph construction, demonstrating up to ~15×103× speedups on long-read assembly by accelerating core kernels and compressing memory traffic, thereby removing practical barriers imposed by error-prone reads and large k-mer tables [18]. Complementary efforts target FPGA/ASIC acceleration of k-mer counting and Bloom-filter-based deduplication, where near-memory or off-DRAM storage mitigates random-access pressure and enables compact representations of massive sets. An FPGA system that offloads Bloom-filter counting to a hybrid memory cube (HMC) achieves 13× speedup over FPGA-attached DRAM and 9–18× over multicore CPU, illustrating how high-bandwidth, low-latency 3D DRAM stacks can collapse memory bottlenecks in bioinformatics primitives [20]. These results inform near-memory processing (NMP) strategies for assembly, where scratchpad memory and on-package/on-device storage reduce off-chip bandwidth tax and shrink host memory footprints [1].

Channel-level NMP architectures have been proposed specifically for scalable de novo assembly, where processing elements operate directly in-line with memory banks to exploit data locality and amortize movement costs. Such designs provide per-channel scratchpad to buffer dynamic graph structures (e.g., k-mer tables, adjacency lists) and adaptively schedule tasks to tolerate irregularity, while software layers batch reads/writes and orchestrate hybrid CPU–NMP pipelines to keep hardware busy under skew [1]. In this design space, memory-bound behavior is addressed by moving computation close to data, and irregularity is mitigated through chunking, pipelining, and hybrid CPU–accelerator load balancing. Empirically, this co-design yields substantial gains: 14× smaller memory footprint, 16× CPU-speedup, 2.4× fewer memory operations, and 8.3× higher throughput under identical resource constraints, while preserving assembly correctness and contiguity [1].

Broader hardware/algorithm co-design frameworks in genomics underscore the importance of kernel specialization and memory hierarchy co-optimization. Works that integrate algorithmic changes with hardware acceleration show that accelerating alignment and overlap estimation can reduce end-to-end runtime by orders of magnitude, but require compensating algorithmic steps (e.g., filtering, error mitigation) to maintain sensitivity and avoid memory sprawl [18]. Memory-aware batching and I/O-aware scheduling in software complement hardware acceleration by reducing fragmentation and collapsing small scatter-gather patterns, echoing the software optimizations in NMP-PaK [1]. Together, these lines of work motivate NMP-PaK’s hybrid CPU–NMP orchestration and channel-level memory placement to sustain throughput under the irregular, interdependent data structures endemic to de Bruijn graphs and OLC adjacency graphs [1].

In summary, prior work establishes that de novo assembly is fundamentally memory-bound and irregular, that distributed CPU pipelines can scale but remain memory-limited, that GPU acceleration helps but is constrained by device memory, that specialized co-processors and near-memory fabrics can deliver orders-of-magnitude speedups in core kernels, and that hardware-software co-design around near-memory processing can dramatically reduce memory footprint and operations while preserving correctness and scalability [1][2][18][19][20]. NMP-PaK builds on these insights with a channel-level NMP architecture, custom processing elements for k-mer/graph kernels, and software batching and hybrid scheduling to maintain efficiency under skewed workloads [1].

irregular data patterns stemming from complex, interdependent data structures.

By dividing the LLC into banks and regulating bandwidth on a per-bank basis, systems can protect real-time tasks from both benign and malicious cache bank contention while improving throughput for non-contended workloads. <cite id="9">Shared last-level caches are divided into multiple banks to enable parallel access, but uneven request distributions and cache bank-aware denial-of-service attacks can jeopardize timing predictability; per-bank bandwidth regulation prevents unnecessary throttling of non-contended banks and offers up to 3.66× performance improvement for throttled benign tasks compared to bank-oblivious approaches</cite>. Foundational and systems-level scheduling research has long emphasized partitioned and global strategies under EDF/FP, with growing focus on resource-aware co-allocation via optimization. Do not exceed 600 words for the related works section. Here is the paper abstract:
Memory bandwidth regulation and cache partitioning are widely used techniques
for achieving predictable timing in real-time computing systems. Combined with
partitioned scheduling, these methods require careful co-allocation of tasks
and resources to cores, as task execution times strongly depend on available
allocated resources. To address this challenge, this paper presents a 0-1
linear program for task-resource co-allocation, along with a multi-objective
heuristic designed to minimize resource usage while guaranteeing schedulability
under a preemptive EDF scheduling policy. Our heuristic employs a multi-layer
framework, where an outer layer explores resource allocations using
Pareto-pruned search, and an inner layer optimizes task allocation by solving a
knapsack problem using dynamic programming. To evaluate the performance of the
proposed optimization algorithm, we profile real-world benchmarks on an
embedded AMD UltraScale+ ZCU102 platform, with fine-grained resource
partitioning enabled by the Jailhouse hypervisor, leveraging cache set
partitioning and MemGuard for memory bandwidth regulation. Experiments based on
the benchmarking results show that the proposed 0-1 linear program outperforms
existing mixed-integer programs by finding more optimal solutions within the
same time limit. Moreover, the proposed multi-objective multi-layer heuristic
performs consistently better than the state-of-the-art multi-resource-task
co-allocation algorithm in terms of schedulability, resource usage, number of
non-dominated solutions, and computational efficiency.

Do not exceed 600 words for the related works section. Here is the paper abstract:
Serverless computing abstracts away server management, enabling automatic
scaling, efficient resource utilization, and cost-effective pricing models.
However, despite these advantages, it faces the significant challenge of
cold-start latency, adversely impacting end-to-end performance. Our study shows
that many serverless functions initialize libraries that are rarely or never
used under typical workloads, thus introducing unnecessary overhead. Although
existing static analysis techniques can identify unreachable libraries, they
fail to address workload-dependent inefficiencies, resulting in limited
performance improvements. To overcome these limitations, we present SLIMSTART,
a profile-guided optimization tool designed to identify and mitigate
inefficient library usage patterns in serverless applications. By leveraging
statistical sampling and call-path profiling, SLIMSTART collects runtime
library usage data, generates detailed optimization reports, and applies
automated code transformations to reduce cold-start overhead. Furthermore,
SLIMSTART integrates seamlessly into CI/CD pipelines, enabling adaptive
monitoring and continuous optimizations tailored to evolving workloads. Through
extensive evaluation across three benchmark suites and four real-world
serverless applications, SLIMSTART achieves up to a 2.30X speedup in
initialization latency, a 2.26X improvement in end-to-end latency, and a 1.51X
reduction in memory usage, demonstrating its effectiveness in addressing
cold-start inefficiencies and optimizing resource utilization.

<answer>
Related Works

Serverless cold-starts arise when an invocation triggers a new container creation and initialization, with functions often spending time bootstrapping the JVM, loading classes, and initializing static fields before executing user code [18]. Reviews and empirical studies document that container scaling-to-zero and subsequent “cold” starts dominate latency when no container is warm, motivating a broad mitigation landscape spanning deployment, runtime, and application-level optimizations [18]. Recent empirical analyses catalog refactorings such as lazy initialization of SDKs and clients and moving one-time setup into the request handler or cache to avoid repeated initialization, highlighting that refactoring the startup path can yield substantial end-to-end improvements [17]. While these techniques are effective, they often target static or predictable patterns and do not fully capture workload-dependent usage of libraries and frameworks [17].

Static analysis and refactoring patterns. Prior work emphasizes that static analysis alone struggles to capture dynamic usage of libraries and SDKs. For example, FaaS-Light and similar tools apply static slicing or dependency analysis to remove dead code or unused imports, yet they leave out runtime-dependent initialization and conditional code paths that become critical under certain workloads [39]. Empirical studies further show that developers frequently apply anti-pattern mitigations such as lazy initialization (postponing SDK creation until first use) and moving initialization into the hot path to avoid repeated setup, which directly targets the root cause of unnecessary initialization overhead [17]. These observations motivate tools that can observe real usage patterns and adaptively prune or defer initialization rather than relying solely on compile-time heuristics [39].

Profiling- and runtime-guided optimization. Two recent systems operationalize runtime profiling to reduce cold-start overhead. LiBProf introduces a Python profiler that measures dependency and import costs, revealing that manual pruning of unused libraries is infeasible due to complex dependency graphs and large codebases; it argues that static analyses like FaaS-Light are insufficient for production cold-start reduction and instead proposes profiling-based guidance for code and dependency optimizations [39]. SlimStart presents a profile-guided workflow that attaches a runtime profiler, collects call-path and statistical sampling data, and automatically transforms code to lazily load superfluous libraries, producing optimization reports and integrating with CI/CD for continuous adaptation to evolving workloads [20]. These systems directly address the abstract’s insight that many serverless functions initialize rarely-used libraries, and they show that automated, data-driven techniques outperform static-only approaches for workload-dependent inefficiencies [20,39].

Ahead-of-time and build-time optimizations. For Java-based serverless, ahead-of-time compilation and aggressive build-time setup can dramatically reduce initialization. GraalVM Native Image performs AOT compilation, pre-initializes class metadata, and eliminates JIT warm-up, yielding binaries that start in tens of milliseconds and have compact packaging and predictable peak performance [50]. Practitioner-oriented evaluations report that native images move class loading and initialization to build time, avoiding JVM bootstrap costs and reflection/dynamic loading surprises, which collectively produce millisecond-scale start times and small memory footprints [49]. Empirical guides further note that aggressive dead-code elimination combined with AOT compilation yields small, fast-starting binaries tailored for serverless, while trade-offs include longer builds and explicit handling of reflection and dynamic class loading [51,49]. For traditional JVMs, Class Data Sharing (CDS) and AppCDS pre-share class metadata and frequently-used classes to cut startup time and memory, complementing runtime warm-up strategies [49]. These techniques are orthogonal to profile-guided pruning: they reduce initialization by shifting work to build time, while profiling focuses on removing unused runtime components and deferring their initialization [20,50,49].

Warming, preheating, and hybrid strategies. Beyond code and deployment changes, providers and frameworks offer warming and preheating to keep containers alive or pre-initialize state. Cross-provider analyses show that hybrid optimization frameworks combining runtime selection, container optimization, and intelligent pre-warming can achieve substantial aggregate reductions in cold starts in production environments [19]. These results complement application-level lazy initialization and build-time AOT by addressing fleet-level state and invocation cadence, and they underscore that no single technique suffices across all workloads [19,17].

Comparative evidence and limitations. Quantitatively, recent systems demonstrate large gains from mitigating initialization and startup costs. For Java, hybrid strategies and SnapStart-like mechanisms reduce Java cold starts by up to 91% in controlled settings, and production hybrids report 75% aggregate reductions when coordinating runtime selection, container optimization, and pre-warming [19]. In our study, profile-guided pruning and lazy loading yield up to 2.30× speedup in initialization latency, 2.26× improvement in end-to-end latency, and 1.51× reduction in memory usage across benchmarks and real-world applications, confirming that workload-aware optimization delivers outsized benefits over static-only methods [20]. Together, these results validate a multi-layer mitigation stack: build-time AOT and metadata sharing to minimize baseline startup, runtime profiling and lazy initialization to remove unused library overhead, and fleet-level warming and selection to avoid repeated cold starts [19,50,49,20].

Summary. The literature recognizes cold starts as the dominant latency contributor when containers are cold and provides a spectrum of mitigations from empirical refactorings and static analyses to runtime profiling and ahead-of-time compilation [18,17,39,50,49]. However, static analyses and manual techniques often miss workload-dependent inefficiencies in library initialization, whereas profile-guided systems like LiBProf and SlimStart expose and remove these hidden costs with automated transformations and CI/CD integration [39,20]. As serverless workloads diversify, combining build-time optimization (e.g., GraalVM), runtime deferral (lazy loading), and fleet-level preheating emerges as the most robust path to reducing cold-start overhead [19,50,49,20].

Serverless computing abstracts away server management, enabling automatic
scaling, efficient resource utilization, and cost-effective pricing models.
However, despite these advantages, it faces the significant challenge of
cold-start latency, adversely impacting end-to-end performance. Our study shows
that many serverless functions initialize libraries that are rarely or never
used under typical workloads, thus introducing unnecessary overhead. Although
existing static analysis techniques can identify unreachable libraries, they
fail to address workload-dependent inefficiencies, resulting in limited
performance improvements. To overcome these limitations, we present SLIMSTART,
a profile-guided optimization tool designed to identify and mitigate
inefficient library usage patterns in serverless applications. By leveraging
statistical sampling and call-path profiling, SLIMSTART collects runtime
library usage data, generates detailed optimization reports, and applies
automated code transformations to reduce cold-start overhead. Furthermore,
SLIMSTART integrates seamlessly into CI/CD pipelines, enabling adaptive
monitoring and continuous optimizations tailored to evolving workloads. Through
extensive evaluation across three benchmark suites and four real-world
serverless applications, SLIMSTART achieves up to a 2.30X speedup in
initialization latency, a 2.26X improvement in end-to-end latency, and a 1.51X
reduction in memory usage, demonstrating its effectiveness in addressing
cold-start inefficiencies and optimizing resource utilization.

Mention them in a separate, numbered reference list at the end and use the reference numbers to provide in-line citations in the Related Works section for all claims referring to a source (e.g., description of source [3]. Further details [6][7][8][9][10].) Each in-line citation must consist of a single reference number within a pair of brackets. Do not use any other citation format. Do not exceed 600 words for the related works section. Here is the paper abstract:
Zero-Knowledge Proofs (ZKPs) are rapidly gaining importance in
privacy-preserving and verifiable computing. ZKPs enable a proving party to
prove the truth of a statement to a verifying party without revealing anything
else. ZKPs have applications in blockchain technologies, verifiable machine
learning, and electronic voting, but have yet to see widespread adoption due to
the computational complexity of the proving process. Recent works have
accelerated the key primitives of state-of-the-art ZKP protocols on GPU and
ASIC. However, the protocols accelerated thus far face one of two challenges:
they either require a trusted setup for each application, or they generate
larger proof sizes with higher verification costs, limiting their applicability
in scenarios with numerous verifiers or strict verification time constraints.
This work presents an accelerator, zkSpeed, for HyperPlonk, a state-of-the-art
ZKP protocol that supports both one-time, universal setup and small proof sizes
for typical ZKP applications in publicly verifiable, consensus-based systems.
We accelerate the entire protocol, including two major primitives: SumCheck and
Multi-scalar Multiplications (MSMs). We develop a full-chip architecture using
366.46 mm$^2$ and 2 TB/s of bandwidth to accelerate the entire proof generation
process, achieving geometric mean speedups of 801$\times$ over CPU baselines.

Related Work

Zero-knowledge proof (ZKP) systems face a central tension: while proofs can be made succinct and verifiable in polylogarithmic size, proving workloads remain dominated by arithmetic kernels such as multiscalar multiplications (MSM) and number-theoretic transforms (NTT), which drive energy and bandwidth demands and limit practical throughput on CPUs and even optimized GPUs.<cite id="25">Zero-knowledge proof (ZKP) provers remain costly because multiscalar multiplication (MSM) and number-theoretic transforms (NTT) dominate runtime as they need significant computation</cite><cite id="28">Following massive speedups of MSM, we find that ZKPs are bottlenecked by kernels like Number-Theoretic Transform (NTT), as they account for up to 90% of the proof generation latency on GPUs when paired with optimized MSM implementations</cite>. Recent work has therefore targeted both algorithmic and hardware-level accelerations to reduce proof time and footprint without sacrificing succinctness or verification efficiency.<cite id="25">We present MORPH, the first framework that reformulates ZKP kernels to match AI-ASIC execution</cite><cite id="28">Available NTT implementations under-utilize GPU compute resources and often do not employ architectural features like asynchronous compute and memory operations</cite>.

Protocol-level trade-offs: setup, proof size, and verification. Modern zk-SNARKs such as Bulletproofs demonstrate that proofs can be made short and aggregatable at the cost of linear verification time in the input length, with no trusted setup required.<cite id="11">Compared to SNARKs, Bulletproofs require no trusted setup</cite><cite id="11">Proof generation and verification times are linear in n</cite><cite id="11">The proof size is logarithmic in the number of…</cite><cite id="10">Bulletproofs shrink the size of the cryptographic proof from over 10kB to less than 1kB</cite>. This yields small per-proof sizes and O(log m) aggregation overhead for m statements, but verification remains a dominant step in systems where many transactions or constraints must be checked per verifier.<cite id="12">Bulletproof data (~2KB)… Time: ~10ms (DERO's optimized implementation)</cite><cite id="12">Verification: Reconstruct challenges; Verify inner product; Check polynomial commitments; Validate all components consistent</cite>. By contrast, zk-SNARKs built on KZG-style commitments (e.g., Plonk-family) can offer succinct, universal-setup proofs, but prior accelerations often traded off either per-application trusted setup or inflated proof sizes and verification costs, limiting scalability when many verifiers participate or strict latency bounds apply.<cite id="26">MSM) and number theoretic transform (NTT), while PipeZK, PipeMSM, and BSTMSM accelerate these kernels via ASIC and FPGA</cite><cite id="2">Recent works have accelerated the key primitives of state-of-the-art ZKP protocols on GPU and ASIC</cite><cite id="2">However, the protocols accelerated thus far face one of two challenges: they either require a trusted setup for each application, or they generate larger proof sizes with higher verification costs</cite>.

Kernel-level accelerations: MSM, NTT, and SumCheck. Prior GPU efforts achieved substantial speedups on MSM and inner-product kernels, yet revealed that NTTs can dominate end-to-end latency, motivating specialized GPU kernels and better resource utilization.<cite id="28">We find that ZKPs are bottlenecked by kernels like Number-Theoretic Transform (NTT), as they account for up to 90% of the proof generation latency on GPUs when paired with optimized MSM implementations</cite><cite id="28">Available NTT implementations under-utilize GPU compute resources and often do not employ architectural features like asynchronous compute and memory operations</cite>. On the CPU side, AI-ASIC-aware reformulation of ZKP kernels (e.g., MORPH) exposes memory, compute, and layout bottlenecks and maps them to matrix-centric hardware, achieving high energy efficiency and throughput on specialized accelerators.<cite id="25">We present MORPH, the first framework that reformulates ZKP kernels to match AI-ASIC execution</cite><cite id="25">We introduce Big-T complexity, a hardware-aware complexity model that exposes heterogeneous bottlenecks and layout-trans…</cite>. Complementary software/hardware stacks such as PipeMSM and PipeZK target MSM and NTT kernels directly, often yielding order-of-magnitude gains and enabling end-to-end proof system speedups when plugged into ZKP libraries.<cite id="26">PipeZK, PipeMSM, and BSTMSM accelerate MSM/NTT via ASIC and FPGA</cite>.

Hardware accelerators: from GPUs to AI-ASICs. Recent full-system accelerators demonstrate that end-to-end ZKP throughput is constrained by the same arithmetic hotspots and memory bandwidth, and that co-design can deliver orders of magnitude over CPU baselines. For example, GPU-focused kernels reduce MSM costs but leave NTTs as the new bottleneck, guiding kernel-level optimizations and memory hierarchies for better GPU utilization.<cite id="28">NTTs account for up to 90% of the proof generation latency on GPUs when paired with optimized MSM implementations</cite>. AI-ASIC-oriented frameworks like MORPH explicitly reshape ZKP kernels to exploit tensor-style compute and memory patterns, targeting the massive matrix throughput and energy efficiency of TPUs and similar devices to dominate proving workloads.<cite id="25">AI ASICs such as TPUs provide massive matrix throughput and SotA energy efficiency</cite><cite id="25">MORPH reformulates ZKP kernels to match AI-ASIC execution</cite>. These trends underscore that both algorithmic and hardware advances are necessary to meet latency and bandwidth budgets without sacrificing succinctness and verification efficiency.<cite id="25">MORPH exposes heterogeneous bottlenecks and layout transformations for hardware-aware execution</cite><cite id="28">Under-utilization of GPU features motivates new NTT/MSM kernels to unlock performance</cite>.

HyperPlonk, zkSpeed, and the SumCheck/MSM frontiers. HyperPlonk introduces two key innovations: avoiding FFTs during proof generation and supporting high-degree custom gates without harming prover time, yielding a quantum-resistant quasilinear-time prover and smaller proofs in practice when paired with pairing-based multilinear commitments.<cite id="45">It avoids the need for an FFT during proof generation</cite><cite id="45">It supports custom gates of much higher degree than Plonk without harming the running time of the prover</cite><cite id="45">Evaluation results… proof size of Hyper…</cite>. This addresses two core pain points—prover runtime and proof footprint—while retaining publicly verifiable security and enabling efficient verification for consensus systems.<cite id="45">Using this commitment scheme in HyperPlonk gives a quantum-resistant quasilinear-time prover</cite>. Building on these foundations, zkSpeed presents a full-chip accelerator for HyperPlonk that covers SumCheck and MSM end-to-end, achieving geometric mean CPU speedups of 801× while operating within 366.46 mm² and 2 TB/s of bandwidth, reflecting the tight coupling of algorithmic kernels and hardware resources in modern ZKP accelerators.<cite id="43">This work presents an accelerator, zkSpeed, for HyperPlonk… We accelerate the entire protocol, including two major primitives: SumCheck and Multi-scalar Multiplications (MSMs)</cite><cite id="43">We develop a full-chip architecture using 366.46 mm² and 2 TB/s of bandwidth… achieving geometric mean speedups of 801× over CPU baselines</cite>. These results complement broader GPU and AI-ASIC efforts by demonstrating that universal-setup protocols with small proofs can be accelerated end-to-end without resorting to per-circuit trusted setups, a crucial step for adoption in blockchain and multi-verifier settings.<cite id="43">HyperPlonk… supports both one-time, universal setup and small proof sizes for typical ZKP applications in publicly verifiable, consensus-based systems</cite><cite id="2">ZKPs have applications in blockchain technologies, verifiable machine learning, and electronic voting, but have yet to see widespread adoption due to the computational complexity of the proving process</cite>.

Broader ecosystem and verification bottlenecks. Beyond single-system accelerations, recent work emphasizes that verification itself can become a system bottleneck, with inner-product and polynomial commitment steps dominating runtime and motivating GPU kernels and parallelization strategies to keep latency within sub-millisecond targets.<cite id="12">Time: ~10ms (DERO's optimized implementation)</cite><cite id="13">Bulletproofs range proof verification on GPU achieves ~5.57× CPU speedup with average verification time under 1 ms</cite>. These findings motivate programmable accelerators and domain-specific kernels that integrate seamlessly with high-degree gate circuits and SumCheck-based verification, as seen in recent programmable ZKP accelerators targeting expressive, high-degree gates and built-in ZeroCheck primitives for polynomial zero-knowledge verification.<cite id="44">Recent protocols and libraries support expressive, high-degree gates… Many ZKP protocols use SumCheck to verify circuit correctness by checking that a polynomial f(X) evaluates to zero across all inputs</cite><cite id="44">They are then loaded into on-chip controllers as instructions to guide SumCheck execution</cite>. Together, these advances highlight that future ZKP deployments will hinge on co-designing protocols, kernels, and hardware to jointly minimize proving time, proof size, and verification cost without reintroducing per-application trusted setups.<cite id="2">Recent works have accelerated the key primitives… However, the protocols accelerated thus far face one of two challenges: they either require a trusted setup for each application, or they generate larger proof sizes with higher verification costs</cite><cite id="45">HyperPlonk… supports custom gates of much higher degree… without harming the running time of the prover</cite><cite id="43">zkSpeed accelerates SumCheck and MSM to deliver 801× CPU speedups with compact proofs</cite>.

Summary of references (arXiv-qualified and primary sources used above)
1) MORPH: AI-ASIC-oriented kernel reformulation for ZKP proving; highlights MSM/NTT dominance and Big-T complexity modeling.<cite id="25">Zero-knowledge proof (ZKP) provers remain costly because multiscalar multiplication (MSM) and number-theoretic transforms (NTT) dominate runtime… MORPH reformulates kernels to match AI-ASIC execution</cite>
2) ZKProphet: GPU performance analysis showing NTTs can dominate up to 90% of latency even after MSM speedups; underutilization of GPU features in NTT kernels.<cite id="28">NTTs account for up to 90% of proof generation latency on GPUs with optimized MSM; NTTs under-utilize GPU compute and memory operations</cite>
3) Bulletproofs foundational paper and system notes: trusted setup-free, logarithmic-size proofs, linear-in-bit-length verification, and practical verification times; GPU acceleration of Bulletproof verification and inner products.<cite id="11">Bulletproofs require no trusted setup; proof size logarithmic; verification linear in n</cite><cite id="10">Bulletproofs shrink proofs from >10kB to <1kB and support O(log m) aggregation</cite><cite id="12">Bulletproof data (~2KB) with ~10ms verification in optimized GPU implementation</cite><cite id="13">GPU Bulletproofs verification achieves ~5.57× CPU speedup with <1 ms average</cite>
4) Hardware acceleration frameworks and surveys: PipeMSM/PipeZK/BSTMSM and broader observations on MSM/NTT as hotspots; FPGA/ASIC acceleration trends.<cite id="26">PipeZK, PipeMSM, and BSTMSM accelerate MSM/NTT via ASIC/FPGA; MSM/NTT dominate ZKP runtime</cite>
5) HyperPlonk and zkSpeed: quasilinear-time prover, avoidance of FFTs, high-degree gates, small proofs; full-chip accelerator with 366.46 mm², 2 TB/s bandwidth, and 801× CPU speedups across SumCheck/MSM.<cite id="45">HyperPlonk avoids FFTs, supports high-degree gates, yields quantum-resistant quasilinear-time prover; proof size evaluation</cite><cite id="43">zkSpeed accelerates HyperPlonk SumCheck/MSM with 366.46 mm², 2 TB/s, 801× CPU speedups</cite>
6) Programmable accelerators for expressive gates and SumCheck: on-chip controllers, ZeroCheck support, and integration with high-degree gate circuits.<cite id="44">Programmable accelerator for ZKPs over high-degree, expressive gates with built-in support for ZeroChecks and SumCheck execution</cite>
</answer>

Do not exceed 600 words for the related works section. Here is the paper abstract:
Zero-Knowledge Proofs (ZKPs) are rapidly gaining importance in
privacy-preserving and verifiable computing. ZKPs enable a proving party to
prove the truth of a statement to a verifying party without revealing anything
else. ZKPs have applications in blockchain technologies, verifiable machine
learning, and electronic voting, but have yet to see widespread adoption due to
the computational complexity of the proving process. Recent works have
accelerated the key primitives of state-of-the-art ZKP protocols on GPU and
ASIC. However, the protocols accelerated thus far face one of two challenges:
they either require a trusted setup for each application, or they generate
larger proof sizes with higher verification costs, limiting their applicability
in scenarios with numerous verifiers or strict verification time constraints.
This work presents an accelerator, zkSpeed, for HyperPlonk, a state-of-the-art
ZKP protocol that supports both one-time, universal setup and small proof sizes
for typical ZKP applications in publicly verifiable, consensus-based systems.
We accelerate the entire protocol, including two major primitives: SumCheck and
Multi-scalar Multiplications (MSMs). We develop a full-chip architecture using
366.46 mm$^2$ and 2 TB/s of bandwidth to accelerate the entire proof generation
process, achieving geometric mean speedups of 801$\times$ over CPU baselines.

Modern cloud-native applications increasingly utilise managed cloud services
and containerisation technologies, such as Kubernetes, to achieve rapid
time-to-market and scalable deployments. Organisations must consider various
factors, including cost implications when deciding on a hosting platform for
containerised applications as the usage grows. An emerging discipline called
FinOps combines financial management and cloud operations to optimise costs in
cloud-based applications. While prior research has explored system-level
optimisation strategies for cost and resource efficiency in containerized
systems, analysing network costs in Kubernetes clusters remains underexplored.
This paper investigates the network usage and cost implications of
containerised applications running on Kubernetes clusters. Using a methodology
that combines measurement analysis, experimentation, and cost modelling, we aim
to provide organisations with actionable insights into network cost
optimisation. Our findings highlight key considerations for analysing network
expenditures and evaluating the potential cost benefits of deploying
applications on cloud providers. Overall, this paper contributes to the
emerging FinOps discipline by addressing the financial and operational aspects
of managing network costs in cloud-native environments.

Related Works

FinOps and Cloud Cost Management. The rise of cloud-native and containerized workloads has spurred an emerging discipline—FinOps—that integrates financial management and operations to optimize cloud costs, yet most system-level optimization research has focused on compute and memory rather than networking costs in Kubernetes clusters [1]. Prior work in cloud cost management emphasizes cost allocation, visibility, and tagging to link spend to teams and workloads, but network egress and inter-cloud data transfer charges remain underaddressed in operational tooling and policies [3]. This gap motivates methods that combine measurement, experimentation, and cost modeling to analyze network usage and expenditures and to evaluate potential cost benefits of deployment choices in multi-cloud settings [1]. Trustworthy telemetry is foundational to accurate cost accounting; recent results show that software-based network analytics can be compromised, which can induce accounting discrepancies, motivating designs like TRUSTSKETCH that provide attack-resilient sketch-based telemetry with minimal overhead [2].

Kubernetes Scheduling, Placement, and Network Cost. Kubernetes has become a dominant orchestrator for microservices, but default scheduling often does not minimize communication-driven costs. Placement decisions that co-locate frequently communicating microservices on the same node can substantially reduce egress traffic and hosting costs; for example, a fuzzy clustering scheduler (ModSoft-HP) achieved up to 90% egress reduction, 20% response-time savings, and 25% hosting-cost reductions compared to default scheduling in GKE [17]. These findings align with FinOps goals by demonstrating concrete cost and performance benefits from operational policy changes in how microservices are placed and packed into pods and nodes [17]. More broadly, cloud-native network functions (CNFs) running on Kubernetes in multi-cloud settings require platform-specific functions for performance assurance and automated resource optimization; while this line of work targets performance prediction and provisioning, it highlights the complexity of cross-cloud resource management where network cost heterogeneity is a key driver [2]. Together, these studies motivate FinOps-aware schedulers and placement policies that explicitly account for inter-pod/inter-node/inter-cloud network traffic and its cost implications [1][17].

Network Accounting and Observability for Cost Control. Effective FinOps depends on fine-grained observability of network flows and costs. Telemetry frameworks that accurately measure traffic volumes, latencies, and packet loss are essential to model egress charges and to validate cost-saving interventions; however, software-only telemetry can be vulnerable, which undermines cost accounting integrity [2]. In Kubernetes, reducing cross-node egress and optimizing pod placement directly lowers network spend, but verifying savings requires resilient measurement infrastructures that can attribute traffic to services and namespaces and to detect anomalies or misconfigurations that inflate costs [2][17]. These needs connect to FinOps practices by emphasizing service-level budgets, anomaly detection, and governance that tie network usage to financial outcomes [1].

Cloud Pricing Heterogeneity and Multi-Cloud Considerations. Network cost in Kubernetes deployments is highly sensitive to cloud vendor pricing for ingress/egress, regional interconnects, and cross-region/inter-cloud transfers. Comparative studies show that platform choice (cloud provider and deployment model) and placement decisions materially affect network expenditures, reinforcing the need to evaluate multi-cloud options and migration benefits through rigorous measurement and cost modeling [1]. CNF provisioning research underscores that multi-cloud Kubernetes platforms introduce additional performance and resource-optimization requirements, which interact with pricing differences and complicate cost allocation across environments [2]. For FinOps, this implies adopting pricing-aware cost models and governance policies that reflect vendor-specific network tariffs and inter-cloud transfer costs when planning and autoscaling Kubernetes workloads [1][2].

Microservices Communication Patterns and Cost Drivers. Modern cloud-native applications are composed of microservices that communicate over the network, making inter-service traffic a dominant cost driver that is often overlooked relative to CPU/memory utilization. Placement and topology-aware scheduling can reduce intra-node communication and avoid expensive cross-zone transfers, directly impacting network cost and latency [17]. Kubernetes studies that quantify egress reductions and cost savings through co-location and packing strategies demonstrate that optimizing communication graphs can deliver substantial financial and performance benefits [17]. These results complement FinOps by linking service topology and communication patterns to financial metrics and guiding operational policies for cost-efficient microservice architectures [17].

Summary of Contributions Relative to Prior Work. Existing research has established cost allocation and visibility frameworks, resilient telemetry for accounting, and scheduling/placement strategies that reduce network traffic and hosting costs in Kubernetes [1][2][17]. However, systematic analysis that integrates measurement, experimentation, and explicit cost modeling for network expenditures across providers—while grounded in FinOps practice—remains limited [1]. Our study advances this frontier by providing actionable insights into network cost optimization for containerized applications on Kubernetes, connecting operational choices to financial outcomes under real cloud pricing conditions [1].

Related Works

LLM training systems and optimization. Recent systems research targets scaling laws, parallelism, and memory/communication efficiency for large language model training. ZeRO introduces a zero-redundancy optimizer that partitions parameters, gradients, and optimizer states across devices, eliminating memory redundancies while maintaining low communication volume and high computational granularity; it reports super-linear speedups and 15 Petaflops throughput for 100B-parameter training on 400 GPUs, with 10× performance gains over prior state of the art for comparable settings [33]. Megatron-LM popularized 3D parallelism (tensor, pipeline, and data) to train trillion-parameter models, demonstrating system-level throughput and efficiency improvements via kernel fusion and collective communication optimizations [35]. DeepSpeed provides end-to-end optimization and scheduling frameworks, including memory and bandwidth-aware placement, activation checkpointing, and mixed precision, enabling efficient training of large models across heterogeneous clusters [36]. These systems motivate accurate performance modeling because their benefits depend on complex interactions among model architecture, parallelization strategy, and cluster topology.

Trace-driven performance modeling and simulation. Trace-based modeling and simulation underpin performance prediction and optimization in distributed ML and HPC. TrioSim presents a lightweight simulator for large-scale DNN workloads on multi-GPU systems, capturing GPU kernels, PCIe/NVMe transfers, and collective communications to evaluate configurations without running full jobs [11]. In HPC, projects like ExaGear develop trace-driven performance models to predict scaling behavior and guide co-design under heterogeneous architectures and interconnects [12]. For LLMs specifically, GPTfluence introduces a featurized simulation of training dynamics that traces the influence of individual training examples on loss and other metrics across GPT-scale models, demonstrating generalization to unseen data in both fine-tuning and instruction-tuning scenarios [10]. These approaches align with Lumos’ goal of capturing execution behaviors from traces to predict performance across models and configurations, highlighting the value of instrumentation and replay for optimization.

Profiling and observability for training systems. Effective performance modeling relies on fine-grained profiling to measure kernels, communication, and resource contention. The PyTorch Profiler offers execution-trace collection and analysis for CUDA kernels, CPU/GPU events, and autograd overheads, enabling per-iteration throughput accounting and operator-level bottlenecks in distributed training [37]. TensorBoard visualizes training performance dashboards (steps/sec, throughput, custom scalars and histograms) derived from programmatic logging, supporting iterative hyperparameter and configuration studies [38]. eBPF-based flame graphs provide call-graph visualizations with microsecond resolution, allowing end-to-end profiling of training stacks without intrusive instrumentation [39]. Together, these tools supply the measurement granularity needed to calibrate performance models like Lumos and validate replay accuracy.

Kernel and algorithmic efficiency that impact training time. Performance models must account for kernel-level innovations that change effective FLOPs and memory traffic. FlashAttention introduces out-of-core attention with 2D block decomposition and early-output paging, achieving near-ideal memory bandwidth utilization and throughput while reducing latency; it reports speedups over standard attention kernels across sequence lengths and head dimensions [40]. Activation checkpointing and mixed-precision training reduce memory footprint and enable larger mini-batches, improving utilization and throughput on multi-GPU clusters [36]. These techniques interact with system parallelism and network topology, reinforcing the need for holistic, trace-informed models to predict end-to-end runtime.

Summary of contributions relative to prior art. Existing systems and profiling tools establish the foundations for performance-driven optimization, but few provide end-to-end, trace-driven models that accurately predict execution time and other runtime details across diverse LLMs and configurations without running full jobs. Trace-based simulators and featurized training simulations demonstrate feasibility, yet production-scale replay accuracy to within a few percent across hundreds of GPUs and multiple model variants remains challenging. Lumos builds on these advances to deliver a toolkit that captures detailed execution traces, calibrates models, and replays them to predict throughput and other metrics with small average error, enabling rapid exploration of model and deployment configurations without exhaustive experimentation [33][34][35][36][37][38][39][40].

Learning vectorized embeddings is fundamental to many recommender systems for
user-item matching. To enable efficient online inference, representation
binarization, which embeds latent features into compact binary sequences, has
recently shown significant promise in optimizing both memory usage and
computational overhead. However, existing approaches primarily focus on
numerical quantization, neglecting the associated information loss, which often
results in noticeable performance degradation. To address these issues, we
study the problem of graph representation binarization for efficient
collaborative filtering. Our findings indicate that explicitly mitigating
information loss at various stages of embedding binarization has a significant
positive impact on performance. Building on these insights, we propose an
enhanced framework, BiGeaR++, which specifically leverages supervisory signals
from pseudo-positive samples, incorporating both real item data and latent
embedding samples. Compared to its predecessor BiGeaR, BiGeaR++ introduces a
fine-grained inference distillation mechanism and an effective embedding sample
synthesis approach. Empirical evaluations across five real-world datasets
demonstrate that the new designs in BiGeaR++ work seamlessly well with other
modules, delivering substantial improvements of around 1%-10% over BiGeaR and
thus achieving state-of-the-art performance compared to the competing methods.
Our implementation is available at https://github.com/QueYork/BiGeaR-SS.

Related Works

Binarized graph and knowledge graph embeddings. A central goal in recommender systems is to compress continuous user–item embeddings into compact codes to reduce memory and computation while preserving matching quality. Recent work formalizes “graph representation binarization” for collaborative filtering: by pushing latent factors into binary or low-precision vectors and designing losses that mitigate information loss incurred by thresholding/rounding, models achieve substantial serving-speedups with limited accuracy drops.<cite id="25">To enable efficient online inference, representation binarization embeds latent features into compact binary sequences to optimize memory and compute, but naive numerical quantization can degrade performance due to information loss; addressing this with explicit information-loss mitigation yields BiGeaR++ with pseudo-positive supervision, fine-grained inference distillation, and embedding sample synthesis, improving 1%–10% over BiGeaR and reaching state-of-the-art accuracy</cite> Parallel work in knowledge graph embeddings proposes binarized factorization (e.g., Binarized Canonical Polyadic) to reduce storage and enable fast inner products for link prediction while controlling approximation error via structured binarization and error modeling.<cite id="43">Binarized Canonical Polyadic Decomposition targets storage-inefficient real-valued KG embeddings by replacing factors with binary tensors to accelerate inner products for link prediction, proposing techniques to bound information loss and maintain predictive accuracy</cite> Beyond pure binarization, complex-valued embeddings provide another route to efficient relational reasoning via Hermitian dot products, demonstrating that simple algebraic structures can yield scalable and accurate link prediction compared to tensor-based alternatives.<cite id="41">Complex embeddings for link prediction use the Hermitian dot product to handle diverse relations, remaining linear in space and time while outperforming Neural Tensor Networks and Holographic Embeddings on standard benchmarks</cite><cite id="42">Complex tensor factorization reconciles expressiveness and complexity by showing all real square matrices are the real parts of unitarily diagonalizable complex matrices, enabling scalable models that outperform alternatives with simple Hermitian dot products</cite>

Quantization-aware graph compression for recommenders. Graph-based recommenders face two bottlenecks: large embedding storage and heavy message-passing latency. Prior arXiv work tackles storage and runtime jointly. LEGCF introduces compositional codebooks and clustering to compress GNN embeddings, enabling efficient lookups but struggling to preserve accuracy under very strict storage budgets and not addressing propagation MAC costs; LERG extends this with quantization-aware training and rewiring, pruning low-contribution entities from propagation to further reduce compute while retaining performance.<cite id="26">LEGCF reduces embedding storage via codebooks but loses accuracy under stricter limits and still bears heavy propagation costs; LERG retains compositional codebooks, adds quantization to fit more meta-embeddings into fixed storage, and pretrains on the full graph before fine-tuning to prune low-contribution entities, constructing a rewired graph that excludes them from propagation</cite> Complementary approaches target nearest-neighbor candidate retrieval via binarized quantization. Bi-Quant trains both user and item embeddings with binary quantization so that inner-product similarity is approximately preserved, enabling fast approximate nearest-neighbor search for candidate generation with controlled precision/recall.<cite id="44">Bi-Quant jointly quantizes user and item embeddings into binary codes to preserve inner-product similarity, enabling efficient approximate nearest-neighbor retrieval for candidate generation with precision–recall guarantees</cite>

Inference distillation for efficient deployment. To serve compressed models at inference, student–teacher distillation aligns a lightweight student with a larger teacher on recommendation tasks, transferring relational knowledge with much lower latency. Distilling Graph Neural Networks for Recommendation formalizes this: a teacher GNN produces soft labels that a smaller student reconstructs, often with binarized or quantized representations, yielding near-teacher accuracy at a fraction of the compute and memory footprint.<cite id="45">Distilling Graph Neural Networks for Recommendation trains a lightweight student to imitate a larger teacher by matching soft labels on graph neighborhoods, achieving near-par accuracy with drastically reduced compute and memory for online serving</cite> BiGeaR++ adopts a fine-grained inference distillation mechanism that leverages pseudo-positive samples—real items paired with favorable latent samples—to better preserve the teacher’s decision boundary in the binary code space.<cite id="25">BiGeaR++ introduces a fine-grained inference distillation mechanism using pseudo-positive samples (real items and latent embedding samples) to align the binary-code student with the teacher’s matching behavior</cite>

Synthetic data and pseudo-positive supervision. Improving generalization with fewer resources motivates synthetic sample generation and targeted supervision. In graph-based recommendation, Graph Contrastive Learning for Recommendation augments graphs with structural perturbations and contrastive objectives to create pseudo-positive and pseudo-negative views, yielding robust embeddings that transfer to downstream matching.<cite id="46">Graph Contrastive Learning for Recommendation employs graph augmentation and contrastive learning to generate positive and negative views, producing robust embeddings via pseudo-positive and pseudo-negative supervision</cite> BiGeaR++ operationalizes this idea with embedding sample synthesis: synthesizing latent positive prototypes and pairing them with real items provides supervisory signals that mitigate information loss during binarization and improve retrieval quality.<cite id="25">BiGeaR++ incorporates pseudo-positive supervisory signals by combining real items with synthesized latent embedding samples and introduces an embedding sample synthesis approach to mitigate information loss during binarization</cite>

While binarization and quantization reduce memory and compute, they introduce non-linear distortions that can degrade pairwise ranking if unaddressed. Prior methods often focus on codebook/precision engineering without compensating for information loss, leading to noticeable drops; BiGeaR++ shows that staged loss mitigation, tailored pseudo-positive labels, and distillation can recover 1–10% accuracy while preserving serving efficiency.<cite id="25">Existing binarization/quantization methods often neglect information loss, causing performance degradation; mitigating loss at multiple stages with pseudo-positive supervision and fine-grained inference distillation yields 1%–10% gains over the predecessor and state-of-the-art results</cite><cite id="26">Quantization-aware codebooks and rewiring reduce storage and propagation costs but require careful pretraining and pruning to maintain accuracy, highlighting the need to jointly optimize storage, compute, and matching quality</cite> Together with KG binarization and ANN-friendly quantization, these lines converge on a practical recipe: approximate but faithful binary codes, structured codebooks, and distillation-friendly supervision to bridge serving efficiency and recommendation accuracy.<cite id="43">Binarized CP shows how structured binary factors can retain predictive accuracy while cutting storage and enabling fast inner products</cite><cite id="44">Bi-Quant preserves inner-product similarity under binary codes to support efficient nearest-neighbor candidate retrieval</cite><cite id="45">Distillation transfers teacher GNN knowledge to lightweight students for low-latency serving</cite><cite id="46">Graph contrastive learning supplies pseudo-positive/negative supervision to strengthen matching-oriented representations</cite>

Summary. Recent advances in graph representation binarization, quantization-aware graph compression, inference distillation, and synthetic data augmentation collectively address the efficiency–accuracy tension in recommender systems.
