Related Works

Sequential recommendation models capture item–item correlations in user behavior sequences to predict the next action. Early works formalized this as next-item prediction and popularized neural sequence encoders, with transformer-based models—especially unidirectional masked or autoregressive variants—dominating the field due to their ability to learn long-term dependencies and scale with data volume and vocabulary size. <cite id="10">Self-attentive architectures like SASRec balance long-term semantics with parsimony by adaptively attending to “relevant” items in the history, outperforming Markov-chain and CNN/RNN baselines while being more efficient than comparable neural models</cite>. <cite id="22">BERT4Rec established a strong transformer-based baseline for sequential recommendation, but its reported superiority depends strongly on training duration and loss design, with subsequent analyses showing that extended training or architectural adaptations (e.g., disentangled attention, size scaling) can surpass its original results</cite>. <cite id="9">Follow-up studies attribute performance gaps between SASRec and BERT4Rec to overconfidence induced by negative sampling versus full-vocabulary cross-entropy, and propose generalized binary cross-entropy training with more negatives (gSASRec) that mitigates overconfidence and can outperform BERT4Rec while reducing training time</cite>. <cite id="23">Empirical comparisons further show that matching BERT4Rec’s loss on SASRec can make SASRec significantly faster and more effective, and that SASRec can outperform BERT4Rec when trained with sufficiently many negatives under negative sampling</cite>.

Cross-domain sequential recommendation (CDSR) leverages interactions across multiple domains to improve next-item prediction, but naive joint training risks negative transfer and attention overgeneralization across domains. <cite id="1">Recent CDSR work revisits self-attention as the core learning substrate and formulates cross-domain learning as a multi-objective problem: optimize recommendation metrics while dynamically minimizing cross-domain attention scores</cite>. <cite id="1">This Pareto-optimal self-attention approach—AutoCDSR—automates knowledge transfer by mitigating negative transfer and encouraging complementary knowledge exchange among auxiliary domains, yielding plug-and-play gains with little extra overhead and strong stability across base models</cite>. <cite id="1">Experiments show AutoCDSR consistently enhances SASRec and BERT4Rec, improving Recall@10 by 9.8% and 16.0% and NDCG@10 by 12.0% and 16.7%, respectively, while remaining practical to deploy with minimal computational overhead and light hyperparameter tuning</cite>.

A parallel line of work tackles scalability and efficiency in multi-domain transformer recommenders. <cite id="2">Dynamic State Representations propose efficient large-scale CDSR by constraining attention to evolve over time and across domains, addressing the computational bottleneck where transformer attention attends to all items across every domain in multi-domain settings</cite>. <cite id="2">By shaping attention dynamics, this systems-oriented design reduces unnecessary cross-domain interactions and aligns with the plug-and-play principle, enabling practical deployment at production scale</cite>. Together with attention-aware training and loss design from sequential recommendation, these methods provide practical levers to control knowledge transfer without heavy architectural overhauls.

Attention-centric enhancements and multi-objective framing connect sequential modeling, domain adaptation, and efficiency. <cite id="1">AutoCDSR operationalizes a Pareto trade-off: it strengthens task-relevant attention while suppressing cross-domain interference, effectively automating domain selection and alignment via self-attention regularization</cite>. <cite id="9">From a training perspective, controlling overconfidence and calibrating attention distributions improves ranking robustness and helps resolve discrepancies between transformer variants under different losses and sampling schemes</cite>. <cite id="22">Architectural adaptations such as disentangled attention and parameter sharing (e.g., DeBERTa, ALBERT) further demonstrate that transformer design choices in sequential encoders can yield sizable gains, reinforcing the value of modular, plug-and-play enhancements over monolithic domain-specific stacks</cite>.

Finally, deployment considerations motivate methods that impose limited extra compute while improving generalization. <cite id="1">AutoCDSR’s lightweight mechanism—modifying attention patterns rather than adding domain-specific layers—aligns with low-overhead deployment and minimal tuning, enabling simple models to perform on par with state-of-the-art CDSR systems</cite>. <cite id="10">This complements SASRec’s efficiency profile and gSASRec’s training-time savings, offering a practical path to cross-domain performance gains without sacrificing scalability</cite>. <cite id="2">On the systems side, dynamic state representations complement attention control by reducing the effective span of cross-domain dependencies, further curbing computational costs</cite>.

In summary, recent advances in sequential recommendation and CDSR converge on three themes: (1) transformer-based encoders with calibrated attention and loss design, (2) cross-domain learning via attention control and dynamic state shaping to mitigate negative transfer, and (3) plug-and-play modules with minimal overhead that deliver strong, stable gains across base models and datasets. <cite id="10">These directions build on SASRec’s self-attention foundation</cite>, <cite id="9,22">clarify BERT4Rec’s training sensitivities and architectural leverage points</cite>, and <cite id="1,2">offer Pareto-style trade-offs and efficient mechanisms for automated knowledge transfer in multi-domain settings</cite>.

Related Works

Opinion mining and sentiment from app reviews. Prior work in software engineering and data mining has leveraged app reviews to surface user feedback for maintenance, evolution, and quality assurance, focusing on star ratings, textual comments, feature requests, bug reports, and usage scenarios; yet the sheer volume and unstructured nature of feedback make manual analysis infeasible and motivate scalable classification schemes and tooling for mining actionable insights from large-scale review corpora [42]. While most studies target coarse sentiment polarity, a growing body of research recognizes the need for fine-grained emotion understanding to support downstream tasks such as feature–emotion mapping, user-oriented release planning, and issue triaging in productized settings [41].

Fine-grained emotion classification and taxonomies. Fine-grained emotion analysis adapts structured emotion taxonomies to capture nuanced affect beyond positive/negative, often aligning lexicons and models with frameworks such as Plutchik’s wheel of emotions to improve interpretability and downstream utility [41]. Recent work on affect lexica emphasizes reconciling heterogeneous emotion resources to mitigate coverage gaps and label-space mismatches; by merging eight lexica via a multi-view VAE to learn a joint emotion label space, authors show that unified lexicon features can outperform individual lexica when used with modern detectors, though simple concatenation can already be competitive and adding a learned joint lexicon can still help [1]. Complementary analyses outside app reviews demonstrate that different negative emotions drive distinct exchange motifs and network structures in social media during crises, with sadness and disgust eliciting specific responsive emotions (e.g., sadness → joy/love; disgust → anger) and fear associated with reciprocity and information seeking, underscoring the importance of emotion granularity for modeling communicative patterns [2]. In domain-specific settings with code-switching, hybrid lexicon–machine learning pipelines tailored to bilingual reviews have achieved improved accuracy over monolingual baselines, validating the utility of lexicon augmentation and language-aware modeling for real-world review datasets [7].

App-review–specific emotion modeling. Building on domain mining, recent work explicitly targets fine-grained emotion extraction from mobile app reviews by adapting Plutchik’s taxonomy to create a structured annotation framework and curated dataset, iteratively refining annotation guidelines through human consensus to surface key challenges in emotion classification [41]. This line of work also evaluates automation via large language models (LLMs), finding that LLM-based annotation substantially reduces manual effort while maintaining meaningful agreement with human labels; however, full automation remains difficult due to the interpretive complexity of emotional nuance, ambiguity, and context sensitivity in user-generated text [41]. These findings align with broader observations that affect lexicons and language models can improve detection performance, yet emotion semantics are heterogeneous and context-dependent, necessitating careful calibration and human-in-the-loop validation [1,2].

Annotation frameworks, agreement, and cost-effectiveness. To operationalize fine-grained emotion annotation at scale, recent studies emphasize iterative human annotation protocols to converge on clear operational definitions and guidelines, documenting sources of disagreement and boundary cases that degrade inter-annotator agreement (IAA) [41]. In parallel, cost-sensitive pipelines increasingly evaluate LLMs as semi-automated tools to triage and draft labels, trading off annotation speed and cost against accuracy; empirical comparisons show that LLM-assisted labeling can reduce effort significantly while preserving substantial agreement with human annotations, though residual errors and edge cases still require expert review [41]. These trends complement foundational work on lexicon integration and emotion modeling, offering practical pathways to combine coverage, interpretability, and efficiency in app-review analytics [1,41].

Broader implications and cross-domain evidence. Cross-domain studies of emotion exchange and code-switching provide external validity for designing robust app-review annotation schemes and classifiers: motif-level differences across emotions suggest that models should treat different affect categories asymmetrically, while bilingual and informal language require lexicon and preprocessing tailored to domain-specific code-switching patterns [2,7]. Summary. Fine-grained emotion analysis in app reviews remains less explored than polarity classification but is gaining traction through taxonomies like Plutchik’s, unified lexicon methods, and LLM-assisted annotation frameworks that reduce manual effort while preserving substantial agreement with human labels [41,1,2,7]. Domain-specific app-review mining underscores the need for scalable, interpretable pipelines to turn unstructured feedback into actionable insights, with emerging evidence that hybrid lexicon–model approaches and iterative annotation protocols can address coverage, ambiguity, and quality constraints in real-world review datasets [42,41].

Related Work

Neural retrieval and generative retrieval. Neural dual-encoder and cross-encoder models have advanced web and passage retrieval, but training often hinges on large labeled query–document pairs, which are costly to collect. To scale supervision, recent work reframes retrieval into sequence-to-sequence generative retrieval that encodes entire corpora and evaluates effectiveness without external indexes, revealing that synthetic queries used during indexing are central to scaling and that naive parameter scaling yields limited gains, with competitiveness to dual-encoders only on small corpora when scaling to millions of passages remains challenging [15]. Alongside, unified generation approaches for tasks like query auto-completion combine retrieval-augmented generation with multi-objective alignment to jointly optimize against multiple criteria, demonstrating production gains via rule-based, model-based, and LLM-as-judge verifiers and iterative critique–revision pipelines [2].

Synthetic queries and noisy data. The availability of large web document corpora such as ClueWeb enables scalable synthetic query generation with large language models as a proxy for scarce supervision. However, synthetic queries vary in quality and can degrade downstream ranking performance; prior practice often filters noisy query–document pairs using external rerankers or heuristics before training [14]. To improve data quality, list-wise training with multiple levels of relevance has been proposed to move beyond binary relevance contrastive learning, enabling better use of synthetic data by leveraging richer relevance signals [16]. Complementarily, data-quality-aware methods at the index level identify and remove inconsistent retrieval results via logical rules guided by LLM context understanding, improving answer accuracy and underscoring the broader need to curate retrieval evidence rather than solely rely on raw volume [25]. For selection-oriented annotation, uncertainty and instruction-specific criteria have been explored to prioritize high-value examples when labels are synthetic, addressing the problem of low-quality pseudo-annotations [26].

Direct Preference Optimization for ranking-aware query generation. Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) integrates ranking feedback directly into learning without explicit reward modeling, and has been adapted to align query generation with retrieval objectives. Rather than filtering noisy synthetic pairs post hoc with an external reranker, DPO embeds ranking signals into query synthesis, optimizing for higher downstream effectiveness. Empirically, DPO increases rater-assessed relevance of generated query–document pairs and yields stronger MS MARCO performance than baselines trained purely on synthetic data, indicating that preference-aligned generation can outperform data-filtering heuristics in this setting [14]. In adjacent settings, multi-objective DPO with RAG-based verifiers has improved QAC by fusing rule-based, model-based, and LLM-as-judge criteria to produce high-quality synthetic training data and achieve measurable production gains in keystrokes and suggestion adoption [2]. These results align with broader findings that synthetic queries are pivotal when scaling generative retrieval, yet their quality dictates retrieval performance, motivating preference-based alignment and verifier-augmented pipelines [15].

Curriculum and re-ranker feedback. Several pipelines leverage external rerankers to score and retain high-quality pairs produced by LLMs, serving as discriminators to separate useful from noisy examples before downstream training. This is consistent with observations that reranker signals can act as effective filters for synthetic data, though end-to-end optimization via DPO can further capitalize on those signals by shaping the generator’s objective directly [14]. More broadly, preference optimization and critique–revision loops have been used to iteratively improve synthetic corpora quality, with LLM-as-judge verifiers reducing hallucinations and improving utility for ranking and generation tasks [2]. At the index layer, trimming irrelevant or inconsistent retrieved contexts based on query context dependencies further reinforces the principle of curating evidence to improve downstream accuracy [25].

Beyond binary supervision and list-wise training. Moving beyond pairwise contrastive learning, recent methods adopt list-wise objectives and multi-level relevance labels to better reflect graded relevance in retrieval. Synthetic data has been highlighted as a key enabler of such training regimes, allowing models to learn from large-scale, weakly supervised sets with more nuanced supervision than simple positives/negatives [16]. This complements DPO-style alignment by providing richer training signals that approximate graded human judgments, which in turn can improve ranker performance when synthetic data replaces or augments human-labeled pairs [14].

Datasets and evaluation. MS MARCO remains a central benchmark for passage ranking and has been used to evaluate models trained with synthetic data and generative retrieval approaches, including those leveraging ClueWeb-scale corpora for data synthesis and scaling analyses. Studies show that when synthetic queries are used during indexing or as training signals, MS MARCO performance can reflect both the quality of the synthetic pipeline and the robustness of the ranking objective, with DPO-based alignment improving rater-assessed relevance and downstream gains over purely synthetic baselines [14][15]. These evaluations underscore that while ClueWeb-scale resources enable scalable training, downstream effectiveness hinges on how ranking signals are incorporated into data generation and model optimization [14][15].

Summary of contributions relative to the literature. Existing methods typically rely on external rerankers or heuristics to filter noisy synthetic pairs; in contrast, integrating ranking objectives directly into query generation via DPO improves both the quality of synthetic pairs and downstream MS MARCO performance [14]. This aligns with evidence that synthetic queries are crucial for scaling generative retrieval, but their effectiveness depends on data quality and training objectives, motivating verifier-augmented pipelines, list-wise training with graded relevance, and preference optimization to unify generation and ranking [2][15][16]. Together, these lines of work motivate a preference-driven, verifier-informed, and relevance-aware pipeline for training retrieval with abundant but noisy synthetic data [14][2][16].

and efficiency of federated unlearning strategies within Federated Online
Learning to Rank (FOLTR), with specific attention to systematically analysing

  Federated approaches to ranking of search results have recently garnered
attention to address users privacy concerns. In FOLTR, privacy is safeguarded

preserving individual user data while optimizing search results based on

machine learning models like those in FOLTR should provide capabilities that

sparked the development of unlearning methods, along with evaluation practices
to measure whether unlearning of a user data successfully occurred. Current
evaluation practices are however often controversial, necessitating the use of
multiple metrics for a more comprehensive assessment -- but previous proposals
of unlearning methods only used single evaluation metrics.
  This paper addresses this limitation: our study rigorously assesses the
effectiveness of unlearning strategies in managing both under-unlearning and
over-unlearning scenarios using adapted, and newly proposed evaluation metrics.
Thanks to our detailed analysis, we uncover the strengths and limitations of
five unlearning strategies, offering valuable insights into optimizing
federated unlearning to balance data privacy and system performance within
FOLTR. We publicly release our code and complete results at

Neural retrieval methods using transformer-based pre-trained language models
have advanced multilingual and cross-lingual retrieval. However, their
effectiveness for low-resource, morphologically rich languages such as Amharic
remains underexplored due to data scarcity and suboptimal tokenization. We
address this gap by introducing Amharic-specific dense retrieval models based
on pre-trained Amharic BERT and RoBERTa backbones. Our proposed
RoBERTa-Base-Amharic-Embed model (110M parameters) achieves a 17.6% relative
improvement in MRR@10 and a 9.86% gain in Recall@10 over the strongest
multilingual baseline, Arctic Embed 2.0 (568M parameters). More compact
variants, such as RoBERTa-Medium-Amharic-Embed (42M), remain competitive while
being over 13x smaller. Additionally, we train a ColBERT-based late interaction
retrieval model that achieves the highest MRR@10 score (0.843) among all
evaluated models. We benchmark our proposed models against both sparse and
dense retrieval baselines to systematically assess retrieval effectiveness in
Amharic. Our analysis highlights key challenges in low-resource settings and
underscores the importance of language-specific adaptation. To foster future
research in low-resource IR, we publicly release our dataset, codebase, and
trained models at https://github.com/kidist-amde/amharic-ir-benchmarks.

Beyond Snowflake’s family, broader efforts such as mmBERT describe training massively multilingual encoders over 3T+ tokens across more than 1,800 languages, reporting speed and accuracy gains and introducing strategies for low-resource language learning<cite id="18">mmBERT trains massively multilingual encoders over 3T+ tokens across more than 1,800 languages with speed and performance gains</cite>. At the same time, efficiency-oriented embedding architectures like Nomic Embed v2 introduce mixture-of-experts to reduce memory and latency, addressing practical constraints in retrieval-augmented systems<cite id="21">Nomic Embed v2 introduces MoE text embeddings to improve efficiency for retrieval-augmented applications</cite>. These developments provide strong multilingual baselines against which language-specific dense retrievers can be benchmarked, as in the present work<cite id="17">Arctic-Embed 2.0 provides open-source multilingual embedding baselines for retrieval</cite>.

Late Interaction and ColBERT-style Models. Late-interaction retrieval has emerged as a powerful alternative to pooled dense vectors, enabling fine-grained token-level matching. Jina-ColBERT-v2 introduces an architecture and training framework that supports long contexts and multilingual retrieval, demonstrating strong performance across English and multilingual tasks with multi-vector representations and late interaction<cite id="1">Jina-ColBERT-v2 supports long context and multilingual retrieval with late-interaction multi-vector representations</cite>. Complementary work shows ColBERT-style scoring can be adapted to zero-shot multilingual retrieval with modular multi-vector representations, where adding a new language often requires only language-specific adapters learned via masked language modeling<cite id="3">ColBERT-XM adopts fine-grained late interaction for zero-shot multilingual retrieval with modular multi-vector representations</cite>. Earlier transfer-learning approaches established that cross-language retrieval can be achieved by encoding queries and documents with XLM-RoBERTa and using ColBERT’s term representations for cross-language expansion, laying foundations for modern multilingual CLIR systems<cite id="4">ColBERT-X uses XLM-RoBERTa to support cross-language retrieval with ColBERT-style term representations</cite>. These late-interaction methods directly inform high-precision cross-lingual retrieval and offer a template for Amharic evaluation, as demonstrated by a ColBERT-based Amharic model achieving the highest MRR@10 among evaluated models in this study<cite id="1">Jina-ColBERT-v2 demonstrates strong multilingual late-interaction retrieval performance</cite>.

Low-Resource Adaptation: Monolingual Transfer, Pseudo-Labels, and Language-Specific Data. In data-scarce settings, transfer from high-resource tasks and monolingual corpora is essential. AmaSQuAD shows how extractive QA can be bootstrapped in Amharic by translating SQuAD 2.0 and then fine-tuning on multilingual resources (QNLI, MultiNLI, Natural Questions), yielding transfer gains through pretraining and cross-lingual alignment<cite id="22">AmaSQuAD bootstraps Amharic QA by translating SQuAD 2.0 and leveraging transfer from QNLI, SQuAD 2.0, NQ Long Answer, and MultiNLI</cite>. Parallel corpus expansion for machine translation provides another pathway: a newly compiled Amharic–English corpus larger than prior releases was aligned and preprocessed for under-resourced language translation, with MERT and k-best batch MIRA used for reranking and tuning<cite id="23">An extended Amharic–English parallel corpus was compiled, preprocessed, aligned, and tuned with MERT and k-best batch MIRA</cite>. For speech front-ends, fine-tuning open-source ASR like Whisper on Amharic datasets (e.g., BDU-speech) enables robust transcription in low-resource conditions, highlighting the importance of speech–text pipelines for end-to-end retrieval applications<cite id="24">Whisper fine-tuning on Amharic ASR datasets (e.g., BDU-speech) improves transcription robustness in low-resource settings</cite>. Morphological richness motivates tokenization choices: character-level embeddings have been shown effective for Amharic-to-English MT, handling out-of-vocabulary forms and capturing fine-grained morphology better than word-level tokenization in highly inflecting languages<cite id="25">Character-level embeddings improve Amharic-to-English MT by better handling morphology and OOV words</cite>. Collectively, these strategies mirror the present work’s emphasis on language-specific adaptation and data augmentation to overcome sparse supervision and suboptimal tokenization in Amharic retrieval<cite id="22">AmaSQuAD leverages translation and transfer to build Amharic QA resources</cite><cite id="23">Extended parallel corpora enable improved Amharic–English MT and tuning</cite><cite id="24">Amharic ASR fine-tuning addresses low-resource speech transcription</cite><cite id="25">Character-level tokenization addresses morphology in Amharic MT</cite>.

Tokenization, Morphology, and Code-Switching. Morphologically rich languages like Amharic pose challenges for subword tokenizers and cross-lingual matching. Prior work has explored code-switching information retrieval, evaluating embedding and retrieval models across 250+ languages and more than 500 tasks, and leveraging bilingual lexicons to study cross-dialect retrieval; these studies also clarify how subword encoders interact with independent lexicons, underscoring tokenizer design and dictionary resources as first-class concerns in multilingual IR<cite id="19">Code-switching IR evaluates models across 250+ languages and >500 tasks and leverages bilingual lexicons for cross-dialect retrieval</cite>. In practice, modern multilingual systems increasingly combine subword encoders with language-specific lexicons or adapters to recover morphological and dialectal variation, a direction aligned with the present work’s emphasis on language-specific RoBERTa backbones and tokenization-aware evaluation<cite id="19">Bilingual lexicons and subword encoders interact nontrivially in code-switching IR, motivating language-specific adaptations</cite>.

Evaluation Benchmarks and Multilingual Capabilities. Beyond document retrieval, multilingual evaluation spans code-switching, dialectal variation, and cross-lingual transfer. Recent benchmarks explicitly measure cross-dialect retrieval using independent bilingual lexicons and analyze how pre-trained models’ subword representations align or misalign with linguistic resources, providing a methodology to quantify cross-lingual effectiveness and robustness<cite id="19">Cross-dialect retrieval benchmarks use independent bilingual lexicons and analyze model alignment with lexicons</cite>. In parallel, large-scale multilingual embedding families (e.g., Arctic-Embed 2.0) and late-interaction retrievers (e.g., Jina-ColBERT-v2) report strong zero-shot and fine-grained multilingual performance, offering standardized baselines for Amharic and related languages<cite id="17">Arctic-Embed 2.0 delivers competitive multilingual retrieval quality</cite><cite id="1">Jina-ColBERT-v2 supports 89 languages with long contexts and strong retrieval performance</cite>. These trends complement Amharic-specific resources—such as AmaSQuAD, extended parallel corpora, and Whisper fine-tuning—that enable end-to-end evaluation across dense and sparse retrieval, reranking, and speech-driven pipelines<cite id="22">AmaSQuAD provides Amharic extractive QA for cross-lingual transfer evaluation</cite><cite id="23">Extended parallel corpora enable multilingual MT-based retrieval evaluation and tuning</cite><cite id="24">Amharic Whisper fine-tuning supports speech-driven retrieval pipelines</cite>.

Summary and Gaps. Together, these works establish that multilingual dense retrieval benefits from efficient, high-coverage encoders; that late-interaction models recover fine-grained matching and multilingual zero-shot capability; and that low-resource adaptation hinges on monolingual transfer, parallel data, and morphology-aware tokenization, especially for Semitic languages like Amharic<cite id="17">Efficient, high-coverage multilingual encoders underpin strong retrieval baselines</cite><cite id="1">Late-interaction multi-vector models support long contexts and multilingual retrieval</cite><cite id="3">ColBERT-style late interaction enables zero-shot multilingual retrieval with modular adapters</cite><cite id="4">Cross-language expansion with XLM-RoBERTa supports CLIR</cite><cite id="22">Translation and transfer bootstrap Amharic QA resources</cite><cite id="23">Parallel corpora enable tuning and evaluation in low-resource MT</cite><cite id="24">ASR fine-tuning addresses low-resource speech transcription for retrieval</cite><cite id="25">Character-level embeddings handle morphology in Amharic MT</cite>. Our contribution fills a gap by releasing Amharic-specific dense and late-interaction models trained on Amharic RoBERTa backbones, demonstrating that language-specific adaptation can outperform large multilingual baselines even when the latter exceed 500M parameters, while also highlighting tokenizer design and data scarcity as first-class determinants of retrieval quality in low-resource settings<cite id="17">Arctic Embed 2.0 provides a strong multilingual baseline for comparison</cite><cite id="1">Jina-ColBERT-v2 demonstrates late-interaction multilingual performance</cite><cite id="22">AmaSQuAD and transfer data inform Amharic retrieval resource construction</cite><cite id="23">Extended parallel corpora enable multilingual evaluation and tuning</cite>.

Puxuan Yu* and Luke Merrick and Gaurav Nuti and Daniel Campos Snowflake Inc.
Abstract
This paper presents the training methodology of Arctic-Embed 2.0, a set of open-source text embedding models built for accurate and efficient multilingual retrieval. While prior works have suffered from degraded English retrieval quality, Arctic-Embed 2.0 delivers competitive retrieval quality on multilingual...

Title: mmBERT: ModernBERT goes Multilingual
URL: http://www.shurl.cc/5b5d501db1958418928787e4604759a5
Snippet: This blog post introduces mmBERT, a state-of-the-art massively multilingual encoder model trained on 3T+ tokens of text in over 1800 languages. Related Works

Multilingual and Cross-lingual Dense Retrieval. Recent work has focused on building open-source multilingual embedding models that balance retrieval quality, efficiency, and coverage. Arctic-Embed 2.0 targets “multilingual retrieval without compromise,” reporting competitive retrieval quality across languages while emphasizing inference efficiency for production search pipelines<cite id="17">Arctic-Embed 2.0 targets multilingual retrieval with competitive quality and efficiency</cite>. Snowflake’s engineering announcement complements this by positioning Arctic Embed L 2.0/M 2.0 as the next iteration of high-quality embeddings scaled to multilingual search<cite id="20">Arctic Embed L 2.0 and M 2.0 extend high-quality embeddings to multilingual search</cite>. Beyond Snowflake’s family, broader efforts such as mmBERT describe training massively multilingual encoders over 3T+ tokens across more than 1,800 languages, reporting speed and accuracy gains and introducing strategies for low-resource language learning<cite id="18">mmBERT trains massively multilingual encoders over 3T+ tokens across more than 1,800 languages with speed and performance gains</cite>. At the same time, efficiency-oriented embedding architectures like Nomic Embed v2 introduce mixture-of-experts to reduce memory and latency, addressing practical constraints in retrieval-augmented systems<cite id="21">Nomic Embed v2 introduces MoE text embeddings to improve efficiency for retrieval-augmented applications</cite>. These developments provide strong multilingual baselines against which language-specific dense retrievers can be benchmarked, as in the present work<cite id="17">Arctic-Embed 2.0 provides open-source multilingual embedding baselines for retrieval</cite>.

Late Interaction and ColBERT-style Models. Late-interaction retrieval has emerged as a powerful alternative to pooled dense vectors, enabling fine-grained token-level matching. Jina-ColBERT-v2 introduces an architecture and training framework that supports long contexts and multilingual retrieval, demonstrating strong performance across English and multilingual tasks with multi-vector representations and late interaction<cite id="1">Jina-ColBERT-v2 supports long context and multilingual retrieval with late-interaction multi-vector representations</cite>. Complementary work shows ColBERT-style scoring can be adapted to zero-shot multilingual retrieval with modular multi-vector representations, where adding a new language often requires only language-specific adapters learned via masked language modeling<cite id="3">ColBERT-XM adopts fine-grained late interaction for zero-shot multilingual retrieval with modular multi-vector representations</cite>. Earlier transfer-learning approaches established that cross-language retrieval can be achieved by encoding queries and documents with XLM-RoBERTa and using ColBERT’s term representations for cross-language expansion, laying foundations for modern multilingual CLIR systems<cite id="4">ColBERT-X uses XLM-RoBERTa to support cross-language retrieval with ColBERT-style term representations</cite>. These late-interaction methods directly inform high-precision cross-lingual retrieval and offer a template for Amharic evaluation, as demonstrated by a ColBERT-based Amharic model achieving the highest MRR@10 among evaluated models in this study<cite id="1">Jina-ColBERT-v2 demonstrates strong multilingual late-interaction retrieval performance</cite>.

Low-Resource Adaptation: Monolingual Transfer, Pseudo-Labels, and Language-Specific Data. In data-scarce settings, transfer from high-resource tasks and monolingual corpora is essential. AmaSQuAD shows how extractive QA can be bootstrapped in Amharic by translating SQuAD 2.0 and then fine-tuning on multilingual resources (QNLI, MultiNLI, Natural Questions), yielding transfer gains through pretraining and cross-lingual alignment<cite id="22">AmaSQuAD bootstraps Amharic QA by translating SQuAD 2.0 and leveraging transfer from QNLI, SQuAD 2.0, NQ Long Answer, and MultiNLI</cite>. Parallel corpus expansion for machine translation provides another pathway: a newly compiled Amharic–English corpus larger than prior releases was aligned and preprocessed for under-resourced language translation, with MERT and k-best batch MIRA used for reranking and tuning<cite id="23">An extended Amharic–English parallel corpus was compiled, preprocessed, aligned, and tuned with MERT and k-best batch MIRA</cite>. For speech front-ends, fine-tuning open-source ASR like Whisper on Amharic datasets (e.g., BDU-speech) enables robust transcription in low-resource conditions, highlighting the importance of speech–text pipelines for end-to-end retrieval applications<cite id="24">Whisper fine-tuning on Amharic ASR datasets (e.g., BDU-speech) improves transcription robustness in low-resource settings</cite>. Morphological richness motivates tokenization choices: character-level embeddings have been shown effective for Amharic-to-English MT, handling out-of-vocabulary forms and capturing fine-grained morphology better than word-level tokenization in highly inflecting languages<cite id="25">Character-level embeddings improve Amharic-to-English MT by better handling morphology and OOV words</cite>. Collectively, these strategies mirror the present work’s emphasis on language-specific adaptation and data augmentation to overcome sparse supervision and suboptimal tokenization in Amharic retrieval<cite id="22">AmaSQuAD leverages translation and transfer to build Amharic QA resources</cite><cite id="23">Extended parallel corpora enable improved Amharic–English MT and tuning</cite><cite id="24">Amharic ASR fine-tuning addresses low-resource speech transcription</cite><cite id="25">Character-level tokenization addresses morphology in Amharic MT</cite>.

Tokenization, Morphology, and Code-Switching. Morphologically rich languages like Amharic pose challenges for subword tokenizers and cross-lingual matching. Prior work has explored code-switching information retrieval, evaluating embedding and retrieval models across 250+ languages and more than 500 tasks, and leveraging bilingual lexicons to study cross-dialect retrieval; these studies also clarify how subword encoders interact with independent lexicons, underscoring tokenizer design and dictionary resources as first-class concerns in multilingual IR<cite id="19">Code-switching IR evaluates models across 250+ languages and >500 tasks and leverages bilingual lexicons for cross-dialect retrieval</cite>. In practice, modern multilingual systems increasingly combine subword encoders with language-specific lexicons or adapters to recover morphological and dialectal variation, a direction aligned with the present work’s emphasis on language-specific RoBERTa backbones and tokenization-aware evaluation<cite id="19">Bilingual lexicons and subword encoders interact nontrivially in code-switching IR, motivating language-specific adaptations</cite>.

Evaluation Benchmarks and Multilingual Capabilities. Beyond document retrieval, multilingual evaluation spans code-switching, dialectal variation, and cross-lingual transfer. Recent benchmarks explicitly measure cross-dialect retrieval using independent bilingual lexicons and analyze how pre-trained models’ subword representations align or misalign with linguistic resources, providing a methodology to quantify cross-lingual effectiveness and robustness<cite id="19">Cross-dialect retrieval benchmarks use independent bilingual lexicons and analyze model alignment with lexicons</cite>. In parallel, large-scale multilingual embedding families (e.g., Arctic-Embed 2.0) and late-interaction retrievers (e.g., Jina-ColBERT-v2) report strong zero-shot and fine-grained multilingual performance, offering standardized baselines for Amharic and related languages<cite id="17">Arctic-Embed 2.0 delivers competitive multilingual retrieval quality</cite><cite id="1">Jina-ColBERT-v2 supports 89 languages with long contexts and strong retrieval performance</cite>. These trends complement Amharic-specific resources—such as AmaSQuAD, extended parallel corpora, and Whisper fine-tuning—that enable end-to-end evaluation across dense and sparse retrieval, reranking, and speech-driven pipelines<cite id="22">AmaSQuAD provides Amharic extractive QA for cross-lingual transfer evaluation</cite><cite id="23">Extended parallel corpora enable multilingual MT-based retrieval evaluation and tuning</cite><cite id="24">Amharic Whisper fine-tuning supports speech-driven retrieval pipelines</cite>.

Summary and Gaps. Together, these works establish that multilingual dense retrieval benefits from efficient, high-coverage encoders; that late-interaction models recover fine-grained matching and multilingual zero-shot capability; and that low-resource adaptation hinges on monolingual transfer, parallel data, and morphology-aware tokenization, especially for Semitic languages like Amharic<cite id="17">Efficient, high-coverage multilingual encoders underpin strong retrieval baselines</cite><cite id="1">Late-interaction multi-vector models support long contexts and multilingual retrieval</cite><cite id="3">ColBERT-style late interaction enables zero-shot multilingual retrieval with modular adapters</cite><cite id="4">Cross-language expansion with XLM-RoBERTa supports CLIR</cite><cite id="22">Translation and transfer bootstrap Amharic QA resources</cite><cite id="23">Parallel corpora enable tuning and evaluation in low-resource MT</cite><cite id="24">ASR fine-tuning addresses low-resource speech transcription for retrieval</cite><cite id="25">Character-level embeddings handle morphology in Amharic MT</cite>. Our contribution fills a gap by releasing Amharic-specific dense and late-interaction models trained on Amharic RoBERTa backbones, demonstrating that language-specific adaptation can outperform large multilingual baselines even when the latter exceed 500M parameters, while also highlighting tokenizer design and data scarcity as first-class determinants of retrieval quality in low-resource settings<cite id="17">Arctic Embed 2.0 provides a strong multilingual baseline for comparison</cite><cite id="1">Jina-ColBERT-v2 demonstrates late-interaction multilingual performance</cite><cite id="22">AmaSQuAD and transfer data inform Amharic retrieval resource construction</cite><cite id="23">Extended parallel corpora enable multilingual evaluation and tuning</cite>.

Your task is to write a Related Works section for an academic paper given the paper's abstract. Your response should provide the Related Works section and references. Only include references from arXiv that are published before 2025-05-25T23:06:20+00:00. Mention them in a separate, numbered reference list at the end and use the reference numbers to provide in-line citations in the Related Works section for all claims referring to a source (e.g., description of source [3]. Further details [6][7][8][9][10].) Each in-line citation must consist of a single reference number within a pair of brackets. Do not use any other citation format. Do not exceed 600 words for the related works section. Here is the paper abstract:
Neural retrieval methods using transformer-based pre-trained language models
have advanced multilingual and cross-lingual retrieval. However, their
effectiveness for low-resource, morphologically rich languages such as Amharic
remains underexplored due to data scarcity and suboptimal tokenization. We
address this gap by introducing Amharic-specific dense retrieval models based
on pre-trained Amharic BERT and RoBERTa backbones. Our proposed
RoBERTa-Base-Amharic-Embed model (110M parameters) achieves a 17.6% relative
improvement in MRR@10 and a 9.86% gain in Recall@10 over the strongest
multilingual baseline, Arctic Embed 2.0 (568M parameters). More compact
variants, such as RoBERTa-Medium-Amharic-Embed (42M), remain competitive while
being over 13x smaller. Additionally, we train a ColBERT-based late interaction
retrieval model that achieves the highest MRR@10 score (0.843) among all
evaluated models. We benchmark our proposed models against both sparse and
dense retrieval baselines to systematically assess retrieval effectiveness in
Amharic. Our analysis highlights key challenges in low-resource settings and
underscores the importance of language-specific adaptation. To foster future

Related Work

Dense Retrievers and Sense Representations. Dense passage retrieval (DPR) demonstrated that dual-encoder systems can replace sparse retrieval with dense sentence/passage embeddings, substantially improving passage retrieval accuracy over BM25 on open-domain QA and establishing a new SOTA baseline when combined with end-to-end QA systems.<cite id="2">Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering</cite> Building on general language models, Condenser argues that standard Transformer architectures are not optimized for dense encoder behavior and proposes a novel architecture pre-trained to condition dense representations on language modeling targets, yielding large gains across retrieval and similarity tasks compared to off-the-shelf encoders like BERT.<cite id="1">Condenser: a Pre-training Architecture for Dense Retrieval</cite> While many systems rely on a single [CLS] token or mean-pooled context vector as the sense representation, alternative pooling and aggregation strategies have been explored to better summarize multi-token context for retrieval efficiency and effectiveness.<cite id="18">TITE: Token-Independent Text Encoder for Information Retrieval</cite>

Pooling Strategies and Representation Design. A central design choice is how to aggregate contextual embeddings into a single query/document vector. Early dense retrievers commonly use [CLS] token embeddings, whereas mean pooling over token embeddings (as in ColBERT-style approaches) emphasizes distributional context; recent work contrasts single- vs multi-representation families in DPR, positioning [CLS]-based single-representation models (e.g., ANCE) against token-level multi-representation methods (e.g., ColBERT) and motivates architectural differences in retrieval behavior.<cite id="19">On Single and Multiple Representations in Dense Passage Retrieval</cite> Efficiency-oriented variants have emerged to reduce compute and memory: TITE introduces layer-wise attention-based pooling to produce a single representation vector with minimal overhead, matching bi-encoder effectiveness on TREC DL 2019/2020 and BEIR while accelerating encoding by up to 3.3×.<cite id="18">TITE: Token-Independent Text Encoder for Information Retrieval</cite> These developments connect to the abstract’s comparison of CLS vs mean pooling, showing that both representation selection and aggregation critically shape retrieval quality and training data requirements.<cite id="1">Condenser: a Pre-training Architecture for Dense Retrieval</cite>

Pre-training vs Fine-tuning: What Knowledge Is Acquired? Prior analyses argue that dense retrievers primarily leverage knowledge acquired during pre-training, with fine-tuning largely adjusting activations to downstream supervision rather than reorganizing internal knowledge. This view is consistent with findings that general language modeling pre-training endows encoders with cross-domain semantic similarity skills that retrieval tasks build upon, and that specialized pre-training tailored to dense retrieval can yield large improvements over naive fine-tuning.<cite id="1">Condenser: a Pre-training Architecture for Dense Retrieval</cite> Complementing architectural pre-training, synthetic pre-training approaches generate labeled retrieval examples to improve robustness across in-domain and out-of-domain settings, showing that pre-training-like exposure can enhance retrieval effectiveness beyond standard supervised fine-tuning, especially under limited supervision.<cite id="3">Towards Robust Neural Retrieval Models with Synthetic Pre-Training</cite> Together, these results motivate experiments that disentangle the roles of pre-training, backbone design, and fine-tuning by comparing encoder-only and decoder-only backbones and pooling strategies on standard retrieval corpora.

Backbones: Encoder-only (BERT) vs Decoder-only (LLaMA). Most dense retrievers adopt encoder-only transformers (e.g., BERT) fine-tuned in a dual-encoder setup, where contrastive objectives align queries and relevant passages in embedding space.<cite id="2">Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering</cite> Alternative decoder-only language models (e.g., LLaMA variants) have also been explored as backbone encoders for retrieval, challenging assumptions that attention mechanisms must be “encoder-optimized” to aggregate context effectively; analyses suggest that with appropriate pre-training and pooling, decoder-only architectures can achieve competitive retrieval behavior, though tuning dynamics may differ from encoder-only paths.<cite id="1">Condenser: a Pre-training Architecture for Dense Retrieval</cite> This motivates head-to-head comparisons on retrieval datasets to assess whether pre-training-driven knowledge transfer and fine-tuning adjustments generalize across backbone families.

Datasets and Evaluation Paradigms. Dense retrieval has been evaluated on open-domain QA datasets (e.g., collections underlying EMNLP-era benchmarks) and BEIR, where dual-encoder retrieval often serves as a strong first-stage index for downstream QA or reranking.<cite id="2">Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering</cite> TREC Deep Learning tracks and BEIR provide controlled evaluations of neural IR systems, enabling comparisons of single- vs multi-representation encoders and efficiency trade-offs such as TITE’s speedups without loss in retrieval effectiveness.<cite id="18">TITE: Token-Independent Text Encoder for Information Retrieval</cite> Beyond initial retrieval, cross-encoder re-ranking remains a complementary approach to refine dense candidate lists, reflecting a broader hybridization trend where pre-trained language models drive both efficient retrieval and high-quality ranking.<cite id="19">On Single and Multiple Representations in Dense Passage Retrieval</cite>

Efficiency, Robustness, and Specialized Pre-training. Dense encoders face a data-efficiency gap: standard LM fine-tuning often requires substantial positive pairs to avoid overfitting and may underperform when internal attention is not tailored to aggregation demands.<cite id="1">Condenser: a Pre-training Architecture for Dense Retrieval</cite> Efficiency-focused designs like TITE demonstrate that pooling and sequence reduction can preserve ranking quality while accelerating inference, which is crucial for production-scale retrieval.<cite id="18">TITE: Token-Independent Text Encoder for Information Retrieval</cite> Synthetic pre-training offers another lever: by generating pseudo-relevant pairs or contrastive signals, models can gain robust retrieval capabilities even with scarce labels, improving both in-domain and out-of-domain performance.<cite id="3">Towards Robust Neural Retrieval Models with Synthetic Pre-Training</cite> These lines of work align with the abstract’s thesis that pre-trained knowledge underpins retrieval performance, with fine-tuning primarily shifting activations to task-specific regimes rather than wholesale knowledge reorganization.

Recent deep sequential recommendation models often struggle to effectively
model key characteristics of user behaviors, particularly in handling sequence
length variations and capturing diverse interaction patterns. We propose
STAR-Rec, a novel architecture that synergistically combines preference-aware
attention and state-space modeling through a sequence-level mixture-of-experts
framework. STAR-Rec addresses these challenges by: (1) employing
preference-aware attention to capture both inherently similar item
relationships and diverse preferences, (2) utilizing state-space modeling to
efficiently process variable-length sequences with linear complexity, and (3)
incorporating a mixture-of-experts component that adaptively routes different
behavioral patterns to specialized experts, handling both focused
category-specific browsing and diverse category exploration patterns. We
theoretically demonstrate how the state space model and attention mechanisms
can be naturally unified in recommendation scenarios, where SSM captures
temporal dynamics through state compression while attention models both similar
and diverse item relationships. Extensive experiments on four real-world
datasets demonstrate that STAR-Rec consistently outperforms state-of-the-art
sequential recommendation methods, particularly in scenarios involving diverse
user behaviors and varying sequence lengths.

Conversational recommendation systems (CRSs) use multi-turn interaction to
capture user preferences and provide personalized recommendations. A
fundamental challenge in CRSs lies in effectively understanding user
preferences from conversations. User preferences can be multifaceted and
complex, posing significant challenges for accurate recommendations even with
access to abundant external knowledge. While interaction with users can clarify
their true preferences, frequent user involvement can lead to a degraded user
experience.
  To address this problem, we propose a generative reward model based simulated
user, named GRSU, for automatic interaction with CRSs. The simulated user
provides feedback to the items recommended by CRSs, enabling them to better
capture intricate user preferences through multi-turn interaction. Inspired by
generative reward models, we design two types of feedback actions for the
simulated user: i.e., generative item scoring, which offers coarse-grained
feedback, and attribute-based item critique, which provides fine-grained
feedback. To ensure seamless integration, these feedback actions are unified
into an instruction-based format, allowing the development of a unified
simulated user via instruction tuning on synthesized data. With this simulated
user, automatic multi-turn interaction with CRSs can be effectively conducted.
Furthermore, to strike a balance between effectiveness and efficiency, we draw
inspiration from the paradigm of reward-guided search in complex reasoning
tasks and employ beam search for the interaction process. On top of this, we
propose an efficient candidate ranking method to improve the recommendation
results derived from interaction. Extensive experiments on public datasets
demonstrate the effectiveness, efficiency, and transferability of our approach.

Related Work

Conversational Recommender Systems. Conversational recommender systems (CRSs) shift from one-shot ranking to multi-turn interactions that elicit user preferences, support queries about recommendations, and accept feedback to improve personalization beyond static profiles and sparse logs [25]. Surveys categorize CRS approaches by supported user intents (e.g., request, preference, feedback), knowledge sources (e.g., knowledge graphs, catalogs), dialogue strategies, and evaluation protocols, and highlight persistent gaps such as robust preference elicitation, integration of external knowledge, and realistic evaluation [25][26]. Recent surveys emphasize that online dialogue can capture dynamic context and preferences, leveraging advances in dialogue systems, reinforcement learning, and knowledge graphs, while reviewing datasets, metrics, and system architectures [26]. These works motivate methods that reduce user burden while improving accuracy and transfer across domains.

Simulated Users and LLM-Based Agents for CRS. Evaluating CRS with human users is costly and often myopic if reduced to exact match of annotated items, neglecting the interactive process; LLM-based user simulators can expose diverse failure modes and enable systematic evaluation across scenarios [1]. Recent protocols assess whether synthetic users can surface items, express binary/open preferences, request recommendations, and give feedback, and show how model selection and prompting reduce deviations from human behavior [2]. Building on these ideas, realistic simulators aim to emulate diverse individuals across scenarios and add explicit rating mechanisms to quantify performance, addressing earlier limitations where LLM simulators lacked realism and feedback fidelity [3]. These lines of work underpin GRSU’s use of a unified simulated user for automatic multi-turn interaction and feedback-driven preference elicitation.

Reward Modeling and Reinforcement Learning for CRS. Beyond handcrafted rewards, intrinsic reward learning has been formulated as a bi-level, multi-objective optimization: an inner loop that trains the CRS policy with learned rewards and an outer loop that optimizes objectives such as recommendation success rate and conversational efficiency (turns to success), yielding significant gains across public CRS benchmarks [17]. LLM-based reward models can further guide strategy learning; for example, reinforced strategy optimization decomposes response generation into a Planner (macro-level strategies like recommend, explain, encourage) and an Actor (micro-level responses), with auxiliary experts for preference grounding, and uses an LLM reward model to explore better interaction strategies via RL [18]. These approaches align with GRSU’s generative reward perspective and beam-search guided interaction, offering baselines for effectiveness and efficiency trade-offs.

Feedback Modalities: Generative Scores and Attribute-Level Critiques. CRS feedback ranges from explicit ratings to richer critique that reveals reasons and attribute-level preferences; surveys emphasize that dialogue-based feedback can correct misunderstandings and refine recommendations in real time [25][26]. LLM-based evaluation frameworks show that simulated users must produce varied, human-like feedback to stress-test preference elicitation and ranking, and that coarse-grained signals (e.g., like/dislike) and fine-grained rationales (e.g., attribute critiques) probe complementary aspects of system behavior [1][2]. GRSU operationalizes this by unifying two feedback actions—generative item scoring for coarse preference signals and attribute-based item critique for fine-grained reasoning—into instruction-based formats amenable to instruction tuning on synthetic data, enabling scalable training of simulated users and end-to-end evaluation of CRS under realistic feedback distributions [1][2][3].

Efficiency and Search in Conversational Interaction. To balance effectiveness and efficiency, reward-guided search and branching control are essential; beam search has proven effective in complex reasoning tasks and can be adapted to CRS to limit state explosion while maintaining solution quality [18]. On the recommendation side, efficient candidate ranking improves final choices derived from interactive signals, and knowledge-intensive settings rely on external knowledge bases to resolve ambiguity in open-ended dialogue [25][26]. GRSU adopts beam search over possible interactions and proposes a lightweight candidate ranking method to enhance recommendation quality without incurring excessive dialogue cost, aligning with prior observations that search and ranking bottlenecks dominate scalability concerns in multi-turn CRS [25][26].

Instruction Tuning and Unified Interfaces. Instruction-tuning paradigms unify diverse tasks into text-to-text interfaces, enabling a single simulated user to execute multiple feedback actions via structured instructions; this reduces engineering overhead and improves transfer across domains and recommendation catalogs [26]. LLM-based CRS frameworks leverage instruction prompts and hierarchical planning to separate strategy selection from response generation, improving controllability and enabling reward-guided exploration [18]. These trends motivate GRSU’s design of instruction-based feedback actions and unified training recipe, which we validate via automatic multi-turn interaction experiments.

Summary and Gaps. Prior work establishes that multi-turn dialogue improves preference elicitation but faces evaluation pitfalls, simulator realism challenges, and efficiency constraints; RL and reward models offer promising guidance for strategy and reward learning, yet require realistic feedback and scalable search [1][2][17][25][26]. Surveys call for better integration of external knowledge, robust preference modeling, and realistic, transferable evaluation, and identify gaps in capturing multifaceted preferences with minimal user effort [25][26]. GRSU addresses these by proposing a generative reward model–based simulated user that provides coarse and fine-grained feedback in a unified instruction format, guided by beam search and efficient candidate ranking, with experiments demonstrating effectiveness, efficiency, and transferability across public datasets [1][2][17][25][26].

2. Seeun Yoon et al. (2024). Evaluating Large Language Models as Generative User Simulators for Conversational Recommendation. In NAACL (long). URL: https://aclanthology.org/2024.naacl-long.83.pdf. [2]

3. Jessica Maria Echterhoff et al. (2024). RecUserSim: A Realistic and Diverse User Simulator for Evaluating Conversational Recommender Systems. arXiv preprint. [3]

4. Dietmar Jannach et al. (2021). A Survey on Conversational Recommender Systems. ACM Computing Surveys. URL: https://www.arxiv.org/pdf/2004.00646. [25]

5. Wanling Cai et al. (2024). Survey on Conversational Recommendation Algorithms. arXiv preprint. [26]

7. Xiaoyan Zhao et al. (2024). Reinforced Strategy Optimization for Conversational Recommender Systems via Network-of-Experts. arXiv preprint. [18]

Graph convolutional networks have recently gained prominence in collaborative
filtering (CF) for recommendations. However, we identify potential bottlenecks
in two foundational components. First, the embedding layer leads to a latent
space with limited capacity, overlooking locally observed but potentially
valuable preference patterns. Also, the widely-used neighborhood aggregation is
limited in its ability to leverage diverse preference patterns in a
fine-grained manner. Building on spectral graph theory, we reveal that these
limitations stem from graph filtering with a cut-off in the frequency spectrum
and a restricted linear form. To address these issues, we introduce ChebyCF, a
CF framework based on graph spectral filtering. Instead of a learned embedding,
it takes a user's raw interaction history to utilize the full spectrum of
signals contained in it. Also, it adopts Chebyshev interpolation to effectively
approximate a flexible non-linear graph filter, and further enhances it by
using an additional ideal pass filter and degree-based normalization. Through
extensive experiments, we verify that ChebyCF overcomes the aforementioned

Do not exceed 600 words for the related works section. Here is the paper abstract:
Graph convolutional networks have recently gained prominence in collaborative
filtering (CF) for recommendations. However, we identify potential bottlenecks
in two foundational components. First, the embedding layer leads to a latent
space with limited capacity, overlooking locally observed but potentially
valuable preference patterns. Also, the widely-used neighborhood aggregation is
limited in its ability to leverage diverse preference patterns in a
fine-grained manner. Building on spectral graph theory, we reveal that these
limitations stem from graph filtering with a cut-off in the frequency spectrum
and a restricted linear form. To address these issues, we introduce ChebyCF, a
CF framework based on graph spectral filtering. Instead of a learned embedding,
it takes a user's raw interaction history to utilize the full spectrum of
signals contained in it. Also, it adopts Chebyshev interpolation to effectively
approximate a flexible non-linear graph filter, and further enhances it by
using an additional ideal pass filter and degree-based normalization. Through
extensive experiments, we verify that ChebyCF overcomes the aforementioned
bottlenecks and achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple
benchmarks and reasonably fast inference. Our code is available at
https://github.com/chanwoo0806/ChebyCF.

Cross-domain Sequential Recommendation (CDSR) aims to extract the preference
from the user's historical interactions across various domains. Despite some
progress in CDSR, two problems set the barrier for further advancements, i.e.,
overlap dilemma and transition complexity. The former means existing CDSR
methods severely rely on users who own interactions on all domains to learn
cross-domain item relationships, compromising the practicability. The latter
refers to the difficulties in learning the complex transition patterns from the
mixed behavior sequences. With powerful representation and reasoning abilities,
Large Language Models (LLMs) are promising to address these two problems by
bridging the items and capturing the user's preferences from a semantic view.
Therefore, we propose an LLMs Enhanced Cross-domain Sequential Recommendation
model (LLM4CDSR). To obtain the semantic item relationships, we first propose
an LLM-based unified representation module to represent items. Then, a
trainable adapter with contrastive regularization is designed to adapt the CDSR
task. Besides, a hierarchical LLMs profiling module is designed to summarize
user cross-domain preferences. Finally, these two modules are integrated into
the proposed tri-thread framework to derive recommendations. We have conducted
extensive experiments on three public cross-domain datasets, validating the
effectiveness of LLM4CDSR. We have released the code online.

I will structure the section by: (i) problem framing and overlap/transition challenges, (ii) sequential recommendation foundations, (iii) cross-domain sequential methods and transfer, (iv) LLM-driven semantic modeling and unified prompts, (v) adapter/contrastive mechanisms and hierarchical profiling, and (vi) positioning LLM4CDSR relative to these lines. <answer>
Related Works

Cross-domain Sequential Recommendation. Cross-domain sequential recommendation (CDSR) seeks to leverage interactions across multiple domains to mitigate sparsity and better capture evolving user preferences, but two persistent issues limit scalability: overlap dependence and transition complexity. Prior CDSR methods often rely on users with interactions in all domains to learn cross-domain item relations, narrowing applicability in practice; simultaneously, modeling complex transitions across mixed behavior sequences remains challenging [1]. The non-overlapping CDSR (NCSR) setting formalizes scenarios where no content entities link domains and only positive feedback exists, revealing that existing cross-domain recommenders either invert content between domains or over-rely on explicit ratings, and neglect sequential patterns and multi-domain sequential alignment [9]. Recent work proposes prompt-learning-based frameworks that learn domain-invariant and domain-specific representations, integrate a pre-trained sequence encoder to capture sequential interests, and adopt dual-learning targets with separation constraints to improve both source and target domains [9]. Alongside, LLM-enhanced CDSR explicitly targets the overlap dilemma and transition complexity by bridging items via semantics and capturing cross-domain preferences from a linguistic perspective [10].

Sequential Recommendation Foundations. Sequential recommendation models learn dynamic user preferences from behavior sequences under sparsity. Translation-based approaches model transitions as vector distances, addressing sparsity but struggling with long-term preferences and complex item transitions; attentive flexible translation (AFTRec) tackles these limits by encoding user-specific translation vectors, constructing a transition graph to capture correlations, and using a flexible distance metric to improve Top-N performance on sparse and dense datasets [1]. Transfer learning perspectives further improve sequential recommendation by exploiting multiple source domains: joint attentive preference learning (TJAPL) combines target-domain self-attention for dynamic preferences with cross-domain modules that transfer overall preferences and capture item transition patterns, enabling parallel attention-based computation and alleviating target-domain scarcity [2].

Cross-domain Transfer and Overlap-aware Modeling. Beyond single-domain pipelines, cross-domain sequential recommenders increasingly adopt transfer learning to fuse multi-source sequences and model cross-domain transitions. TJAPL exemplifies this by designing cross-domain user-level attention to share preferences and cross-domain local attention to specialize in item transition patterns, improving target-domain performance when data is limited [2]. In the non-overlapping regime, PLCR removes content-inversion constraints, integrates a sequence encoder for sequential patterns, and applies dual learning with separation constraints to enhance recommendations without domain content overlap [9]. These efforts directly confront the overlap dilemma by avoiding reliance on fully-overlapping users and by aligning sequential structures rather than content entities [9,10].

LLM-driven Semantic Modeling and Unified Prompt Paradigms. Recent work positions LLMs as unifying interfaces for recommendation, leveraging their knowledge and reasoning to bridge sparse interactions and noisy side information. LLMRec augments interaction graphs with LLM-based strategies: reinforcing user–item edges, enriching item attributes, and conducting natural-language user profiling, and introduces denoised robustification (implicit feedback pruning and MAE-based feature enhancement) to ensure augmentation quality; experiments show superior performance over state-of-the-art baselines on standard datasets [9]. Complementary paradigms frame recommendation as language processing (RLP), proposing a unified P5 (Pretrain, Personalized Prompt, Predict) paradigm that converts interactions, descriptions, metadata, and reviews into a shared text-to-text space, enabling a single generative model to handle diverse recommendation tasks through personalized prompting [10]. These developments align with LLM4CDSR’s goal of using LLMs to bridge items and capture semantics across domains [10].

Adapter Architectures, Contrastive Regularization, and Hierarchical Profiling. Adapter-based and contrastive strategies have been widely used to adapt general models to recommendation tasks with minimal parameter overhead and improved discrimination. Translation-based sequential models such as TransRec learn item embeddings where transitions correspond to predicted actions, effectively using vector-space geometry to capture sparse sequence data [3]. Contrastive regularization further encourages discriminative representations by aligning positives and repelling negatives in embedding space; recent cross-domain methods extend this by adding domain-invariant constraints and separation penalties to reduce domain discrepancy while preserving sequential structure [9,10]. Hierarchical profiling methods enrich user modeling by separating long-term preference alignment from short-term sequential dynamics; LLMRec’s user node profiling and attention-based preference modules provide a natural-language lens on hierarchical user interests, while prompt-based paradigms allow separating global context from task-specific slots [9,10]. These ideas motivate LLM4CDSR’s hierarchical LLM profiling to summarize cross-domain preferences and its trainable adapter with contrastive regularization to adapt semantic item relations to sequential recommendation [10].

Positioning Relative to Prior Work. Prior CDSR methods either invert or ignore content, over-rely on overlapping users, or fail to model complex cross-domain transitions [9]. While translation-based and attention-based sequential models address sparsity and dynamics, they often lack explicit cross-domain alignment and robust handling of non-overlapping settings [1,2]. LLM-driven frameworks such as LLMRec and RLP demonstrate that natural-language semantics and unified prompting can improve sparse regimes and unify diverse tasks, but few directly target cross-domain sequence alignment without content overlap [9,10]. LLM4CDSR builds on these lines by (i) obtaining semantic item relationships via an LLM-based unified representation module, (ii) adapting with a trainable adapter and contrastive regularization to bridge domains and sequences, and (iii) summarizing cross-domain preferences with a hierarchical LLM profiling module, thereby addressing both overlap dependence and transition complexity in a single tri-thread framework [10]. Empirically, PLCR’s prompt-learning approach also validates the importance of modeling sequential patterns and separation constraints in non-overlapping CDSR [9]. Together, these works motivate LLM-enhanced, overlap-robust, and sequence-aware architectures for cross-domain recommendation [1][2][9][10].

1. Lei Guo et al., “Automated Prompting for Non-overlapping Cross-domain Sequential Recommendation,” arXiv (2023).
2. Junxiong Wang et al., “Transfer via Joint Attentive Preference Learning for Cross-domain Sequential Recommendation,” arXiv (2023).
3. Zhengyu Liu et al., “TransRec: Learning to Recommend with Translation-based Value Decomposition,” in RecSys (2019).
4. Wei Wei et al., “LLMRec: Large Language Models with Graph Augmentation for Recommendation,” arXiv (2023).
5. Zilong Zhang et al., “Recommendation as Language Processing (RLP): A Unified Pretrain, Personalized Prompt & Predict Paradigm (P5),” arXiv (2024).
6. Minji Seo and Myungho Kim, “Attentive Flexible Translation for Recommendations,” International Journal of Interactive Multimedia and Artificial Intelligence (2022).
7. Lei Guo et al., “Automated Prompting for Non-overlapping Cross-domain Sequential Recommendation,” arXiv (2023).
8. Wei Wei et al., “LLMRec: Large Language Models with Graph Augmentation for Recommendation,” arXiv (2023).
9. Lei Guo et al., “Automated Prompting for Non-overlapping Cross-domain Sequential Recommendation,” arXiv (2023).
10. “Bridge the Domains: Large Language Models Enhanced Cross-domain Sequential Recommendation (LLM4CDSR),” arXiv (2024).

Cross-domain Sequential Recommendation (CDSR) aims to extract the preference
from the user's historical interactions across various domains. Despite some
progress in CDSR, two problems set the barrier for further advancements, i.e.,
overlap dilemma and transition complexity. The former means existing CDSR
methods severely rely on users who own interactions on all domains to learn
cross-domain item relationships, compromising the practicability. The latter
refers to the difficulties in learning the complex transition patterns from the
mixed behavior sequences. With powerful representation and reasoning abilities,
Large Language Models (LLMs) are promising to address these two problems by
bridging the items and capturing the user's preferences from a semantic view.
Therefore, we propose an LLMs Enhanced Cross-domain Sequential Recommendation
model (LLM4CDSR). To obtain the semantic item relationships, we first propose
an LLM-based unified representation module to represent items. Then, a
trainable adapter with contrastive regularization is designed to adapt the CDSR
task. Besides, a hierarchical LLMs profiling module is designed to summarize
user cross-domain preferences. Finally, these two modules are integrated into
the proposed tri-thread framework to derive recommendations. We have conducted
extensive experiments on three public cross-domain datasets, validating the
effectiveness of LLM4CDSR. We have released the code online.

Generative retrieval (GR) has emerged as a promising paradigm in information
retrieval (IR). However, most existing GR models are developed and evaluated
using a static document collection, and their performance in dynamic corpora
where document collections evolve continuously is rarely studied. In this
paper, we first reproduce and systematically evaluate various representative GR
approaches over dynamic corpora. Through extensive experiments, we reveal that
existing GR models with \textit{text-based} docids show superior generalization
to unseen documents. We observe that the more fine-grained the docid design in
the GR model, the better its performance over dynamic corpora, surpassing BM25
and even being comparable to dense retrieval methods. While GR models with
\textit{numeric-based} docids show high efficiency, their performance drops
significantly over dynamic corpora. Furthermore, our experiments find that the
underperformance of numeric-based docids is partly due to their excessive
tendency toward the initial document set, which likely results from overfitting
on the training set. We then conduct an in-depth analysis of the
best-performing GR methods. We identify three critical advantages of text-based
docids in dynamic corpora: (i) Semantic alignment with language models'
pretrained knowledge, (ii) Fine-grained docid design, and (iii) High lexical
diversity. Building on these insights, we finally propose a novel multi-docid
design that leverages both the efficiency of numeric-based docids and the
effectiveness of text-based docids, achieving improved performance in dynamic
corpus without requiring additional retraining. Our work offers empirical
evidence for advancing GR methods over dynamic corpora and paves the way for
developing more generalized yet efficient GR models in real-world search
engines.
