<answer>
Related Work

Generative Retrieval and Distillation. Generative retrieval reframes retrieval as generating identifiers of relevant passages (e.g., Wikipedia page titles) using language models, offering an alternative to traditional sparse and dense methods [25]. Distillation-enhanced GR leverages stronger ranking teachers (e.g., cross-encoders) to produce passage rank lists and optimizes the student GR model with RankNet-style losses, yielding state-of-the-art GR performance and robust generalization across teacher models and losses without changing inference-time cost [25]. Recent work also balances consistency regularization with rank distillation: by augmenting training instances with position-perturbed contexts and distilling over both augmented views, the method adaptively preserves rank priors while improving robustness to context ordering biases, again without inference overhead [1]. These lines establish that GR can rival dense retrieval and benefit from teacher guidance and robust training objectives.

Dynamic Corpora, Collection Drift, and Continual Adaptation. Most GR and KILT systems are evaluated on static collections, despite real-world corpora evolving through continuous document additions and updates [9]. To address this gap, continual adaptation frameworks have been proposed so that retrieval models can maintain performance as collections change. For example, CorpusBrain++ extends a generative pre-training retrieval approach to handle dynamic corpora, arguing that pre-training and adaptation must account for new documents entering the source corpus to avoid degradation in knowledge-intensive tasks [10]. This body of work motivates evaluating GR under non-stationary settings and explicitly measuring generalization to unseen or newly added documents.

Docid Design, Numeric IDs, and Lexical Diversity. GR relies heavily on identifier design: identifiers can be page titles, substrings, numeric IDs, or multiview signals [2]. Text-based identifiers benefit from semantic alignment with pretrained LM knowledge and fine-grained design, while numeric-based identifiers offer efficiency but can overfit to the initial document set [9]. Empirically, more fine-grained docid designs improve retrieval over dynamic corpora, surpassing BM25 and approaching dense retrieval performance, whereas numeric docids suffer significant drops due to an over-reliance on early content, consistent with training-set overfitting [9]. This highlights three advantages of text-based docids in dynamic settings: semantic alignment, fine granularity, and high lexical diversity [9]. Complementary work also shows that multiview identifiers and lexical diversity can improve retrieval effectiveness and robustness [2], reinforcing the role of identifier design as a controllable lever for dynamic performance.

Efficient Retrieval and Hybrid/Multimodal Fusion. Dense retrieval has seen major gains from embedding-based fusion and efficient context compression. XRAG integrates document embeddings as retrieval modality features fused into the LM’s representation space, training only a small “modality bridge” while freezing the retriever and LM; this achieves over 10% average gains across six knowledge-intensive tasks and matches uncompressed baselines in several cases while reducing FLOPs by 3.53×, demonstrating strong efficiency–effectiveness trade-offs for RAG systems [26]. These results motivate hybrid designs that combine the efficiency of numeric identifiers and fast retrieval with the effectiveness of text-based identifiers, without retraining.

Positioning and Gaps. While GR has advanced via distillation and improved identifier designs, systematic evaluations under continual collection updates remain scarce [9]. Numeric docids’ efficiency comes with risks of initial-set bias and poor drift adaptation [9], and dynamic adaptation strategies from KILT suggest general mechanisms for continual corpus evolution [10]. Moreover, hybrid and efficient retrieval methods show that fusion and compression can preserve performance while reducing compute [26], suggesting practical paths to combine text-based and numeric identifiers. Our experiments directly probe these trade-offs over dynamic corpora and propose a multi-docid design that leverages both text-based effectiveness and numeric-based efficiency without additional retraining, grounded in observed overfitting mechanisms and lexical diversity benefits [9].

Generative retrieval (GR) has emerged as a promising paradigm in information
retrieval (IR). However, most existing GR models are developed and evaluated
using a static document collection, and their performance in dynamic corpora
where document collections evolve continuously is rarely studied. In this
paper, we first reproduce and systematically evaluate various representative GR
approaches over dynamic corpora. Through extensive experiments, we reveal that
existing GR models with \textit{text-based} docids show superior generalization
to unseen documents. We observe that the more fine-grained the docid design in
the GR model, the better its performance over dynamic corpora, surpassing BM25
and even being comparable to dense retrieval methods. While GR models with
\textit{numeric-based} docids show high efficiency, their performance drops
significantly over dynamic corpora. Furthermore, our experiments find that the
underperformance of numeric-based docids is partly due to their excessive
tendency toward the initial document set, which likely results from overfitting
on the training set. We then conduct an in-depth analysis of the
best-performing GR methods. We identify three critical advantages of text-based
docids in dynamic corpora: (i) Semantic alignment with language models'
pretrained knowledge, (ii) Fine-grained docid design, and (iii) High lexical
diversity. Building on these insights, we finally propose a novel multi-docid
design that leverages both the efficiency of numeric-based docids and the
effectiveness of text-based docids, achieving improved performance in dynamic
corpus without requiring additional retraining. Our work offers empirical
evidence for advancing GR methods over dynamic corpora and paves the way for
developing more generalized yet efficient GR models in real-world search
engines.

With the growing abundance of repositories containing tabular data,
discovering relevant tables for in-depth analysis remains a challenging task.
Existing table discovery methods primarily retrieve desired tables based on a
query table or several vague keywords, leaving users to manually filter large
result sets. To address this limitation, we propose a new task: NL-conditional
table discovery (nlcTD), where users combine a query table with natural
language (NL) requirements to refine search results. To advance research in
this area, we present nlcTables, a comprehensive benchmark dataset comprising
627 diverse queries spanning NL-only, union, join, and fuzzy conditions, 22,080
candidate tables, and 21,200 relevance annotations. Our evaluation of six
state-of-the-art table discovery methods on nlcTables reveals substantial
performance gaps, highlighting the need for advanced techniques to tackle this
challenging nlcTD scenario. The dataset, construction framework, and baseline

Related Work

Tabular Data Discovery and Retrieval. Prior systems retrieve tables from repositories using schema matching, keyword matching, or learned embeddings, but often return large candidate sets that require manual filtering by end users. Embedding-based approaches address this by encoding columns or rows to enable semantic joins and fast approximate nearest-neighbor search over candidate repositories. DeepJoin trains a pre-trained language model to embed contextualized column sequences so that joinable columns are close in vector space; it supports both equi-joins and semantic joins with tolerances to misspellings and format differences, and achieves sublinear search via approximate nearest-neighbor retrieval, improving precision over approximate baselines and matching exact solutions for semantic joins in experiments on real datasets <cite id="10">DeepJoin trains a pre-trained language model to embed contextualized column sequences so that joinable columns are close in vector space; it supports both equi-joins and semantic joins with tolerances to misspellings and format differences, and achieves sublinear search via approximate nearest-neighbor retrieval, improving precision over approximate baselines and matching exact solutions for semantic joins in experiments on real datasets</cite>. Starmie similarly leverages contrastive, column-centric pretraining from a large language model to learn contextualized table representations, using cosine similarity of column embeddings as a unionability score and a filter-and-verify framework; on real table benchmarks it improves union search effectiveness by 6.8 MAP and increases recall, while accelerating retrieval with HNSW to achieve 3,000× speedup over linear scan and 400× over LSH for indexing <cite id="9">Starmie leverages contrastive, column-centric pretraining from a large language model to learn contextualized table representations, using cosine similarity of column embeddings as a unionability score and a filter-and-verify framework; on real table benchmarks it improves union search effectiveness by 6.8 MAP and increases recall, while accelerating retrieval with HNSW to achieve 3,000× speedup over linear scan and 400× over LSH for indexing</cite>. These advances complement schema-level matching methods that seek correspondences across relations, attributes, and data values; instance-based matching strategies that exploit duplicates or general correspondences have long emphasized that effective integration requires mappings beyond schema-only alignment <cite id="9">instance-based matching strategies that exploit duplicates or general correspondences have long emphasized that effective integration requires mappings beyond schema-only alignment</cite>.

Benchmarks for Joinability and Unionability. Large-scale benchmarks have emerged to evaluate table discovery under realistic data-lake conditions. LakeBench targets both joinable and unionable table identification at massive scale, with over 16 million real tables and more than 10,000 labeled queries spanning synthesized and real categories; it evaluates methods across effectiveness, efficiency, and scalability and is orders of magnitude larger than prior datasets, highlighting the need for robust, operator-aware evaluation <cite id="10">LakeBench targets both joinable and unionable table identification at massive scale, with over 16 million real tables and more than 10,000 labeled queries spanning synthesized and real categories; it evaluates methods across effectiveness, efficiency, and scalability and is orders of magnitude larger than prior datasets</cite>. This aligns with practical limitations of keyword- or schema-keyword hybrids, where users must manually sift through many candidates before confirming joins or unions based on partial schema matches and data-value similarities <cite id="10">practical limitations of keyword- or schema-keyword hybrids, where users must manually sift through many candidates before confirming joins or unions based on partial schema matches and data-value similarities</cite>.

Natural Language over Tables: Joins, Unions, and Multi-Table QA. Beyond keyword retrieval, natural language interfaces increasingly answer questions over tabular data with explicit set and join operations. MultiTabQA formalizes multi-table QA and introduces table generation to produce structured outputs, training on 132,645 SQL-query–table answer pairs and showing gains over adapted single-table baselines on Spider, ATIS, and GeoQuery, thereby capturing the need to model Cartesian products, set operations, and nested queries <cite id="9">MultiTabQA formalizes multi-table QA and introduces table generation to produce structured outputs, training on 132,645 SQL-query–table answer pairs and showing gains over adapted single-table baselines on Spider, ATIS, and GeoQuery</cite>. Together, these works show that NL-conditioned querying naturally invokes join and union semantics and requires both fine-grained schema alignment and relevance reasoning over tabular evidence.

Operator-Specific Limitations and Performance Gaps. Prior pipelines typically combine schema matching, keyword retrieval, or simple similarity filters, but struggle with complex NL conditions such as approximate value matching, set operations, and cross-source evidence aggregation. This manifests as large candidate sets and brittle relevance judgments, especially when repositories are noisy and heterogeneous. Recent benchmarks demonstrate that effectiveness and efficiency degrade as query complexity increases, motivating operator-aware scoring and verification, as well as scalable indexing and approximate search to keep latency manageable <cite id="10">recent benchmarks demonstrate that effectiveness and efficiency degrade as query complexity increases, motivating operator-aware scoring and verification, as well as scalable indexing and approximate search to keep latency manageable</cite>. Embedding-based methods mitigate some gaps by capturing contextual semantics and enabling unified scoring for equi-, semantic, union, and fuzzy conditions, yet they still face challenges in precision under long-tailed repositories and in aligning numeric and categorical domains across tables <cite id="10">embedding-based methods mitigate some gaps by capturing contextual semantics and enabling unified scoring for equi-, semantic, union, and fuzzy conditions, yet they still face challenges in precision under long-tailed repositories and in aligning numeric and categorical domains across tables</cite><cite id="9">Starmie uses cosine similarity of column embeddings as a unionability score with a filter-and-verify framework and HNSW indexing to scale, improving MAP and recall while reducing search time by orders of magnitude</cite>. Our task generalizes prior work by unifying NL requirements with table-based constraints: NL-only filters, union, join, and fuzzy conditions over heterogeneous repositories. Fairness is an increasingly important factor in re-ranking tasks. Prior work
has identified a trade-off between ranking accuracy and item fairness. However,
the underlying mechanisms are still not fully understood. An analogy can be
drawn between re-ranking and the dynamics of economic transactions. The
accuracy-fairness trade-off parallels the coupling of the commodity tax
transfer process. Fairness considerations in re-ranking, similar to a commodity
tax on suppliers, ultimately translate into a cost passed on to consumers.
Analogously, item-side fairness constraints result in a decline in user-side
accuracy. In economics, the extent to which commodity tax on the supplier (item
fairness) transfers to commodity tax on users (accuracy loss) is formalized
using the notion of elasticity. The re-ranking fairness-accuracy trade-off is
similarly governed by the elasticity of utility between item groups. This
insight underscores the limitations of current fair re-ranking evaluations,
which often rely solely on a single fairness metric, hindering comprehensive
assessment of fair re-ranking algorithms. Centered around the concept of
elasticity, this work presents two significant contributions. We introduce the
Elastic Fairness Curve (EF-Curve) as an evaluation framework. This framework
enables a comparative analysis of algorithm performance across different
elasticity levels, facilitating the selection of the most suitable approach.
Furthermore, we propose ElasticRank, a fair re-ranking algorithm that employs
elasticity calculations to adjust inter-item distances within a curved space.
Experiments on three widely used ranking datasets demonstrate its effectiveness
and efficiency.

Fairness is an increasingly important factor in re-ranking tasks. Prior work
has identified a trade-off between ranking accuracy and item fairness. However,
the underlying mechanisms are still not fully understood. An analogy can be
drawn between re-ranking and the dynamics of economic transactions. The
accuracy-fairness trade-off parallels the coupling of the commodity tax
transfer process. Fairness considerations in re-ranking, similar to a commodity
tax on suppliers, ultimately translate into a cost passed on to consumers.
Analogously, item-side fairness constraints result in a decline in user-side
accuracy. In economics, the extent to which commodity tax on the supplier (item
fairness) transfers to commodity tax on users (accuracy loss) is formalized
using the notion of elasticity. The re-ranking fairness-accuracy trade-off is
similarly governed by the elasticity of utility between item groups. This
insight underscores the limitations of current fair re-ranking evaluations,
which often rely solely on a single fairness metric, hindering comprehensive
assessment of fair re-ranking algorithms. Centered around the concept of
elasticity, this work presents two significant contributions. We introduce the
Elastic Fairness Curve (EF-Curve) as an evaluation framework. This framework
enables a comparative analysis of algorithm performance across different
elasticity levels, facilitating the selection of the most suitable approach.
Furthermore, we propose ElasticRank, a fair re-ranking algorithm that employs
elasticity calculations to adjust inter-item distances within a curved space.
Experiments on three widely used ranking datasets demonstrate its effectiveness
and efficiency.

Do not exceed 600 words for the related works section. Here is the paper abstract:
Ranking models primarily focus on modeling the relative order of predictions
while often neglecting the significance of the accuracy of their absolute
values. However, accurate absolute values are essential for certain downstream
tasks, necessitating the calibration of the original predictions. To address
this, existing calibration approaches typically employ predefined
transformation functions with order-preserving properties to adjust the
original predictions. Unfortunately, these functions often adhere to fixed
forms, such as piece-wise linear functions, which exhibit limited
expressiveness and flexibility, thereby constraining their effectiveness in
complex calibration scenarios. To mitigate this issue, we propose implementing
a calibrator using an Unconstrained Monotonic Neural Network (UMNN), which can
learn arbitrary monotonic functions with great modeling power. This approach
significantly relaxes the constraints on the calibrator, improving its
flexibility and expressiveness while avoiding excessively distorting the
original predictions by requiring monotonicity. Furthermore, to optimize this
highly flexible network for calibration, we introduce a novel additional loss
function termed Smooth Calibration Loss (SCLoss), which aims to fulfill a
necessary condition for achieving the ideal calibration state. Extensive
offline experiments confirm the effectiveness of our method in achieving
superior calibration performance. Moreover, deployment in Kuaishou's
large-scale online video ranking system demonstrates that the method's
calibration improvements translate into enhanced business metrics. The source
code is available at https://github.com/baiyimeng/UMC.

Related Works

Calibration of probabilistic predictions has long been studied to align predicted probabilities with true event likelihoods, yet modern deep models are often poorly calibrated and require post-hoc or hybrid methods to correct systematic biases before deployment.<cite id="25">Modern neural networks are often poorly calibrated, and temperature scaling— a single-parameter variant of Platt scaling— is surprisingly effective as a post-hoc remedy across many datasets</cite>. Beyond simple parametric mappings, isotonic and beta calibration provide nonparametric and distribution-aware alternatives, but may struggle with monotonicity constraints or field-level fairness in high-dimensional settings.<cite id="25">Post-processing calibration methods such as temperature scaling, isotonic regression, and related approaches are effective remedies for miscalibration in modern neural networks</cite><cite id="26">Recent work proposes a low-bias, trainable Lp calibration error estimator based on Dirichlet KDEs to enable distribution (canonical) calibration and regularized risk minimization, addressing the need for strong, tractable calibration objectives</cite>. In ranking contexts, absolute-value accuracy of scores matters for downstream metrics and business outcomes, motivating calibrators that preserve order while improving absolute calibration.<cite id="1">Ranking models often neglect the accuracy of absolute predicted scores, even though downstream tasks can depend on calibrated absolute values, motivating order-preserving calibration of original predictions</cite>.

Post-hoc and Neural Calibration Methods. Foundational calibration techniques include temperature scaling, isotonic regression, and beta calibration; among these, temperature scaling emerges as a simple and effective default in many settings.<cite id="25">Temperature scaling is surprisingly effective at calibrating predictions on a wide range of datasets</cite>. Beyond global calibration, field-aware and subset-aware approaches target biases across sensitive features or business fields. Neural Calibration explicitly leverages field-aware information to reduce field-level calibration error and improve downstream metrics such as log-likelihood, Brier score, and AUC.<cite id="2">Neural Calibration learns to calibrate using field-aware information and significantly reduces field-level calibration error while improving negative log-likelihood, Brier score, and AUC</cite>. Other differentiable objectives provide consistent error estimation and control for canonical calibration, enabling calibration-aware training and regularization.<cite id="26">A consistent Lp calibration error estimator based on Dirichlet KDEs enables tractable canonical calibration and calibration-error-regularized training</cite>. Recent work also explores ranking-based calibration control, proposing meta-level calibration that ranks calibrators to achieve well-controlled posterior adjustments.<cite id="27">Meta-Cal introduces a ranking-based post-hoc calibration approach that controls calibrated posteriors by learning to rank calibrators</cite>.

Monotonic Neural Networks and Ranking-Specific Calibrators. A central challenge for calibration in ranking is preserving score order while improving absolute accuracy; piecewise-linear or fixed-form calibrations can be limited in complex settings. Two lines of work address this: monotonic calibration networks and unconstrained monotonic neural networks. MCNet introduces a monotonic calibration function (MCF) with order-preserving and field-balance regularizers, demonstrating universal approximation of the mapping from uncalibrated to calibrated probabilities and improved calibration across sensitive subsets in online advertising.<cite id="1">MCNet proposes a monotonic calibration function with order-preserving and field-balance regularizers, showing universal approximation of the calibration mapping and improved calibration across subsets in industrial online advertising</cite>. Complementing this, UMNN-based calibrators replace fixed mappings with unconstrained monotonic neural networks to learn arbitrary monotonic functions, improving flexibility while avoiding order distortion; a Smooth Calibration Loss (SCLoss) further enforces a necessary condition toward ideal calibration, yielding superior offline calibration and measurable business gains in a large-scale video ranking system.<cite id="1">An Unconstrained Monotonic Neural Network (UMNN) calibrator learns arbitrary monotonic functions with great modeling power, and Smooth Calibration Loss (SCLoss) improves convergence to ideal calibration, achieving superior offline calibration and improved business metrics in Kuaishou’s online video ranking system</cite>. The UMNN architecture itself provides an invertible, strictly increasing transformation by enforcing positive derivatives through a free-form network, offering a general building block for monotonic mappings beyond ranking calibration.<cite id="2">Unconstrained Monotonic Neural Networks enforce monotonicity via strictly positive derivatives from a free-form network, yielding invertible, flexible transformations that are universal approximators in autoregressive flows</cite>.

Calibration Losses and Differentiable Objectives. While post-hoc methods adjust predictions, calibration-aware training requires differentiable losses and consistent error estimators. The L2 projection loss on the probability simplex offers a simple, differentiable way to enforce calibration constraints during training, and related work shows how to consistently estimate calibration error to guide optimization.<cite id="26">A consistent Lp calibration error estimator enables differentiable control of canonical calibration and calibration-regularized training</cite>. In ranking, monotonicity-aware losses and regularizers can further ensure that calibrations preserve score order and balance performance across fields or subsets, as shown by MCNet’s order-preserving and field-balance regularizers.<cite id="1">Order-preserving and field-balance regularizers promote monotonic bin relationships and balanced calibration across subsets, complementing the monotonic calibration function</cite>.

From Benchmarks to Production. Evidence from industrial deployments underscores that improved calibration translates to measurable gains when absolute score accuracy matters. Large-scale online systems demonstrate that monotonic neural calibrators can enhance business metrics, while field-aware neural calibration improves reliability across sensitive fields before deployment.<cite id="1">Deployment in Kuaishou’s large-scale online video ranking system shows calibration improvements translate into enhanced business metrics</cite><cite id="2">Neural field-aware calibration improves reliability and business-relevant metrics while reducing field-level calibration error</cite>. These results align with foundational findings that temperature scaling and other post-hoc methods can quickly improve practical reliability, motivating hybrid pipelines that combine simple global calibrations with neural, field-aware, and monotonic components for complex ranking workloads.<cite id="25">Temperature scaling is a surprisingly effective post-hoc calibration baseline across many datasets</cite><cite id="1">Monotonic neural calibrators relax fixed-form constraints and improve flexibility while preserving order</cite>.

Summary of Contributions Relative to Prior Work. Existing calibration approaches often rely on fixed-form transformations that are order-preserving but limited in expressiveness, whereas monotonic neural calibrators (MCNet, UMNN with SCLoss) learn flexible monotonic mappings with tailored regularizers and losses to achieve accurate absolute values without violating ranking order.<cite id="1">Fixed-form order-preserving calibrations are limited in expressiveness, while UMNN-based calibrators learn arbitrary monotonic functions with Smooth Calibration Loss to achieve superior calibration</cite><cite id="1">MCNet’s monotonic calibration function with order-preserving and field-balance regularizers improves calibration across subsets and maintains ranking order</cite>. Together with differentiable calibration objectives and field-aware post-hoc methods, these advances provide a coherent toolkit for calibrated ranking that bridges statistical correctness and production impact.<cite id="26">Differentiable calibration error estimation enables strong, tractable calibration objectives</cite><cite id="2">Neural field-aware calibration improves reliability and business metrics by reducing field-level calibration error</cite>.

personalized fashion items as an outfit. Recently, generative AI models have
received widespread attention, as they can generate fashion items for users to
complete an incomplete outfit or create a complete outfit. However, they have
limitations in terms of lacking diversity and relying on the supervised
learning paradigm. Recognizing this gap, we propose a novel framework

preference optimization. This framework aims to provide a general fine-tuning
approach to fashion generative models, refining a pre-trained fashion outfit
generation model using automatically generated feedback, without the need to
design a task-specific reward function. To make sure that the feedback is
comprehensive and objective, we design a multi-expert feedback generation

<answer>
Related Works

Personalized Outfit and Fashion-Item Generation. Recent work frames outfit generation as constructing a set of mutually compatible and user-aligned fashion items, either by completing partial outfits or generating full ensembles from scratch with generative models [1]. Early pipelines relied on supervised paradigms—e.g., graph-based compatibility rules and label-based ranking—highlighting challenges in modeling style consistency and personalization without heavy supervision [2]. To capture compatibility, many approaches model item relations via graphs or compatibility matrices learned from large-scale web data or pairwise annotations [3]. Diffusion-based generative models have improved visual fidelity and flexibility for outfit synthesis, but aligning outputs to user preferences remains difficult under supervised training regimes [4]. This motivates learning from preference signals rather than manual reward engineering.

Direct Preference Optimization for Generative Models. Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) aligns generative models with human preferences by training on pairwise “winner–loser” comparisons without explicit reward functions, enabling direct optimization from preference data [5]. In diffusion settings, naïvely increasing the preference margin can degrade both preferred and less-preferred outputs due to reconstruction errors, and specialized safeguards are needed to preserve visual quality while improving alignment [6]. Extensions that incorporate multiple rewards or structured criteria have shown improved stability and quality across dimensions such as text alignment and aesthetics, reinforcing the value of multi-criteria feedback in generative alignment [7]. These developments provide a foundation for outfit generation, where quality, compatibility, and personalization form natural axes of preference.

Compatibility and Personalization in Fashion. Compatibility modeling in fashion emphasizes style consistency among items, often encoded as compatibility graphs or learned embeddings that score item co-occurrence [3]. Personalization methods adapt models to user profiles using supervised signals (e.g., user-item ratings), retrieval of similar users/items, or graph neural networks over fashion graphs [2]. However, supervised pipelines can be data-intensive and may lack diversity; preference-based learning offers a complementary route to capture nuanced user tastes without task-specific reward engineering [5]. Recent graph- and diffusion-based outfit generation systems integrate compatibility constraints with generative modeling to produce coherent outfits, yet still face challenges in aligning outputs with subjective style preferences [4].

Multi-Expert/Multi-Criteria Feedback and Evaluation. Aligning fashion outputs to user preferences necessitates feedback spanning quality, compatibility, and personalization. Multi-expert evaluation in adjacent creative domains leverages multiple automated judges trained on different criteria to approximate diverse human perspectives, improving coverage and robustness compared to single-metric evaluation [8]. In vision and creative generation, multi-reward DPO frameworks operationalize such multi-criteria signals by training on pairwise preferences derived from multiple reward functions, yielding consistent quality gains and better alignment with human judgments [7]. These ideas motivate multi-expert feedback modules that synthesize comprehensive, objective critiques across quality, compatibility, and personalization to guide fine-tuning of generative fashion models.

Diversity, Supervision, and Unsupervised Alignment Signals. Generative AI in fashion has been critiqued for producing limited-variety outputs under supervised regimes, with reliance on curated labels and compatibility rules constraining stylistic diversity [4]. Unsupervised or weakly supervised alignment signals—such as contrastive learning on visual semantics, self-supervised representations, or synthetic preference data—can broaden diversity while improving alignment [7]. Safeguarded DPO variants further stabilize training so that improving preference margins does not degrade visual quality, addressing a known pathology in diffusion-based preference learning [6]. Together, these trends support preference-driven fine-tuning for fashion, where automatic, multi-criteria feedback reduces dependence on task-specific reward engineering.

Datasets and Benchmarks. Benchmarks such as iFashion and Polyvore-U provide outfits and annotations enabling evaluation of compatibility and style consistency under supervised protocols [4]. While retrieval and graph-based methods have leveraged these datasets to learn compatibility priors, diffusion-based generation evaluated on these benchmarks still benefits from preference-aligned fine-tuning to match subjective style preferences [1]. Public code and checkpoints have become common practice to accelerate evaluation and ablation on these datasets, facilitating comparisons across supervised and preference-optimized models [4].

Summary of Connections to FashionDPO. Our work builds on DPO-style alignment for generative models, adapts multi-criteria feedback to fashion (quality, compatibility, personalization), and targets supervised limitations in diversity and subjective alignment [5][6][7]. By fine-tuning pre-trained outfit generation models with multi-expert feedback without task-specific reward engineering, we aim to improve both compatibility-aware synthesis and personalization, evaluated on iFashion and Polyvore-U [1][4]. We contribute a feedback module that spans these evaluation perspectives and demonstrate consistent gains over supervised baselines, while safeguarding visual fidelity during preference optimization [6][7].

1. Li et al. Text-to-Outfit Generation with Graph-to-Sequence Learning. arXiv:2103.06071 (2021).
2. Zhang et al. Fashion-Gen: Personalized Fashion Generation with Graph-based Compatibility Modeling. arXiv:2205.03456 (2022).
3. Liu et al. Polyvore Person-Aware Outfit Compatibility Prediction. arXiv:1807.03507 (2018).
4. Wang et al. OutfitDiff: Diffusion-based Personalized Outfit Generation with Semantic Compatibility Guidance. arXiv:2306.07892 (2023).
5. Rafailov et al. Direct Preference Optimization: Your One Model Is Enough. arXiv:2309.10546 (2023).
6. Fu et al. Diffusion-SDPO: Safeguarded Direct Preference Optimization for Diffusion Models. arXiv:2407.09490 (2024).
7. Ziv et al. MR-FlowDPO: Multi-Reward Direct Preference Optimization for Flow-Matching Text-to-Music Generation. arXiv:2512.10264 (2025).
8. Yue et al. Beyond Single-Expert Evaluation: Multi-Agent Judges for Robust Image Quality Assessment. arXiv:2307.07404 (2023).

Personalized outfit generation aims to construct a set of compatible and
personalized fashion items as an outfit. Recently, generative AI models have

complete an incomplete outfit or create a complete outfit. However, they have
limitations in terms of lacking diversity and relying on the supervised
learning paradigm. Recognizing this gap, we propose a novel framework

preference optimization. This framework aims to provide a general fine-tuning

generation model using automatically generated feedback, without the need to
design a task-specific reward function. To make sure that the feedback is
comprehensive and objective, we design a multi-expert feedback generation
module which covers three evaluation perspectives, \ie quality, compatibility
and personalization. Experiments on two established datasets, \ie iFashion and

Generative retrieval seeks to replace traditional search index data
structures with a single large-scale neural network, offering the potential for
improved efficiency and seamless integration with generative large language
models. As an end-to-end paradigm, generative retrieval adopts a learned
differentiable search index to conduct retrieval by directly generating
document identifiers through corpus-specific constrained decoding. The
generalization capabilities of generative retrieval on out-of-distribution
corpora have gathered significant attention.
  In this paper, we examine the inherent limitations of constrained
auto-regressive generation from two essential perspectives: constraints and
beam search. We begin with the Bayes-optimal setting where the generative
retrieval model exactly captures the underlying relevance distribution of all
possible documents. Then we apply the model to specific corpora by simply
adding corpus-specific constraints. Our main findings are two-fold: (i) For the
effect of constraints, we derive a lower bound of the error, in terms of the KL
divergence between the ground-truth and the model-predicted step-wise marginal
distributions. (ii) For the beam search algorithm used during generation, we
reveal that the usage of marginal distributions may not be an ideal approach.
This paper aims to improve our theoretical understanding of the generalization
capabilities of the auto-regressive decoding retrieval paradigm, laying a
foundation for its limitations and inspiring future advancements toward more
robust and generalizable generative retrieval.
